Global Warming and Climate Change

The summer of 2024 was the hottest ever recorded on Earth, and it was the first calendar year in which the global average temperature was more than 1.5 °C above pre-industrial levels. In India, temperatures crossed 50 °C in parts of Rajasthan and Delhi, and heat waves killed hundreds of people. Glaciers in the Himalaya are retreating, sea levels are rising, and floods, droughts and cyclones are becoming more frequent and intense. Global warming is no longer a forecast; it is the reality of our times.

What is happening and why

Global warming is the long-term rise in the Earth's average surface temperature, caused mainly by human activities that release greenhouse gases — carbon dioxide from burning coal, oil and gas, methane from agriculture, landfills and fossil fuel extraction, and nitrous oxide from fertilisers. These gases trap heat in the atmosphere like a blanket. Deforestation adds to the problem by removing the trees that absorb carbon dioxide. The concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere is now higher than at any time in at least two million years.

Climate change is the broader set of changes that follow: shifts in rainfall, more extreme weather, melting ice, rising and warming oceans, and changes in ecosystems. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) has concluded that it is "unequivocal" that human influence has warmed the planet.

The impacts

  • Heat waves: more frequent and deadly, reducing labour productivity and harming health.
  • Water: erratic monsoons, melting glaciers and falling groundwater threaten water security for hundreds of millions.
  • Agriculture: heat and erratic rain reduce yields of wheat and rice; farmers face greater risk and debt.
  • Disasters: heavier rainfall causes floods and landslides; warmer seas fuel stronger cyclones.
  • Coasts: rising seas erode coastlines and push salt water into farmland in the Sundarbans and elsewhere.
  • Health: spread of vector-borne diseases like dengue and malaria; heat stress.
  • Biodiversity: coral reefs bleach; species are pushed to extinction.
  • Inequality: the poor, who contribute least to emissions, suffer most; climate change may push millions into poverty and migration.

The response

The world responded through the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (1992), the Kyoto Protocol and the Paris Agreement (2015), under which countries aim to limit warming to well below 2 °C and pursue 1.5 °C. But current pledges still put the world on course for well over 2 °C of warming.

Mitigation — cutting emissions — requires a shift to renewable energy, energy efficiency, electric transport, sustainable agriculture and protection of forests. Adaptation — coping with unavoidable changes — requires drought-resistant crops, early warning systems, heat action plans, resilient infrastructure and water conservation.

India's role

India is the world's third-largest emitter in total, but its per-capita emissions are less than half the global average. It has pledged net zero by 2070, and in 2025 non-fossil sources crossed half of its installed power capacity. It leads the International Solar Alliance, runs a National Green Hydrogen Mission, and promotes Mission LiFE — a movement for sustainable lifestyles. India also insists on climate justice: developed countries, responsible for most past emissions, must lead in cutting emissions and provide finance and technology to developing countries.

What each of us can do

Individuals matter too: saving electricity, using public transport, reducing waste, eating sustainably, planting trees and supporting climate-friendly policies. Collective action begins with personal responsibility.

Conclusion

Climate change is the defining challenge of our century. It tests our science, our economies and above all our sense of responsibility towards the poor and towards future generations. As the saying goes, we do not inherit the Earth from our ancestors; we borrow it from our children. The technologies to solve the crisis exist and are becoming cheaper every year. What we need now is urgency, cooperation and justice — before the window to act closes.

What Lies Ahead for the Indian Economy?

India is today one of the world's fastest-growing large economies and among its five largest. It has a young population, a vibrant digital public infrastructure, a large domestic market and ambitious goals — to become a developed nation, "Viksit Bharat", by 2047. Yet it also faces deep challenges: creating jobs for millions of young people, raising incomes of farmers and informal workers, and growing sustainably in a world of climate change and geopolitical uncertainty. What lies ahead depends on how these opportunities and challenges are handled.

Strengths that point to a bright future

First, demography. About two-thirds of Indians are of working age, and this demographic window will remain open for about two more decades.

Second, digital public infrastructure. Aadhaar, UPI, DigiLocker and the Account Aggregator framework have made payments, identity and data-sharing cheap and universal. UPI now handles billions of transactions every month, bringing millions into the formal economy.

Third, infrastructure investment. Public capital spending on highways, railways, ports, airports, power and urban transport has risen sharply, lowering logistics costs and attracting private investment.

Fourth, services strength. India is a global leader in IT services and global capability centres, and its services exports continue to grow.

Fifth, manufacturing push. Production Linked Incentive schemes have made India the second-largest mobile phone manufacturer, and companies seeking to diversify away from China are investing in electronics, pharmaceuticals and renewable equipment.

Sixth, macroeconomic stability. Banks have cleaned up their balance sheets, inflation is under control, and foreign exchange reserves are large.

Challenges ahead

  • Jobs: growth has not created enough good-quality jobs; many young people are underemployed, and women's participation in work is low.
  • Agriculture: nearly half the workforce depends on farming, which produces only about a sixth of output.
  • Human capital: learning levels, health and skills need major improvement.
  • Inequality: gains are concentrated among a few, and rural consumption lags.
  • Private investment has been slow to pick up.
  • Climate risks: heat waves, floods and droughts threaten agriculture, health and infrastructure.
  • Global uncertainty: trade wars, tariffs, wars and supply-chain disruptions.
  • Fiscal pressures: high public debt limits room for spending.

What should be done

  • Labour-intensive manufacturing — textiles, footwear, food processing, electronics assembly — to absorb workers moving out of agriculture.
  • Education and skilling reform focused on foundational learning and job-ready skills.
  • Agricultural reform: productivity, diversification, markets and climate resilience.
  • Ease of doing business: simpler regulations, faster courts, land and labour reforms at State level.
  • Women's participation: safety, childcare and flexible work.
  • Green growth: renewable energy, electric mobility and green hydrogen can become new engines of growth and jobs.
  • Trade integration: trade agreements to join global value chains.

Conclusion

The Indian economy stands at a turning point. If India uses its demographic dividend, digital strength and infrastructure push to build human capital and create jobs, it can become a developed nation within a generation. If it fails, growth may remain uneven and fragile. The future is not predetermined; it will be shaped by the choices of policymakers, businesses and citizens. With wise reforms and inclusive growth, what lies ahead can be India's most prosperous era.

Quality Education as an Indicator of Social Development

A society's progress cannot be measured by its wealth alone. The truer test is how well it develops the abilities of its people — and nothing does this more than education. But it is not enough for children merely to attend school; they must learn. Quality education, more than enrolment figures, is the clearest indicator of social development.

Why education reflects development

Education is both an end and a means. It is an end because the ability to read, reason and understand the world is valuable in itself — part of what Amartya Sen calls human capabilities. It is a means because it improves almost every other aspect of social life. The Human Development Index includes education along with health and income for this reason.

  • Health: educated mothers have healthier children; infant mortality and malnutrition fall as female education rises.
  • Income and mobility: education opens better jobs and allows children of poor families to rise.
  • Gender equality: educated women marry later, have fewer children, earn more and participate more in public life.
  • Democracy: educated citizens are better informed, more tolerant and more likely to participate.
  • Social cohesion: schools bring together children of different castes, religions and classes.
  • Innovation and growth: a skilled workforce drives productivity and research.

Kerala's experience shows this: its early investment in schooling, especially for girls, helped it achieve health and social indicators comparable to developed countries despite modest income.

Quantity is not quality

India has achieved nearly universal enrolment in primary school. But surveys such as ASER have repeatedly shown that many children in Class V cannot read a Class II text or do simple division. The National Achievement Survey reveals similar gaps. Children who cannot read by the age of ten struggle for the rest of their education. Learning gaps are widest for poor, rural, tribal and Dalit children, and for girls in some regions — so poor-quality schooling deepens inequality instead of reducing it.

What quality education means

Quality education involves:

  • Foundational literacy and numeracy for every child.
  • Competent, motivated teachers with good training and support.
  • Child-centred, activity-based learning rather than rote memorisation.
  • Learning in the mother tongue in the early years.
  • Safe, inclusive schools with toilets, libraries, laboratories and nutrition.
  • Critical thinking, creativity and values — not just marks.
  • Relevance to life and work, including vocational skills.

India's efforts

The Right to Education Act (2009) made schooling a right. The National Education Policy 2020 shifts the focus from enrolment to learning, with the NIPUN Bharat Mission aiming for foundational literacy and numeracy for all children by Class 3. Programmes for teacher training, digital content (DIKSHA) and assessment reform (PARAKH) support this goal. Yet implementation, teacher shortages and low public spending remain challenges.

Conclusion

The United Nations' Sustainable Development Goal 4 calls for inclusive and equitable quality education for all. It rightly recognises that education is the foundation of all other development goals. A society that ensures every child learns well — whatever their caste, gender or class — is building a future of health, prosperity, equality and democracy. That is why the quality of a nation's classrooms is perhaps the best mirror of its social development.

OpportunitiesDigital addictionMisinformationDigital citizenship

The Influence of the Internet on Youth

For India's young people, the internet is not a tool they pick up occasionally — it is the world they live in. With cheap data and over 90 crore internet users, a teenager in a small town can watch lectures from world-class teachers, start an online business, follow global news and chat with friends across continents. Yet the same internet can also distract, deceive, isolate and harm. Its influence on youth is profound — and double-edged.

The positive influence

First, education and knowledge. Free online courses (SWAYAM, YouTube lessons, open textbooks) democratise learning. During the pandemic, the internet kept education going for those with access.

Second, careers and enterprise. Young people find jobs online, freelance for global clients, and build start-ups and creative careers as content creators, designers and coders. India's start-up ecosystem is driven by digitally fluent youth.

Third, voice and participation. Social media allows young people to express opinions, mobilise for causes, and hold authorities accountable.

Fourth, connection and support. The internet connects young people with friends, mentors and communities who share their interests, and can help those who feel isolated find support.

Fifth, access to services: digital payments, health information, government services and skill programmes.

The negative influence

First, addiction and distraction. Endless scrolling, gaming and short videos can consume hours, affecting sleep, studies, physical activity and concentration.

Second, mental health. Comparison with idealised lives on social media, cyberbullying and online harassment have been linked to anxiety, depression and low self-esteem among adolescents.

Third, misinformation and radicalisation. Fake news, conspiracy theories and hate speech spread rapidly; algorithms can trap young users in echo chambers.

Fourth, online risks: cyber fraud, sextortion, online gambling and exposure to harmful content. Many young people fall victim to scams.

Fifth, privacy. Young people often share personal data without understanding the consequences.

Sixth, the digital divide. Youth without access — often rural, poor or female — fall further behind.

Finding the balance

The answer is not to keep young people off the internet but to help them use it wisely:

  • Digital literacy in schools: evaluating information, protecting privacy, recognising scams and respecting others online.
  • Parental guidance and open conversations rather than only restrictions.
  • Platform responsibility: safety by design, age-appropriate content, quick removal of harmful material; India's data protection law requires verifiable parental consent for processing children's data.
  • Healthy habits: screen-time limits, digital detox, sport and offline friendships.
  • Mental-health support through school counsellors and helplines such as Tele-MANAS.
  • Bridging the divide through affordable devices and connectivity for rural youth and girls.

Conclusion

The internet is like fire: it can cook our food or burn down our house. For India's youth, it can be a ladder to knowledge, opportunity and global citizenship — or a trap of distraction and deception. The difference lies in how they are prepared to use it. If we educate young people to be responsible, critical and creative digital citizens, the internet will become one of the greatest forces for empowering the next generation.

XYZ XYZ Locality

16 November 2019

The Editor XYZ (an English newspaper) City

Subject: Lack of basic amenities for garbage disposal in our locality

Sir/Madam,

Through the columns of your esteemed newspaper, I wish to draw the attention of the municipal authorities to the lack of basic facilities for the disposal of garbage in our locality.

There are no community bins or door-to-door collection in most streets of our area. As a result, residents throw garbage on vacant plots and roadsides. Heaps of rotting waste lie uncleared for days, attracting stray dogs, cattle, flies and mosquitoes. The stench is unbearable, and the waste often blocks drains, causing water to stagnate. Some people burn the garbage, filling the air with smoke. Cases of dengue, malaria and stomach infections have risen in recent months, and children and the elderly are the worst affected.

Residents have complained to the municipal office several times, but no action has been taken.

I request the authorities to: 1. start daily door-to-door collection of garbage; 2. place covered bins for wet and dry waste at suitable points; 3. clear the existing dumps and clean the drains immediately; 4. set up a composting unit for wet waste; 5. take action against open burning and littering, and run awareness campaigns on segregation.

I hope this letter will move the authorities to act before the situation leads to an outbreak of disease.

Yours faithfully, XYZ

Programme on "Renewable Energy Sources are the Need of the Hour"

By XYZ

The Environment Club of XYZ Institute organised a day-long programme on the theme "Renewable Energy Sources are the Need of the Hour" on its campus last Saturday. Over 300 students, faculty members and local residents took part.

The programme began with a keynote address by a scientist from a renewable energy research centre, who explained that coal, oil and gas are limited resources and the main cause of air pollution and climate change. He spoke about India's rapid growth in solar and wind power and its target of net zero emissions by 2070.

A panel discussion followed with an engineer, an entrepreneur running a solar business and a farmer who uses a solar irrigation pump. They discussed the benefits of rooftop solar, solar pumps, biogas plants and electric vehicles, as well as challenges such as cost, storage and grid integration.

Students presented working models of a solar cooker, a small wind turbine, a biogas plant and a solar-powered street light. A poster and slogan competition on clean energy drew enthusiastic participation, and the winners received prizes.

The institute announced that it would install rooftop solar panels on its buildings and switch to LED lighting. Students took a pledge to save electricity and spread awareness about renewable energy in their neighbourhoods.

The programme ended with a vote of thanks by the club's coordinator, who said that the shift to clean energy is essential for a healthy and sustainable future.

The habit of reading must be cultivated; it gives pleasure along with knowledge, vocabulary and new styles of expression. Not everyone enjoys it, as it demands intelligence, interest, language skills and the ability to concentrate in solitude.

Childhood is the best time to form this habit, but reading today is limited to notes, guides and guess papers meant only for passing examinations, and is being replaced by television, the internet and mobile phones, which cannot enrich knowledge as books do. Books make the mind richer, while phones make it shallow; reading is food for the mind.

Reading may be light or serious. Newspapers and journals keep us informed about a globalised world where distant events affect us. Books on travel and adventure inspire courage and take us beyond dull routine. Religious and philosophical works enlighten the soul and teach morals, while literature and history reveal our culture, past and society, enrich our knowledge and broaden our outlook.

free.ifm-2019-ge-4a:
The passage discusses two kinds of educational research:

  • Research from within the field of education, which asks questions informed by educational thought, epistemic issues, the aims and practices of education, and the perspectives of students, teachers and communities.
  • Research from other disciplines — economics, political science, sociology and so on — which takes the aims and practices of education for granted and studies education through the lenses of those disciplines and of social policy.
free.ifm-2019-ge-4b: Epistemic issues concern knowledge — what knowledge is, how it is acquired, justified and understood. In education, they include questions such as what children should learn, how they come to know and understand things, and how knowledge should be organised and taught. Research informed by epistemic issues examines the nature of learning and knowledge itself, not merely outcomes such as enrolment or costs.
free.ifm-2019-ge-4c: The author says so because much research on education in India is done from the perspective of other disciplines, not from within education. Since education is not its primary perspective, it tends to focus on issues such as enrolment, expenditure or economic returns, which are peripheral to the reality of education — what actually happens between teachers and students in classrooms. Yet such research gets disproportionate attention from policymakers and the public.
free.ifm-2019-ge-4d: Teachers often handle about thirty children of ages six to ten across Classes I to V together, many of whose parents never went to school, who speak a language different from the medium of instruction, who depend on the mid-day meal and have household chores. The passage suggests there is no single right method; teachers must use multiple, flexible approaches suited to their context — handling several languages, giving extra support to the most deprived children, and continually reflecting on their experience to develop operating principles that can be adapted to changing situations.
free.ifm-2019-ge-4e: In my opinion, the author says this because education is a social and human process that varies enormously with children's backgrounds, languages, poverty, the community and the teacher, and these factors keep changing over time. What works in one classroom may fail in another. Hence no fixed formula can apply everywhere; teachers need flexible, context-sensitive approaches and principles developed through experience and rigorous reflection, which themselves must be constantly questioned.

Monsoon windsMuziris and ArikameduUttarapatha and DakshinapathaPepper and gold

In the post-Mauryan period (c. 200 BCE–300 CE), trade between India and the Roman Empire flourished, especially after the discovery of the monsoon winds (attributed to the Greek sailor Hippalus, 1st century BCE), which allowed ships to cross the Arabian Sea directly. Our sources include the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, Pliny's Natural History, Ptolemy's Geography, Sangam literature (which mentions the Yavanas) and archaeological finds of Roman coins and pottery.

1. Main ports

Arikamedu has yielded Roman amphorae, Arretine pottery and glass, showing a Roman trading station.

2. Internal trade routes

  • Uttarapatha: from Taxila through Mathura and Kaushambi to Pataliputra and Tamralipti — linked to the Silk Route through the Kushana empire.
  • Dakshinapatha: from Ujjain to Pratishthana (Paithan) and Tagara (Ter), bringing goods to Barygaza.
  • Routes across the Deccan to the east and west coasts under the Satavahanas; river routes on the Ganga.
  • Guilds (shrenis) organised production and trade; merchants donated to Buddhist caves along these routes (Karle, Nashik).

3. Commodities

4. Significance

  • Balance of trade favoured India: Pliny complained that India drained Rome of about 50 million sesterces a year.
  • Hoards of Roman coins in south India (Coimbatore, Madurai) and the use of gold coins by the Kushanas show the inflow of gold.
  • Prosperity of urban centres, guilds and Buddhist monasteries; spread of Indian culture abroad.
  • The trade declined in the 3rd century CE with the crisis of the Roman Empire.

Alvars and NayanarsShankaraMadhvaSaguna and nirguna

1. Rise of the Bhakti Movement

  • It began in south India (6th–9th centuries) with the Tamil Alvars (devotees of Vishnu) and Nayanars (devotees of Shiva), who sang in Tamil, opposed ritualism and welcomed all castes and women (Andal, Karaikkal Ammaiyar).
  • It was given a philosophical base by acharyas: Shankaracharya (Advaita, 8th century), Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita, 11th–12th), Madhvacharya (Dvaita, 13th), Nimbarka and Vallabha.
  • It spread north from the 14th century: Ramananda, Kabir, Ravidas, Guru Nanak (nirguna), and Tulsidas, Surdas, Mirabai, Chaitanya (saguna); in Maharashtra Jnaneshwar, Namdev and Tukaram; in Karnataka the Virashaivas (Basavanna).

2. Nature of the movement

  • Devotion (bhakti) to a personal god as the path to salvation, more than rituals or knowledge.
  • Equality: rejection of caste and gender barriers; many saints came from lower castes.
  • Vernacular languages: Tamil, Kannada, Marathi, Hindi, Bengali, Punjabi — creating rich literature.
  • Criticism of ritualism, idol worship (nirguna saints) and priestly control.
  • Synthesis with Sufism, promoting Hindu–Muslim harmony.

3. Advaita and Dvaita

  • Advaita gave a philosophical basis to nirguna bhakti — devotion to a formless God, as in Kabir.
  • Dvaita and Vishishtadvaita gave strong support to saguna bhakti — loving devotion to a personal God like Krishna or Rama; Madhva's ideas influenced the Haridasa movement in Karnataka and the Chaitanya tradition in Bengal.

The Bhakti movement thus combined deep philosophy with popular devotion and social reform, shaping Indian religion and culture for centuries.

AmuktamalyadaNayankara systemRevenue and irrigationAshtadiggajas

Krishnadevaraya (1509–1529) of the Tuluva dynasty was the greatest ruler of the Vijayanagara Empire. Accounts of Portuguese travellers Domingo Paes and Fernao Nuniz and his own Telugu work Amuktamalyada describe his administration.

Administrative policies

  • Ideal of kingship: in Amuktamalyada he advised kings to protect subjects, develop trade and irrigation, and rule justly.
  • Nayankara system: military chiefs (nayakas) received land (amaram) and had to maintain troops and pay tribute to the king.
  • Provinces and villages: the empire was divided into rajyas, nadus and villages; villages were run by the ayagar system of twelve functionaries.
  • Revenue: land revenue based on land quality, with taxes on trade, property and professions.
  • Irrigation and agriculture: large tanks and canals (such as at Nagalapura); encouragement to clear forests for cultivation.
  • Trade: good relations with the Portuguese for the import of horses; ports on the west coast.
  • Military: a large army with cavalry and artillery; victory over Bijapur at Raichur (1520).
  • Justice and tolerance: fair justice; though a Vaishnava, he respected all faiths.
  • Patron of culture: the Ashtadiggajas (eight poets, including Allasani Peddana); temples such as the Vitthala and Hazara Rama.

His policies combined strong military control with prosperity and cultural growth, making his reign the high point of Vijayanagara.

Moral codeToleranceNon-violenceWelfare

Ashoka's Dhamma was a set of ethical principles he adopted after the Kalinga war (c. 261 BCE) and spread through his rock and pillar edicts. It was a code of conduct for all, not a sectarian religion.

Main tenets

  • Respect for elders, parents and teachers; kindness to servants and slaves.
  • Non-violence (ahimsa): restrictions on killing animals, a ban on sacrifices (Rock Edict I).
  • Religious tolerance: respect for all sects; restraint in speech about others' faiths (Rock Edict XII).
  • Generosity to Brahmanas, Shramanas, the poor and the aged.
  • Self-control and purity of thought; avoiding anger, cruelty, jealousy and pride.
  • Welfare of all beings: medical treatment for humans and animals, wells and trees along roads (Rock Edict II).
  • Conquest by Dhamma rather than by war (Rock Edict XIII).

Means of spreading it

  • Dhamma mahamattas, Dhamma yatras, edicts in local languages, and missions to Sri Lanka and western Asia.

Ashoka's Dhamma aimed at social harmony and moral governance in a vast, diverse empire, and remains a symbol of ethical rule.

Recession and slowdownCorporate tax cutBank mergersMonetary easing

1. What is a recession?

A recession is a significant and widespread decline in economic activity. A common rule is two consecutive quarters of falling real GDP. A slowdown is a fall in the rate of growth while GDP still grows.

In 2019, India was in a slowdown, not a technical recession: GDP growth fell from over 8% in 2017-18 to about 4.5% in July–September 2019, the lowest in six years. Causes included weak consumer demand, stress in non-banking financial companies (the IL&FS crisis), bad loans, falling rural incomes and weak private investment.

2. Steps taken by the Government (2019)

  • Corporate tax cut (September 2019): from 30% to 22% for existing companies and 15% for new manufacturing firms.
  • Bank mergers: ten public sector banks merged into four; ₹70,000 crore recapitalisation.
  • Real estate: a ₹25,000 crore fund (SWAMIH) for stalled housing projects.
  • Automobile sector: relaxations in vehicle purchase by government departments, higher depreciation.
  • Exports: a new export incentive scheme (RoDTEP) and easier credit.
  • Withdrawal of the surcharge on foreign portfolio investors.
  • National Infrastructure Pipeline of over ₹100 lakh crore (December 2019).
  • PM-KISAN income support to farmers; GST rate cuts on some goods.

3. Monetary steps by the RBI

  • Repo rate cuts of 135 basis points in 2019 (from 6.5% to 5.15%).
  • Linking of loan rates to external benchmarks for faster transmission.
  • Liquidity support for NBFCs.

4. Assessment

These measures improved supply-side conditions, but demand remained weak, and the economy was then hit by COVID-19 in 2020, causing a real contraction. Recovery came later through monetary easing, higher public capital spending and reforms.

Pollution lawsNGTNCAPImplementation gaps

1. Major environmental laws and policies

2. Are they sufficient? Not fully.

Strengths

  • A comprehensive legal framework; strong judicial support (M.C. Mehta cases, Vellore Citizens' Welfare Forum, 1996).
  • Some successes: forest and tree cover has increased; tiger numbers have doubled; LPG for cooking (Ujjwala) and BS-VI fuel cut emissions.

Weaknesses

  • Weak enforcement: State Pollution Control Boards lack staff, funds and independence.
  • Air quality remains among the worst in the world; NCAP targets are only partly met.
  • Rivers remain polluted because sewage treatment capacity lags.
  • Dilution of EIA and post-facto approvals; projects in fragile areas (Himalaya, Western Ghats).
  • Fragmented approach across ministries and States; dependence on courts.
  • Low public participation and awareness.
  • Growth pressures often override environmental concerns.

3. What is needed

  • An independent environmental regulator; stronger, well-funded pollution boards.
  • Polluter-pays enforcement and real-time monitoring.
  • Ecosystem-based planning (airsheds, river basins) instead of city-by-city action.
  • Green technology, circular economy and citizen involvement.

Policies are necessary but not sufficient; effective implementation and accountability decide results.

90-day overdue4R strategyIBCRecapitalisation

Non-Performing Assets (NPAs) are loans on which interest or principal has remained overdue for more than 90 days. They stop earning income for banks, reduce profits and capital, and limit fresh lending. Gross NPAs of public sector banks (PSBs) peaked at about 14.6% in March 2018 after the Asset Quality Review (2015) forced banks to recognise hidden bad loans.

Steps taken by the Government and RBI

  • 4R strategy: Recognition, Resolution, Recapitalisation and Reforms.
  • Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (2016): time-bound resolution of stressed companies.
  • Recapitalisation of PSBs with over ₹3 lakh crore (2016–2021).
  • Mergers: 27 PSBs consolidated into 12.
  • Prompt Corrective Action framework for weak banks.
  • SARFAESI Act amendments and Debt Recovery Tribunals strengthened.
  • CRILC database of large borrowers; rules on wilful defaulters; the Fugitive Economic Offenders Act, 2018.
  • EASE reforms for better governance and risk management in PSBs.
  • National Asset Reconstruction Company (2021) to take over large bad loans.

Result: gross NPAs of PSBs fell to below 3% by 2025, and PSBs returned to record profits. Preventing new NPAs needs better credit appraisal and governance.
free.ifm-2019-gk-2d:
CBDR-RCNationally determinedClimate financeEquity

The Paris Agreement (2015) aims to keep warming well below 2 °C and pursue 1.5 °C, with every country submitting Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs).

Why some say it is loaded against developing countries

  • Weakened differentiation: unlike the Kyoto Protocol, which bound only developed countries, all countries must take action; the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities (CBDR) was qualified by "in light of different national circumstances".
  • Finance is not legally binding: the promise of $100 billion a year was missed until 2022, and the new goal of $300 billion a year by 2035 (COP29) is far below needs.
  • Historical responsibility: developed countries used most of the carbon budget, leaving little room for developing countries to grow.
  • Transparency and reporting burdens on countries with limited capacity.
  • Withdrawal by the United States (announced twice) weakens trust.

Why it is not wholly unfair

  • NDCs are self-chosen, so India sets targets according to its capacity.
  • CBDR and equity are recognised; developed countries "shall" provide finance (Article 9) and must take the lead.
  • Flexibility in transparency for developing countries; loss and damage is recognised (Article 8).
  • India has gained through renewable energy growth, the International Solar Alliance, and carbon markets (Article 6).

Conclusion: the Agreement is not fully balanced — finance and technology transfer remain weak — but its bottom-up design protects India's development space. India's task is to press for climate justice while pursuing its own clean-energy goals.
free.ifm-2019-gk-3a:
Article 371Sixth ScheduleInternal minoritiesInter-state migrants

India's federalism is asymmetric: some regions enjoy special autonomy to protect the identity of territorially concentrated ethnic groups.

1. Forms of asymmetric federalism

  • Article 370 (special status of Jammu and Kashmir, abrogated in 2019 and upheld by the Supreme Court in December 2023).
  • Articles 371 and 371A–J: special provisions for Nagaland (customary law and land), Mizoram, Manipur, Sikkim, Assam, Arunachal Pradesh and others.
  • Sixth Schedule: autonomous district councils in Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram.
  • Fifth Schedule and PESA (1996) for Scheduled Areas.
  • Inner Line Permits in Arunachal Pradesh, Nagaland, Mizoram and Manipur.

2. How it has helped

  • Protected tribal identity, land and customs — preventing land alienation and cultural loss.
  • Reduced insurgency by giving self-rule (Mizo Accord, 1986; Bodoland agreements).
  • Accommodated diversity within national unity.

3. Limits for minorities within sub-units

  • "Internal minorities" — smaller tribes or non-dominant groups within autonomous areas — can face exclusion: for example tensions between the Bodos and other communities, the displacement of Brus from Mizoram (resettled in Tripura after a 2020 agreement), the long denial of citizenship to Chakmas and Hajongs in Arunachal Pradesh, and the ethnic violence in Manipur (2023) between Meiteis and Kukis.
  • Dominant ethnic groups may control councils and jobs.
  • Women's rights under customary law (property, representation in Nagaland's local bodies) are sometimes limited.

4. Rights of inter-state migrants

  • ILP regimes, domicile rules and land restrictions limit migrants' rights to settle, own land or get jobs.
  • "Sons of the soil" demands and job quotas for locals (Haryana's 75% private-job reservation law was struck down by the High Court in 2023).
  • Migrants face hostility, as in Assam's anti-foreigner movement and the NRC (2019).
  • Article 19(1)(d)–(e) guarantees freedom of movement and residence, but reasonable restrictions protect Scheduled Tribes.

5. Assessment

Asymmetric federalism has protected group rights and maintained unity, but it has been less successful in protecting internal minorities and migrants. Balancing group autonomy with individual rights requires inclusive councils, safeguards for smaller groups, judicial oversight and protection of the fundamental rights of all citizens.
free.ifm-2019-gk-3b:
Negative and positive rightsReservationsWelfare rightsImplementation gaps

Civil-political rights — freedom of speech, religion, life and liberty — are often called negative rights: the State must not interfere. Social and economic rights — to education, health, food and work — are positive rights: the State must act through laws, spending and institutions.

(In practice, even civil rights need State action — courts, police and elections cost money — so the distinction is not absolute.)

1. India's approach

  • The Constitution puts social rights mainly in the Directive Principles, but courts have read many into Article 21.
  • Affirmative action: reservations in education, jobs and legislatures for SCs, STs and OBCs (and EWS since 2019); abolition of untouchability; land reforms.
  • Rights-based laws: MGNREGA (2005), Right to Education (2009), National Food Security Act (2013), Forest Rights Act (2006).
  • Welfare schemes: Ayushman Bharat, PM Awas Yojana, free food grains, scholarships.

2. Successes

  • Representation: SCs and STs in legislatures, services and education; a growing middle class among them.
  • Poverty reduction: NITI Aayog estimates that about 24.8 crore people escaped multidimensional poverty between 2013-14 and 2022-23.
  • Universal school enrolment, better nutrition and health indicators.
  • Rural employment and food security, especially during COVID-19.

3. Limitations

  • Implementation gaps: leakages, poor quality of schools and hospitals, delayed MGNREGA wages.
  • Benefits captured by the better-off within reserved groups; debates over the creamy layer and sub-classification (allowed for SCs and STs by the Supreme Court in 2024).
  • Private sector — where most jobs are — is outside reservations.
  • Fiscal limits and dependence on political will.
  • Social discrimination persists despite legal equality.
  • Judicial limits: the 50% cap on reservations (Indra Sawhney, 1992), though the EWS quota was upheld (2022).

Conclusion: affirmative State action has expanded social and economic justice considerably, but much remains to be done to make these rights real for the most deprived — through better delivery, quality services and greater accountability.
free.ifm-2019-gk-3c:
Article 123Legislative power of the executiveRe-promulgationJudicial review

Nature of the ordinance-making power

  • Under Article 123, the President can issue an ordinance when either House of Parliament is not in session and circumstances require immediate action.
  • It has the same force as an Act of Parliament but is temporary: it must be laid before Parliament and ceases six weeks after Parliament reassembles, unless approved earlier; Parliament can disapprove it.
  • The President acts on the advice of the Council of Ministers; it is really the Government's power.
  • Ordinances can be made only on subjects on which Parliament can legislate and are subject to the same constitutional limits.
  • Governors have a similar power (Article 213).

Concerns about misuse

  • Bypassing Parliament for laws that need debate.
  • Re-promulgation of the same ordinance repeatedly (as in Bihar between 1967 and 1981).

Safeguards

  • Judicial review: R.C. Cooper (1970) — the President's satisfaction can be challenged on grounds of mala fide; D.C. Wadhwa (1987) — repeated re-promulgation is unconstitutional; Krishna Kumar Singh (2017) — re-promulgation is a "fraud on the Constitution", and ordinances are subject to judicial review.
  • Parliamentary control: disapproval resolutions and the six-week limit.
  • The President can return the advice once for reconsideration.
  • Conventions: using ordinances only in genuine urgency and explaining reasons.

Ordinances are a useful emergency tool, but their frequent use weakens parliamentary democracy.
free.ifm-2019-gk-3d:
73rd AmendmentGram SabhaThree-tier systemDevolution

Panchayats in their institutional framework

  • The 73rd Amendment (1992) added Part IX (Articles 243–243O) and the Eleventh Schedule (29 subjects).
  • Three tiers: village, intermediate (block) and district panchayats (States with less than 20 lakh population may skip the middle tier).
  • Gram Sabha of all village voters.
  • Five-year term, elections by the State Election Commission, State Finance Commissions for funds.
  • Reservations for SCs, STs and at least one-third for women (half in many States).
  • PESA (1996) extends special powers to Gram Sabhas in Scheduled Areas.
  • Supported by the Ministry of Panchayati Raj, Finance Commission grants, eGramSwaraj and SVAMITVA property cards.

Role in democratic decentralisation

  • Government at the doorstep: planning and implementing schemes (Gram Panchayat Development Plans).
  • Participation: about 31 lakh elected representatives, including about 14 lakh women.
  • Empowerment of SCs, STs and women.
  • Accountability: social audits and Gram Sabha meetings.
  • Delivery of services: water (Jal Jeevan Mission), sanitation, roads, MGNREGA.

Constraints: weak devolution of funds, functions and functionaries, dependence on State grants, bureaucratic dominance and proxy leadership. Real decentralisation needs greater financial and administrative autonomy.
free.ifm-2019-gk-4a:
Deforestation firesTipping pointWeak governanceIndigenous stewardship

The Amazon, the world's largest tropical rainforest, spreads across nine countries and holds about 10% of known species. In 2019, Brazil's space agency INPE recorded a sharp rise in fires — about 80% more than in 2018 — drawing global attention.

Why the fires happened

  • Most were set deliberately to clear forest for cattle ranching, soya farming and land grabbing, not natural fires.
  • Weakened enforcement and cuts to environmental agencies in Brazil at that time encouraged illegal clearing.
  • Dry conditions and degraded, fragmented forest made fires spread.
  • Illegal logging and gold mining, and new roads.

Why sustainable management is difficult

  • Vast and remote area across nine countries — hard to monitor and police.
  • Poor soils: most nutrients are in the vegetation; once cleared, land degrades quickly and more forest is cut.
  • Economic pressure: global demand for beef, soya, timber and minerals; poverty in the region.
  • Insecure land rights and land speculation; indigenous territories are invaded.
  • Political changes — policies swing with governments.
  • Tipping point: scientists warn that if 20–25% of the Amazon is lost, large parts may turn into savanna; droughts in 2023–24 led to record fires.
  • Complex ecosystem with little knowledge of species and interactions.
  • Global benefits, local costs: the world gains from the carbon sink, but local people bear the costs of conservation.

What can work

  • Indigenous territories and protected areas have far lower deforestation.
  • Satellite monitoring and strict enforcement — deforestation fell sharply in Brazil in 2004–2012 and again after 2023.
  • Soy Moratorium and deforestation-free supply chains.
  • International finance: the Amazon Fund and the Tropical Forest Forever Facility launched at COP30 in Belém (2025).
  • Sustainable livelihoods: agroforestry, non-timber products and eco-tourism.

The Amazon fires show that sustainable management is difficult but possible when strong governance, local rights and global support come together.
free.ifm-2019-gk-4b:
Market scaleTwo- and three-wheelersBattery cellsCritical minerals

India aims to become a global hub for electric vehicle (EV) manufacturing. It has real advantages, but also important gaps.

1. Competitive advantages

  • Large domestic market: the world's third-largest vehicle market and the largest market for two-wheelers and three-wheelers, which are electrifying fastest.
  • Strong automobile and component industry, with export experience.
  • Low-cost engineering and software talent; frugal innovation.
  • Policy support: PLI for Advanced Chemistry Cell batteries (50 GWh), PLI for automobiles and components, PM E-DRIVE (2024), the scheme for EV car manufacturing with lower import duties for investors (2024), low GST (5%) on EVs.
  • Renewable energy growth makes EVs cleaner.
  • Global interest: "China-plus-one" strategies; Indian-made EVs are being exported to many countries.

2. Weaknesses

  • Battery cells — the most valuable part — are largely imported, mainly from China.
  • Critical minerals (lithium, cobalt, nickel, graphite, rare earths) are imported; China's restrictions on rare-earth magnets in 2025 hit EV makers.
  • Low R&D spending and limited technology in cells, power electronics and motors.
  • Charging infrastructure is limited.
  • Higher costs compared with Chinese manufacturers, who have scale and integrated supply chains.
  • Skills gaps in battery chemistry and electronics.

3. What is needed

  • Domestic cell and component manufacturing at scale.
  • Mineral security through the National Critical Mineral Mission, overseas assets (KABIL) and recycling.
  • R&D in sodium-ion and solid-state batteries.
  • Charging and battery-swapping networks.
  • Trade agreements to access markets and inputs.

Conclusion: India has a competitive advantage in two- and three-wheelers and buses, and a growing base in cars, but to become a global leader it must secure batteries, minerals and technology.
free.ifm-2019-gk-4c:
EscarpmentSahyadriAnamudiDeccan basalt

The Western Ghats (Sahyadri) run for about 1,600 km along the western edge of the peninsula, from the Tapi valley to Kanyakumari.

Topographical characteristics

  • Continuous range broken only by passes — Thal Ghat, Bhor Ghat and the Palghat (Palakkad) Gap.
  • Steep western slope facing the coast and a gentle eastern slope merging with the Deccan Plateau.
  • Height increases southwards: about 900–1,600 m in the north; Anamudi (2,695 m) in the Anaimalai Hills is the highest peak of peninsular India; Doddabetta (2,637 m) in the Nilgiris.
  • They meet the Eastern Ghats at the Nilgiris.
  • Water divide: major rivers (Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri) rise here and flow east; short, swift rivers flow west (Mandovi, Sharavati with Jog Falls, Periyar).
  • Orographic barrier causing heavy rain on the western side and a rain shadow to the east.

Structural characteristics

  • They are not true fold mountains but the faulted, uplifted western edge (escarpment) of the Deccan Plateau, formed when the western part of the peninsula subsided into the Arabian Sea.
  • Northern part: horizontal layers of Deccan basalt (lava flows) with step-like (trap) topography.
  • Southern part: ancient Archaean gneisses, granites and charnockites, with Dharwar rocks.
  • Laterite caps on plateaus due to heavy rain and weathering.

They are a UNESCO World Heritage Site (2012) and a global biodiversity hotspot.
free.ifm-2019-gk-4d:
SRS dataNeonatal deathsEAG StatesRural–urban gap

Infant mortality rate (IMR) is the number of deaths of children under one year per 1,000 live births.

Trends

India's IMR has fallen sharply — from about 80 in 1990 and 40 in 2013 to 25 in 2023 (Sample Registration System), and about 24 in 2024. Yet because of its large population, India still accounts for a large share of the world's infant deaths, and its IMR remains far higher than China's or Sri Lanka's (single digits).

Regional variations

  • EAG States (Bihar, UP, MP, Rajasthan, Chhattisgarh, Odisha, Jharkhand) have higher IMR; southern States, Maharashtra and Punjab lower.
  • Neonatal deaths (first 28 days) account for about three-quarters of infant deaths.
  • Higher among poor, less-educated and tribal families.

Causes

  • Preterm birth and low birth weight, birth asphyxia, infections (pneumonia, diarrhoea, sepsis).
  • Maternal malnutrition and anaemia, early marriage and close birth spacing.
  • Weak health systems in some States — shortage of doctors, newborn care units and referral transport.
  • Poor sanitation and low immunisation in some areas.

Measures

Janani Suraksha Yojana and institutional deliveries, Special Newborn Care Units, Mission Indradhanush, Home-Based Newborn Care by ASHAs, LaQshya, Poshan Abhiyaan, the India Newborn Action Plan, and the SDG target of reducing neonatal mortality to 12.

Reducing regional inequality by strengthening health systems in high-burden States is the key to further progress.
free.ifm-2019-gk-5a:
Bast fibresSeed fibresLeaf fibresNatural and man-made

Sources of plant fibres

Plant fibres are long, thin cells, mostly made of cellulose, obtained from different parts of plants:

  • Seeds and fruits: cotton, kapok, coir (coconut husk).
  • Stems (bast fibres): jute, flax (linen), hemp, ramie, kenaf, sunn hemp.
  • Leaves: sisal, abaca (Manila hemp), pineapple fibre, agave.
  • Wood: pulp fibres for paper and rayon.
  • Grasses and canes: bamboo, sabai grass, munj.

1. Classification based on nature (origin)

2. Classification based on use

  • Textile fibres: fine and flexible — cotton, flax, ramie.
  • Cordage fibres: strong — jute, sisal, hemp, coir — for ropes and sacks.
  • Brush fibres: stiff — palmyra, coconut.
  • Filling fibres: soft — kapok and cotton for mattresses and pillows.
  • Weaving and plaiting fibres: bamboo, cane, grasses for mats and baskets.
  • Paper-making fibres: wood pulp, bamboo, bagasse.

3. Classification based on structure (plant part)

  • Surface fibres: hairs on seeds — cotton, kapok.
  • Soft or bast fibres: from the phloem of stems — jute, flax, hemp.
  • Hard or structural fibres: from leaves — sisal, abaca.
  • Fruit fibres: coir.
  • Wood fibres: xylem — pulp.

Importance in India: India is the largest producer of cotton and jute, a major producer of coir (Kerala) and a leading textile exporter. Natural fibres are biodegradable and support millions of farmers and artisans; schemes such as the National Jute Board and the Golden Fibre Revolution promote them.
free.ifm-2019-gk-5b:
MosquitoesHousefliesCockroachesIntegrated pest management

Household insects affecting human health

Prevention and control

  • Sanitation: proper disposal of garbage, covered drains, clean kitchens, food kept covered.
  • Eliminate breeding sites: remove stagnant water from coolers, tyres, pots and roofs (for Aedes); weekly "dry day".
  • Physical barriers: window screens, insecticide-treated bed nets, repellents and protective clothing.
  • Biological control: larvivorous fish (Gambusia, guppy) in tanks and ponds; Bacillus thuringiensis israelensis against larvae.
  • Chemical control: indoor residual spraying, fogging, baits and gels — used carefully to avoid resistance and health effects.
  • Personal hygiene: regular bathing and washing of clothes and bedding against lice and bed bugs.
  • Rodent control to limit fleas.
  • Integrated vector management under the National Centre for Vector Borne Diseases Control, with community participation and awareness.
free.ifm-2019-gk-5c:
Beta-caroteneVitamin A deficiencyBiofortificationGenetic engineering

How golden rice was developed

  • Normal rice grains contain no beta-carotene (provitamin A) in the endosperm.
  • Ingo Potrykus and Peter Beyer (1999–2000) used genetic engineering to insert genes for the beta-carotene pathway into rice:

- phytoene synthase (psy) from daffodil (later replaced by the more efficient gene from maize in Golden Rice 2, 2005), and - carotene desaturase (crtI) from the soil bacterium Erwinia uredovora.

  • These were transferred using Agrobacterium; the grains turn golden-yellow because of beta-carotene.
  • Golden Rice 2 produces much more beta-carotene (up to about 35 micrograms per gram).

Importance in human nutrition

  • Vitamin A deficiency causes night blindness, weakens immunity and increases child deaths; it affects millions of children in Asia and Africa where rice is the staple.
  • Golden rice can provide a significant part of daily vitamin A needs through the staple food — a cheap, sustainable form of biofortification.
  • It complements supplements and diverse diets.

Status and concerns: approved for food use in some countries and for cultivation in the Philippines (2021), though a court there halted commercial planting in 2024. Concerns include biosafety, acceptance by farmers and consumers, and whether diet diversity is a better solution. India has not approved it; it promotes non-GM biofortified varieties developed by ICAR.
free.ifm-2019-gk-5d:
Plants clean pollutantsPhytoextractionRhizofiltrationLow-cost remediation

Phytoremediation is the use of green plants (with their associated microbes) to remove, degrade or contain pollutants in soil, water and air.

Mechanisms

  • Phytoextraction: plants absorb heavy metals (lead, cadmium, arsenic) and store them in shoots, which are harvested — e.g. Indian mustard (Brassica juncea), sunflower.
  • Rhizofiltration: roots absorb pollutants from water — e.g. water hyacinth, sunflower (used to remove radioactive caesium after Chernobyl).
  • Phytodegradation: plants break down organic pollutants (pesticides, explosives).
  • Phytostabilisation: plants immobilise contaminants in soil, preventing spread — e.g. vetiver grass on mine wastes.
  • Phytovolatilisation: plants convert pollutants (mercury, selenium) into volatile forms released into air.
  • Rhizodegradation: microbes around roots break down petroleum hydrocarbons.

Importance

  • Low-cost and eco-friendly compared with digging and chemical treatment.
  • Treats large areas of mildly polluted land, mine sites and wastewater.
  • Improves soil structure, prevents erosion and beautifies the area.
  • Public acceptance — a "green" solution.
  • Useful in India for arsenic in groundwater, mining areas, industrial effluents and lakes; constructed wetlands treat sewage.

Limitations: it is slow, limited to the depth of roots, works best for moderate pollution, and contaminated plants must be safely disposed of.
free.ifm-2019-gk-6a:
MesophaseAnisotropyElectro-optic effectDisplays and sensors

What are liquid crystals?

Liquid crystals are substances in a state between a liquid and a solid crystal (a mesophase). They flow like liquids, but their molecules — usually rod-shaped or disc-shaped — stay aligned in a particular direction, as in crystals. They were discovered by Friedrich Reinitzer (1888).

Types: nematic (molecules parallel, no layers), smectic (parallel and in layers), and cholesteric (twisted, helical structure); thermotropic (changing with temperature) and lyotropic (in solution — like cell membranes and soap).

Useful features

  • Anisotropy: optical and electrical properties depend on direction.
  • Birefringence: they split light and can rotate polarised light.
  • Electro-optic effect: a small voltage changes the alignment of molecules and therefore how light passes — the basis of displays.
  • Sensitivity to temperature: cholesteric liquid crystals change colour with temperature.
  • Low power use and fast response.

Applications

Liquid crystals thus connect physics, chemistry, biology and technology, and modern display technology depends on them.
free.ifm-2019-gk-6b:
CoherenceMonochromaticCollimatedApplications

1. Similarities between laser light and starlight

  • Both are electromagnetic waves travelling at the speed of light.
  • Both are produced when excited atoms release energy as photons.
  • Both can be reflected, refracted and focused, and both appear as a point source from far away.

2. Differences

3. Uses of lasers

  • Barcode scanners: a low-power laser beam sweeps across the barcode; black bars absorb and white spaces reflect light; a photodetector converts the pattern of reflections into an electric signal that is decoded into numbers. The narrow, coherent beam allows reading from a distance and at angles.
  • Laser printers: a laser beam "draws" the image on a positively charged photosensitive drum, changing the charge where it falls; toner powder sticks to these areas, is transferred to paper and fused by heat. The precision of the laser gives sharp text and images.
  • Cautery instruments (laser surgery): the focused laser beam heats and cuts tissue while sealing blood vessels, reducing bleeding and infection; used in eye surgery (LASIK, retinal repair), removing tumours, skin treatment and dental surgery.

Lasers are also used in fibre-optic communication, cutting and welding, measuring distances, and scientific research.
free.ifm-2019-gk-6c:
Brain-inspired computingSpiking neuronsSynapses and plasticityEnergy efficiency

Neurocomputing (neuromorphic computing) is computing that imitates the structure and working of the brain. Instead of the conventional von Neumann architecture, where memory and processing are separate and data moves back and forth, neuromorphic systems combine memory and processing in networks of artificial neurons and synapses.

Biological inspirations

  • Neurons: the brain has about 86 billion neurons that communicate by electrical spikes; neuromorphic chips use spiking neural networks that process information only when a spike occurs.
  • Synapses: connections whose strength changes with learning (synaptic plasticity); hardware uses devices like memristors to store weights.
  • Massive parallelism: the brain processes many signals at once.
  • Energy efficiency: the brain uses only about 20 watts; neuromorphic chips aim for very low power.
  • Learning from experience and adapting in real time.
  • Fault tolerance: the brain works even when some neurons fail.

Examples: IBM's TrueNorth, Intel's Loihi and research chips in India (IISc and IITs).

Uses: robotics, sensors, self-driving vehicles, edge AI devices, pattern and speech recognition — wherever fast, low-power learning is needed.
free.ifm-2019-gk-6d:
Permanently shadowed cratersWater iceSoft landingChandrayaan-3

Why the lunar south pole was chosen

  • Water ice: permanently shadowed craters near the south pole are extremely cold and may hold water ice — important for science and for future human bases (drinking water, oxygen and rocket fuel).
  • Unexplored region: no mission had landed near the south pole before; it offers new science.
  • Ancient record: the cold traps may preserve a record of the early solar system.
  • Larger area in shadow than at the north pole.
  • Sunlit peaks nearby could provide continuous solar power for future bases.

Key objective demonstrating technological advancement

A key objective of Chandrayaan-2 (launched July 2019) was to demonstrate a soft landing on the Moon with the Vikram lander and to operate the Pragyan rover. This required autonomous navigation, hazard detection and throttleable engines — advanced technologies. The lander crash-landed in September 2019, but the orbiter continues to work and has mapped the Moon in high resolution.

Outcome: the lessons led to Chandrayaan-3, which made India the first country to land near the lunar south pole on 23 August 2023 (now National Space Day), proving India's mastery of soft-landing technology.
free.ifm-2020-ge-1a:
OvershootWater, soil and forestsCircular economyIntergenerational equity

Depletion of Natural Resources: A Threat to Humanity

Every year, a group of scientists calculates Earth Overshoot Day — the date by which humanity has used up all the natural resources that the planet can regenerate in that year. In recent years, it has fallen in late July or early August. For the rest of the year, we live on credit, drawing down forests, fisheries, soils, groundwater and the atmosphere's capacity to absorb carbon. Like a family that spends its savings instead of living on its income, humanity is heading towards bankruptcy — not financial, but ecological.

The scale of depletion

The UN Environment Programme's Global Resources Outlook (2024) reports that the extraction of materials — biomass, fossil fuels, metals and minerals — has more than tripled since 1970 and could rise by another 60% by 2060 if trends continue.

  • Water: groundwater is being pumped faster than it is recharged in India, the United States, China and the Middle East. Rivers like the Colorado and Yellow no longer reach the sea in some seasons; in India, cities like Chennai and Bengaluru have faced severe water crises.
  • Soil: erosion, salinity and loss of organic matter are degrading farmland; about 30% of India's land is degraded.
  • Forests: about ten million hectares are lost worldwide every year.
  • Fisheries: more than a third of the world's fish stocks are overfished.
  • Minerals and energy: oil, gas and high-grade ores are finite; even sand — used in concrete — is being mined so heavily that riverbeds and coasts are damaged.
  • Biodiversity: species are disappearing far faster than the natural rate.

Why depletion threatens humanity

First, food and water security. When aquifers run dry and soils lose fertility, harvests fall. The Green Revolution heartland of Punjab now faces a groundwater crisis.

Second, economic stability. Scarce resources mean rising prices, supply disruptions and slower growth; industries dependent on water, minerals and energy become vulnerable.

Third, conflict and migration. Competition over water, land and minerals fuels tensions within and between countries. Drought and land degradation push people to migrate.

Fourth, climate change. Burning fossil fuels and cutting forests release the greenhouse gases that are warming the planet, which in turn worsens water stress and crop losses.

Fifth, injustice. The poor, who depend directly on forests, fisheries and common lands, suffer first, while a wealthy minority consumes the most. Future generations will inherit a poorer planet — a deep injustice to those who have no voice today.

The causes

The root causes include population growth, rising consumption, especially by the rich, wasteful production, subsidies that encourage overuse (such as free electricity for pumping groundwater), poor regulation and an economic model that counts the use of natural capital as income.

What can be done

  • Efficiency: produce more with less — micro-irrigation, energy-efficient buildings and appliances, precision farming.
  • Circular economy: reduce, reuse, repair and recycle materials; extended producer responsibility for plastics, batteries and e-waste.
  • Renewables: shift from coal and oil to solar, wind and other clean sources.
  • Restoration: reforestation, watershed development, soil conservation and the revival of lakes and wetlands.
  • Pricing nature: remove harmful subsidies and account for natural capital in economic decisions.
  • Community management: local people can manage forests, fisheries and groundwater well, as India's Joint Forest Management and Atal Bhujal Yojana show.
  • Sustainable lifestyles: India's Mission LiFE asks individuals to consume mindfully and avoid waste.
  • Global cooperation on climate, oceans and biodiversity.

Conclusion

Mahatma Gandhi warned that the Earth provides enough for everyone's need but not for everyone's greed. The depletion of natural resources is not a distant problem; it is already shaping our water, food, climate and peace. Humanity has the knowledge and technology to live within the planet's limits. What it needs now is the will to change. The resources we save today are not merely ours; they belong to the generations yet to come.
free.ifm-2020-ge-1b:
Farm lawsMarket accessFPOs and digital agricultureDiversification

Impact of Agricultural Reforms on India's Economic Future

Agriculture employs nearly half of India's workforce but produces only about a sixth of its national output. This gap explains much of rural distress: too many people depend on small, low-productivity farms. India's economic future — its growth, jobs, food security and social stability — therefore depends on reforming agriculture.

The need for reform

Indian farms are small (the average holding is just over one hectare), yields are below world averages, and much of the land depends on rain. Farmers face volatile prices, debt, weak access to markets and storage, and the growing effects of climate change. Public procurement at minimum support prices (MSP) mainly benefits rice and wheat farmers in a few States, encouraging water-intensive crops in water-scarce regions. The sector needs new investment, technology and markets.

The 2020 reforms and their fate

In 2020, Parliament passed three farm laws to allow farmers to sell outside regulated APMC mandis, to promote contract farming and to reduce stock limits under the Essential Commodities Act. Supporters argued that these would widen markets, attract private investment and raise farmers' incomes. But many farmers, especially in Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh, feared the weakening of mandis and MSP, and that large companies would dominate. After a year-long protest, the laws were repealed in November 2021. The episode showed that reforms must be built through consultation and trust.

Reforms that are reshaping agriculture

Even without those laws, several reforms are changing the sector:

  • Income support: PM-KISAN gives ₹6,000 a year to farm families.
  • Markets: the e-NAM platform links mandis online; 10,000 Farmer Producer Organisations help small farmers bargain collectively.
  • Infrastructure: the ₹1 lakh crore Agriculture Infrastructure Fund for storage, cold chains and processing.
  • Digital agriculture: the Digital Agriculture Mission and Agri Stack aim to give farmers digital identities, crop surveys and advisories.
  • Risk cover: crop insurance under PMFBY and higher limits for Kisan Credit Cards.
  • Sustainability: natural farming, micro-irrigation, soil health cards and crop diversification towards pulses, oilseeds and millets.
  • Allied sectors: dairy, fisheries and poultry, which are growing faster than crops.

Impact on India's economic future

If carried through, these reforms can:

  • Raise farm incomes, increasing rural demand for industrial goods and services and supporting overall growth.
  • Create rural non-farm jobs in food processing, logistics and agri-tech, helping to move surplus labour out of farming.
  • Strengthen food and nutrition security while reducing the burden of food subsidies.
  • Boost exports — India is already the largest rice exporter and a major exporter of spices and marine products.
  • Reduce inflation volatility through better storage and supply chains.
  • Protect natural resources, making agriculture resilient to climate change.

Challenges

  • Small holdings and fragmented land records limit scale.
  • Political sensitivity of MSP, subsidies and markets.
  • State subject: agriculture and markets are largely State responsibilities, requiring Centre–State cooperation.
  • Climate risks — heat waves and erratic rain.
  • Skills and capital for farmers to use technology.

Conclusion

Agriculture is not a sector of the past; it is the foundation of India's future. Reforms that raise productivity, open markets fairly, protect farmers from risk and conserve soil and water can turn rural India into an engine of growth. The lesson of recent years is that reforms succeed only when farmers are partners, not mere subjects, of change. A prosperous farmer is the surest guarantee of a prosperous India.

School closuresDigital divideLearning lossFoundational literacy

Virtual Teaching and the Crisis of Primary Education

When the COVID-19 pandemic closed schools in March 2020, Indian classrooms moved to mobile screens almost overnight. Teachers recorded lessons on WhatsApp, governments broadcast classes on television, and platforms like DIKSHA offered digital textbooks. For some children, especially in cities, learning continued online. For millions of others, especially young children in villages and poor homes, school simply stopped. Indian schools remained closed, fully or partly, for well over a year — among the longest closures in the world. The experience exposed both the promise and the limits of virtual teaching, and deepened a crisis in primary education that already existed.

A crisis before the pandemic

Even before COVID-19, India faced a learning crisis. Most children were enrolled, but many were not learning. Surveys such as ASER showed that only about half of Class V children could read a Class II text. Large classes, teacher shortages and rote learning meant that children fell behind early and rarely caught up.

What virtual teaching could not do

First, the digital divide. Many families had no smartphone, or one phone shared among several children and parents. Internet access was patchy in rural areas and data was expensive. Children of migrant workers, tribal communities and the poorest families were cut off.

Second, young children learn differently. Primary education depends on play, interaction, songs, handling objects and the close attention of a teacher. A screen cannot hold the attention of a six-year-old for long, and children learning to read and count need individual guidance.

Third, teachers were unprepared. Most had no training in online teaching, and many lacked devices themselves.

Fourth, home conditions varied. Parents with little education could not help, and many children were drawn into household work or wage labour.

Fifth, lost nutrition and safety. Schools provide mid-day meals, health check-ups and protection; their closure increased malnutrition, child labour and child marriage in some places.

The result: learning loss

ASER 2022 found that the share of Class III children able to read a Class II text fell from about 27% in 2018 to about 20%, wiping out years of slow progress. Children also forgot what they had learnt. The loss was greatest among the poorest children, widening inequality.

What virtual teaching did achieve

The crisis also brought innovation. Television and radio lessons, community classes in open spaces ("mohalla classes"), teachers visiting homes, and digital content in local languages reached children who had nothing else. Teachers and parents became more comfortable with technology, and platforms like DIKSHA and PM eVidya created a foundation for blended learning.

The way forward

  • Foundational learning first: the NIPUN Bharat Mission aims for every child to read and do basic arithmetic by Class 3; remedial programmes such as "Teaching at the Right Level" help children catch up.
  • Blended, not virtual, learning: technology should support teachers in classrooms, not replace them, especially in the early years.
  • Close the digital divide: devices, connectivity and digital content for schools and poor households.
  • Train teachers in digital and activity-based teaching.
  • Mother-tongue instruction in early grades, as NEP 2020 recommends.
  • Protect nutrition and child welfare during emergencies through community delivery of meals and services.
  • Preparedness: plans for continuing learning during future disasters.

Conclusion

The pandemic proved that a screen is no substitute for a school, especially for young children. Virtual teaching was a lifeline for some but a wall for many. The real lesson is not to abandon technology but to use it wisely — to strengthen classrooms, empower teachers and reach every child. If India focuses on foundational learning with determination, the crisis exposed by the pandemic can become the turning point for a stronger primary education system.

NEP 2020Flexibility and choiceSkills and researchImplementation

New Education Policy and the Future of India's Youth

India has the largest youth population in the world. Whether this becomes a demographic dividend or a demographic burden depends above all on education. The National Education Policy (NEP) 2020, the first comprehensive education policy in 34 years, seeks to transform how Indians learn — from early childhood to research. Its success or failure will shape the future of India's youth.

What NEP 2020 proposes

  • New school structure (5+3+3+4), including three years of pre-school, with a strong focus on foundational literacy and numeracy.
  • Mother tongue or local language as the medium of instruction, wherever possible, at least till Class 5.
  • Less rote learning, more conceptual understanding, critical thinking and experiential learning; reformed board examinations.
  • Vocational education from Class 6, with internships, aiming for at least half of learners to have vocational exposure.
  • Flexibility: no rigid separation between arts, science and commerce, or between curricular and extracurricular activities.
  • Higher education: four-year multidisciplinary undergraduate programmes with multiple entry and exit, an Academic Bank of Credits, and a target of 50% gross enrolment by 2035.
  • Research: the Anusandhan National Research Foundation (established by law in 2023) to fund research.
  • Internationalisation: foreign universities can set up campuses in India, and several have begun to do so.
  • Technology in teaching and assessment, and a single higher education regulator.
  • Public spending on education to reach 6% of GDP.

How it can shape the future of youth

First, better foundations. Children who can read, write and reason well in the early years go further in education and life.

Second, freedom to choose. A student can study physics with music, or economics with computer science, and follow her interests rather than a fixed stream. Multiple exits mean that leaving a course does not mean losing everything.

Third, employability. Vocational exposure, internships and skills linked to industry can bridge the gap between degrees and jobs. Many employers say graduates lack practical skills; NEP aims to fix this.

Fourth, innovation and research. Multidisciplinary universities and research funding can help young Indians create knowledge and start enterprises, not merely seek jobs.

Fifth, values and citizenship. NEP stresses ethics, constitutional values, Indian languages and culture, along with global outlook — preparing young people to be responsible citizens of a diverse democracy.

Sixth, inclusion. Special attention to girls, socially disadvantaged groups and regions through gender inclusion funds and special education zones.

Challenges

  • Funding: India still spends less than 5% of GDP on education; reaching 6% requires major increases.
  • Teachers: a vision of creative, multidisciplinary teaching needs well-trained, motivated teachers, but vacancies and poor training persist.
  • Infrastructure and digital divide in rural schools and colleges.
  • Language policy has raised debates, especially in States worried about the imposition of Hindi.
  • Federal concerns: education is a concurrent subject; some States have resisted parts of the policy.
  • Implementation gaps: reforms such as multiple exits and credit banks need institutional capacity.

Conclusion

NEP 2020 is an ambitious vision that could equip India's youth for a rapidly changing world — if it is implemented well. A policy document cannot by itself educate a child; that requires committed teachers, adequate resources and cooperation between the Centre and the States. If these come together, the young people of India can become not only job seekers but job creators, thinkers and leaders who help build a developed India by 2047.

Subject: Growing rowdyism in our locality

Sir/Madam,

Through the columns of your esteemed newspaper, I wish to draw the attention of the police and civic authorities to the growing incidence of rowdyism in our locality.

Last week, a shopkeeper was assaulted when he objected to their behaviour, and there have been several cases of chain-snatching. Women and elderly residents now hesitate to go out after dark, and parents are anxious about children returning from tuition classes.

Residents have complained to the local police station, but patrolling remains irregular and little action has been taken. Poor street lighting near the park makes matters worse.

I request the authorities to: 1. increase police patrolling, especially in the evenings, and set up a police picket near the market; 2. take strict action against public drinking and rash driving; 3. install street lights and CCTV cameras at vulnerable spots; 4. deploy women's safety squads and publicise helpline numbers; 5. involve residents' welfare associations in community policing.

I hope that this letter will prompt quick action so that residents can live without fear.

COVID-19 Awareness Camp held by XYZ NGO

By ABC

The XYZ NGO organised a COVID-19 awareness camp at the community centre of our town on Sunday to help citizens protect themselves and their families from the pandemic. Over 500 people, including daily-wage workers, shopkeepers, students and senior citizens, attended in small groups, following distancing norms.

The camp was inaugurated by a doctor from the local government hospital, who explained how the virus spreads and the importance of wearing masks, washing hands, maintaining physical distance and avoiding crowded places. Volunteers demonstrated the correct way to wear and dispose of masks and to wash hands for twenty seconds.

Health workers checked temperatures and oxygen levels with pulse oximeters and advised people with symptoms to get tested at the nearest centre. A help desk assisted people in registering for vaccination and downloading the Aarogya Setu app. Counsellors spoke about coping with stress and anxiety during the lockdown, and busted common myths about home remedies and vaccines.

Free masks, sanitisers and pamphlets in local languages were distributed. Ration kits were given to the families of migrant workers who had lost their income.

Residents appreciated the camp. "I learnt how to use an oximeter and when to go to hospital," said an elderly participant. The NGO's coordinator announced that similar camps will be held in nearby villages and slum areas in the coming weeks, with the support of the local administration.

Quality seedResearch and food securityBiotechnologyNational Seeds Policy

Good harvests need good seed. Farmers require a reliable supply of quality seeds and seedlings at affordable prices, and new technology is improving their quality and range. Seed is the chief determinant of agricultural potential, on which other inputs depend; suitable varieties for diverse agro-climatic conditions and intensive cropping, and their timely supply, sustain productivity. The seed sector has progressed greatly in three decades: farmers who once saved their own seed now buy improved varieties.

Seed research under the National Agricultural Research System ended food-grain shortages and edible-oil imports and produced drought-tolerant varieties. As farmers readily adopted improved seeds and inputs, food-grain output rose from 50 to over 212 million tonnes, turning shortages into surpluses. The aim now is household food and nutritional security. But growth has been uneven across regions, crops and farmers, and slowed in the 1990s.

Biotechnology promises stress-tolerant, productive and nutritious varieties, needing a supportive climate and investment, while health, biosafety and farmers' concerns are addressed. Amid globalisation, the National Seeds Policy seeks to help the seed industry seize opportunities, protect farmers and conserve agro-biodiversity through a new regulatory system that removes needless controls, assures quality and prevents exploitation.
