free.ifm-2020-ge-4a: According to the writer, Western scholars believe that any borrowing from the West means a loss of Indian identity. They hold the clichéd view that Indian intellectuals, including Nehru, are elitist, imitate the West and lack a sense of what is truly Indian, and imply that the West must tell Indians how to be truly Indian. They ignore Nehru's deep rapport with the rural masses, misunderstand India's economic planning by overlooking its aim of real independence through self-sufficiency, and set up a false opposition between Gandhi as "Indian" and Nehru as "Western".
free.ifm-2020-ge-4b:
Nehru carried forward Gandhian ideas in his own way:

  • His policy of non-alignment was an extension of Gandhi's non-violence in international affairs.
  • His doctrine of import substitution was an extension of the charkha, Gandhi's symbol of self-sufficiency — applied to the nation through industrial and agricultural self-reliance.
  • His economic planning aimed at real independence, free from manipulation and economic imperialism.
  • He kept a close rapport with the rural masses, and Gandhi himself had chosen Nehru as his successor despite their differences.
free.ifm-2020-ge-4c: The "reversal process" is the way in which people exposed to Western education and ideas turn back, at the creative and intellectual level, to rediscover and revive their own Indian roots. For example, Macaulay's education policy aimed to create a class of "brown Englishmen", but these very people became a great force for liberating India from British rule and for the "discovery of India". In the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, in almost every field of creative work, the so-called westernised segment led the movement for Indianisation, turning from European philosophy, literature and art to Indian traditions.
free.ifm-2020-ge-4d: The paradox is that the Western-educated elite, who were expected to lose their Indianness, actually led the rediscovery of Indian tradition and Indianisation. By contrast, those who did not go through this reversal absorbed only cheap Western habits and now combine consumerism with fundamentalism. The implication is that genuine engagement with Western ideas can strengthen a confident Indian identity, whereas superficial imitation produces a dangerous mix that threatens India's unity and integrity, creating new divisions on religious, linguistic and regional lines. It also shows how Western scholars misread Indian modernity.
free.ifm-2020-ge-4e: Developing countries need a synthesis of tradition and modernity so that they can achieve progress without losing their identity. Modern knowledge and institutions are necessary for development, but rejecting tradition leads to rootlessness. On the other hand, an unchanged, unmediated continuity of tradition would destroy itself through its own unawareness, and would end up imitating only the most superficial aspects of Western society. A creative synthesis allows a society to modernise while remaining true to its cultural roots.

First pan-Indian empireSourcesAdministrationArt and Dhamma

The Mauryan period (c. 321–185 BCE) is one of the most important periods of Indian history for several reasons.

1. Political unification

  • Chandragupta Maurya, with Kautilya's help, overthrew the Nandas and built the first empire covering most of the subcontinent, from Afghanistan to Karnataka.
  • He defeated Seleucus Nicator, gaining territories in the north-west and a marriage alliance; Bindusara and Ashoka extended it further (Kalinga, c. 261 BCE).

2. Rich and varied sources

  • Kautilya's Arthashastra on statecraft and economy, Megasthenes' Indica (in fragments), the Ashokan edicts — the first deciphered written records of Indian rulers (read by James Prinsep in 1837) — and Buddhist and Jain texts.

3. Centralised administration

  • A council of ministers (mantriparishad), departments under adhyakshas, provinces under princes (kumaras), city administration at Pataliputra by committees (Megasthenes), a large standing army, and an efficient spy system.

4. Economy

  • State control of agriculture (sita land), mines, forests and trade; punch-marked silver coins; guilds; roads such as the Uttarapatha; growth of towns.

5. Ashoka and Dhamma

  • After Kalinga, Ashoka adopted Dhamma — tolerance, non-violence and welfare — and spread Buddhism to Sri Lanka, Central Asia and South-East Asia.

6. Art and architecture

  • The polished stone pillars with animal capitals — the Sarnath lion capital is India's national emblem; stupas (Sanchi, Bharhut in their early form); rock-cut Barabar caves; the Didarganj Yakshi.

7. International contacts

  • Diplomatic relations with the Hellenistic world; Ashoka's edicts mention Greek kings.

The Mauryan period thus marks the beginning of an imperial tradition, a written history and a pan-Indian culture, which is why it continues to attract historians.

Village assembliesUttaramerurBrihadeeswaraChola bronzes

The Chola Empire (c. 850–1279 CE), founded by Vijayalaya and raised to its height by Rajaraja I (985–1014) and Rajendra I (1014–1044), was the greatest power of south India and controlled sea trade in the Bay of Bengal.

1. Administrative features

  • Monarchy with a council of officials; kings took titles like Rajakesari and Parakesari.
  • Units: the kingdom (rajyam) was divided into mandalams (provinces), valanadus, nadus and villages.
  • Local self-government — the most famous feature:

- Ur — assembly of ordinary villages; - Sabha (mahasabha) — assembly of Brahmana villages (brahmadeyas); - Nagaram — assembly of merchants. - The Uttaramerur inscriptions (919 and 921 CE, under Parantaka I) describe the election of committees by lot (kudavolai system), qualifications of members (property, education, age), and disqualifications. - Committees (variyams) looked after tanks, gardens, justice and temples.

  • Land revenue: Rajaraja ordered a land survey; revenue of about one-third of produce; tax in cash or kind.
  • Strong army and navy: Rajendra I's naval expedition to Srivijaya (1025) and conquests in Sri Lanka and the Maldives; his campaign to the Ganga gave him the title Gangaikondachola.
  • Irrigation: large tanks, such as the Cholagangam tank, and canals from the Kaveri.

2. Cultural features

  • Temple architecture (Dravida style): the Brihadeeswara temple at Thanjavur (1010) with its tall vimana; Gangaikondacholapuram and Airavatesvara (Darasuram) — together the Great Living Chola Temples (UNESCO).
  • Bronze sculpture: the Nataraja and other bronzes made by the lost-wax process are among the finest in the world.
  • Literature: Tamil works such as Kamban's Ramayana, Sekkizhar's Periyapuranam on the Nayanars, and Jayankondar's Kalingattupparani; the compilation of the Shaiva canon (Tirumurai) and Vaishnava hymns.
  • Temples as centres of economy, education, music and dance; devadasis and temple endowments.
  • Bhakti movement of Alvars and Nayanars strengthened.
  • Overseas influence in Sri Lanka and South-East Asia.

The Chola period is regarded as a golden age of Tamil culture and of local self-government in India.

Religious policyDeccan warsRajput alienationStructural crisis

Aurangzeb (1658–1707) contributed significantly to the decline of the Mughal Empire, but he was not solely responsible.

His share of responsibility

  • Religious policy: reimposition of jizya (1679), destruction of some temples and restrictions on Hindu practices alienated many subjects and allies.
  • Rajput policy: interference in Marwar's succession (1679) led to a long war with Marwar and Mewar and lost the Mughals their most loyal allies.
  • Deccan wars (1681–1707): 26 years spent fighting Bijapur, Golconda and the Marathas drained the treasury and armies and left the north neglected.
  • Revolts: Jats, Satnamis, Sikhs (the execution of Guru Tegh Bahadur, 1675) and Marathas.
  • Suspicious and centralising — he did not trust his sons or nobles, so able successors were not trained.

Other causes beyond Aurangzeb

  • Jagirdari crisis: too many mansabdars and too few productive jagirs (Satish Chandra).
  • Agrarian crisis: heavy revenue demands led to peasant flight and revolts (Irfan Habib).
  • Weak successors, wars of succession, court factions and the rise of autonomous provinces after 1707.
  • Foreign invasions (Nadir Shah, 1739) and the rise of European companies.

Conclusion: Aurangzeb's policies hastened the decline by straining the empire's resources and loyalties, but deeper structural weaknesses existed, which his weak successors could not manage.

SavarkarPopular participationHindu–Muslim unityLimits

The Revolt of 1857 began as a sepoy mutiny at Meerut but spread to large parts of north and central India. V.D. Savarkar, in The Indian War of Independence of 1857 (1909), called it the First War of Indian Independence.

Arguments for calling it a war of independence

  • Popular participation: peasants, artisans, zamindars and taluqdars joined in Awadh, Rohilkhand, Bihar and central India.
  • Hindu–Muslim unity: leaders of both communities fought together under the symbolic leadership of Bahadur Shah Zafar.
  • Common enemy: the aim was to end British rule; proclamations called on people to fight the foreigners.
  • Heroic leaders: Rani Lakshmibai, Nana Saheb, Tantia Tope, Kunwar Singh, Begum Hazrat Mahal and Maulvi Ahmadullah Shah.
  • It inspired later nationalists, and its memory became part of the freedom struggle.

Arguments against

  • Limited area: the south, Bengal, Punjab and large parts of the west remained largely unaffected; many rulers helped the British.
  • No common programme or vision of a new India; leaders fought for local grievances and to restore old orders.
  • Not "first": earlier revolts such as the Vellore Mutiny (1806) and tribal and peasant uprisings had taken place.
  • R.C. Majumdar called it "neither the first, nor national, nor a war of independence"; modern education and the middle class stayed away.

Assessment: it was more than a mutiny but less than a fully national war of independence in the modern sense. It was the first large-scale, popular challenge to British rule and laid the groundwork for later nationalism.

ContractionLockdownMonetary easingCapital expenditure

1. Impact of COVID-19 on growth

  • India's GDP contracted by about 24% in April–June 2020 and by about 6% in 2020-21, the first annual contraction in four decades.
  • The lockdown stopped production, transport and trade; migrant workers lost jobs; demand collapsed.
  • MSMEs, tourism, hospitality, aviation and construction were hit hardest.
  • Uncertainty about new waves (the second wave in 2021), vaccination and global demand kept investment low; banks faced the risk of rising bad loans.
  • Growth was already slowing before the pandemic (about 4% in 2019-20).

2. Need for supportive monetary policy

  • The RBI cut the repo rate to 4% (May 2020), cut the CRR and injected liquidity through targeted long-term repo operations.
  • A loan moratorium and restructuring gave relief to borrowers.
  • Low interest rates and ample liquidity reduced borrowing costs and kept credit flowing to businesses.
  • Accommodative guidance gave confidence to investors.

3. Need for strong public investment

  • When private demand is weak, public capital expenditure creates demand, jobs and income (the multiplier effect is higher for capex than for current spending).
  • Crowding in: better roads, railways, ports and power encourage private investment.
  • The Government's Aatmanirbhar Bharat package (about ₹20 lakh crore), the Emergency Credit Line Guarantee Scheme for MSMEs, free food grains (PMGKAY) and a sharp rise in Union capital expenditure — from about ₹3.4 lakh crore in 2019-20 to over ₹11 lakh crore in 2024-25 — supported revival.

4. Outcome

The economy grew by over 9% in 2021-22 and has been among the fastest-growing major economies since. But concerns remain about uneven recovery ("K-shaped"), informal-sector jobs and private consumption. A balanced mix of monetary support, public investment and structural reforms remains essential.
free.ifm-2020-gk-2b:
Glacier meltErratic monsoonGroundwater stressBehavioural nudges

1. Implications of climate change for freshwater in India

  • Himalayan glaciers are retreating; rivers such as the Ganga, Indus and Brahmaputra may first see more flow and floods, then less flow in the dry season.
  • Erratic monsoon: fewer rainy days, more intense downpours, longer dry spells; more droughts and floods.
  • Higher evaporation from reservoirs and soils; higher water demand for crops and cities in hotter weather.
  • Groundwater stress: less recharge because of intense runoff; over-extraction in Punjab, Haryana and Rajasthan.
  • Sea-level rise causes saltwater intrusion in coastal aquifers and deltas.
  • Water quality falls as low flows concentrate pollutants.
  • Conflicts between States and sectors (agriculture, industry, cities); urban crises such as Chennai (2019) and Bengaluru (2024).

NITI Aayog's Composite Water Management Index (2018) warned that about 60 crore Indians face high to extreme water stress.

2. Can behavioural nudges improve water-use efficiency?

Yes, demand-side management through nudges — small changes in how choices are presented, without force — can help, as the Economic Survey 2018-19 argued.

  • Studies abroad have found that comparing a household's use with its neighbours' reduces consumption by a few per cent at almost no cost.
  • Farmers adopt micro-irrigation faster when peers show results.

3. Limits

  • Nudges work best alongside price signals (volumetric pricing), metering, regulation of groundwater, and infrastructure (micro-irrigation, wastewater reuse).
  • Agriculture uses about 80% of water; free power for pumps and MSP-driven paddy in dry areas need policy changes, not just nudges.

Thus nudges can raise end-use efficiency, but they must be part of a wider water management strategy.

JAM trinityUPIDBTAccount Aggregator

Financial inclusion means access to affordable financial services — bank accounts, credit, insurance, pensions and payments — for all, especially the poor. It drives growth by mobilising savings, expanding credit to small businesses, reducing poverty and making welfare delivery efficient.

Role of digital technology

  • JAM trinity: Jan Dhan accounts (over 50 crore), Aadhaar and mobile phones together enable Direct Benefit Transfers, reducing leakages.
  • UPI: instant, low-cost payments — about 20 billion transactions a month — even for street vendors.
  • e-KYC makes opening accounts cheap and quick.
  • Digital credit: the Account Aggregator framework, OCEN and cash-flow-based lending give small firms loans without collateral.
  • Micro-insurance and pensions (PMJJBY, PMSBY, Atal Pension Yojana) enrolled through mobile banking.
  • Business correspondents with micro-ATMs and India Post Payments Bank reach villages.
  • Fintech innovation and digital public infrastructure lower costs.

Challenges: the digital divide, low digital and financial literacy, cyber fraud, dormant accounts and limited formal credit for women and the poor. Digital literacy (PMGDISHA), consumer protection and local language interfaces can make inclusion meaningful.

Non-timber forest products (NTFPs) are all forest products other than timber.

Types

Importance for livelihoods

  • About 27.5 crore people depend on forests; NTFPs are a major source of cash income for tribal households.
  • Seasonal income when there is no farm work; women do most collection.
  • Processing and trade create local enterprise (Van Dhan Vikas Kendras, MSP for MFP).

Importance for food security

  • Direct food: fruits, leaves, tubers, mushrooms and honey supply nutrition, especially during lean seasons and droughts.
  • Income to buy food; medicinal plants for health.

Rights under the Forest Rights Act (2006) and PESA (1996), fair prices and sustainable harvesting make NTFPs a basis of both livelihoods and conservation.
free.ifm-2020-gk-3a:
Article 37Harmonious constructionArticle 21Reasonable restrictions

Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSPs) are not enforceable in courts (Article 37), but they are "fundamental in the governance of the country". Over time, the Supreme Court has used them as a framework of values to interpret Fundamental Rights (FRs).

1. DPSPs as a framework that structures rights

  • Expanding Article 21:

- Bandhua Mukti Morcha (1984): the right to live with dignity draws on Articles 39(e), (f), 41 and 42. - Olga Tellis (1985): right to livelihood (Article 39(a)). - Unni Krishnan (1993): right to education (Articles 41, 45) — later Article 21A. - M.C. Mehta cases: right to a clean environment (Article 48A).

  • Equality: Randhir Singh (1982) — "equal pay for equal work" (Article 39(d)) read into Articles 14 and 16.
  • Legal aid: Article 39A read into Article 21 (Hussainara Khatoon, 1979).

2. DPSPs as values that constrain rights

  • Laws implementing DPSPs are treated as reasonable restrictions on FRs: land reforms; State of Gujarat v. Mirzapur Moti Kureshi (2005) upheld a ban on cow slaughter citing Article 48 as a reasonable restriction on trade (Article 19(1)(g)).
  • Article 31C protects laws giving effect to Article 39(b) and (c) from challenge under Articles 14 and 19.

3. Balance — neither overrides the other

  • Champakam Dorairajan (1951): DPSPs must yield to FRs.
  • Kesavananda Bharati (1973) and Minerva Mills (1980): the Constitution rests on a balance and harmony between Parts III and IV; DPSPs are the ends and FRs the means.
  • Property Owners' Association (2024): a nine-judge bench limited the State's power under Article 39(b), showing that DPSPs guide but do not override rights.

Conclusion: yes, DPSPs are best understood as the value framework for interpreting FRs — giving them social and economic content — while courts maintain a balance so that one does not destroy the other.
free.ifm-2020-gk-3b:
Holding-together federationStrong centrePartition contextCooperative federalism

India's federalism is "holding together" rather than "coming together" (Alfred Stepan): it was created by the Constitution to keep a diverse country united, not by sovereign states joining together.

1. Why a strong Union was chosen

  • Partition and communal violence (1947), the integration of 560-plus princely states, and the threat to unity made the framers prefer a strong Centre.
  • Economic planning and development needed central coordination.
  • Security — wars, insurgencies and external threats.

2. Features of the strong Union

  • "Union of States" (Article 1): States cannot secede.
  • Parliament can alter State boundaries (Article 3) — an "indestructible Union of destructible States".
  • Residuary powers with the Union; the Union List is the longest.
  • Emergency provisions (Articles 352, 356, 360), Article 249 (Parliament legislating on State subjects), Governors appointed by the Centre.
  • All-India services, single citizenship, integrated judiciary, single Constitution.
  • Fiscal dominance of the Centre.

K.C. Wheare called India "quasi-federal"; Ambedkar said it can be federal in normal times and unitary in emergencies.

3. How it has sustained unity

  • Helped integrate princely states, manage linguistic reorganisation and contain separatism in Punjab, Mizoram and Jammu and Kashmir.
  • Coordinated national programmes and responded to crises such as COVID-19.

4. Evolution towards cooperative federalism

  • S.R. Bommai (1994): federalism is a basic feature; limited the misuse of Article 356.
  • Coalition era gave States more voice; Sarkaria (1988) and Punchhi (2010) Commissions recommended better Centre–State relations.
  • GST Council, NITI Aayog and higher tax devolution (41% under the 15th Finance Commission) promote cooperative and competitive federalism.
  • Tensions remain: Governors' role, central agencies, fiscal disputes and the debate over delimitation.

Conclusion: the strong Union has kept India together, but its legitimacy now rests on respecting State autonomy — a balance between unity and diversity.
free.ifm-2020-gk-3c:
Tenth ScheduleVoluntarily giving up membershipSpeaker's roleMerger exception

The 52nd Amendment (1985) added the Tenth Schedule (anti-defection law).

Grounds for disqualification

  • A member of a political party is disqualified if he or she:

- voluntarily gives up membership of the party (this can be inferred from conduct); or - votes or abstains in the House contrary to the party's direction (whip) without prior permission, and the act is not condoned by the party within 15 days.

  • An independent member is disqualified if he or she joins a political party after the election.
  • A nominated member is disqualified if he or she joins a party after six months of taking the seat.

Exceptions: a merger of the party with another, if at least two-thirds of the legislature party agree (the "split" exception of one-third was removed by the 91st Amendment, 2003); the presiding officer giving up party membership.

Decision: by the Speaker or Chairman; Kihoto Hollohan (1992) made it subject to judicial review.

Critique

  • Curbs free speech and dissent: legislators must follow the whip on every vote, weakening debate and accountability to voters.
  • Partisan and delayed decisions by Speakers; the Supreme Court in Keisham Meghachandra Singh (2020) said cases should be decided within three months.
  • Loopholes: mass "mergers" and resignations to topple governments; defectors re-elected in by-elections.
  • Strengthens party leaders over legislators and reduces inner-party democracy.

Reforms suggested: limit the law to confidence and money votes (Dinesh Goswami Committee, Law Commission), let the Election Commission or President decide cases, and set time limits.
free.ifm-2020-gk-3d:
Article 163Hung legislatureArticle 200Article 356

1. The President

The President acts on the advice of the Council of Ministers (Article 74), but has situational discretion:

  • Appointing the Prime Minister when no party or coalition has a clear majority, or when the PM dies suddenly with no obvious successor.
  • Dismissing a Council of Ministers that has lost the confidence of the Lok Sabha but refuses to resign.
  • Dissolving the Lok Sabha when the government has lost its majority.
  • Returning advice for reconsideration once (Article 74(1)).
  • Suspensive veto — returning a non-money bill once (Article 111); pocket veto — no time limit to act on a bill (used by President Zail Singh in 1986 on the Indian Post Office (Amendment) Bill).

2. The Governor

The Governor has both constitutional and situational discretion (Article 163):

  • Reserving a bill for the President's consideration (Article 200).
  • Recommending President's Rule (Article 356).
  • Special responsibilities under Article 371 (for example in Nagaland, Manipur, Sikkim, Maharashtra and Gujarat).
  • Determining royalties to district councils from mining in Sixth Schedule areas (Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, Mizoram).
  • Acting as administrator of a neighbouring Union Territory.
  • Situational: appointing the Chief Minister in a hung assembly, dismissing a ministry that has lost majority, dissolving the assembly, and seeking information from the Chief Minister (Article 167).

Judicial limits: S.R. Bommai (1994) — majority must be tested on the floor of the House; Nabam Rebia (2016) — the Governor's discretion is limited; State of Tamil Nadu v. Governor (2025) — a Governor cannot sit on bills indefinitely; the Presidential Reference opinion (November 2025) held that courts cannot fix rigid timelines for Governors and the President, but prolonged inaction can be reviewed.
free.ifm-2020-gk-4a:
Arctic amplificationSurface melt and calvingGreenland blockingSea-level rise

The Greenland Ice Sheet, the world's second-largest (about 1.7 million km²), holds enough ice to raise the sea level by about 7 metres. Satellite (GRACE) data show it has lost on average about 270 billion tonnes of ice a year since 2002, with a record loss of over 500 billion tonnes in 2019.

1. Global warming and shrinkage

  • Arctic amplification: the Arctic is warming about three to four times faster than the global average.
  • Surface melting and runoff now cause more than half of the mass loss; the melt area has expanded, even to the summit — rain fell at Greenland's Summit station in August 2021 for the first time on record.
  • Albedo feedback: melting exposes darker ice; soot, dust and algae darken the surface further, so it absorbs more heat.
  • Ocean warming: warm water undercuts glacier fronts, speeding up calving and glacier flow (Jakobshavn Isbrae).
  • Meltwater lubrication at the base speeds up ice flow.

2. Role of atmospheric circulation

  • Greenland blocking: persistent high-pressure systems over Greenland bring clear skies, strong sunlight and warm air from the south; such blocking caused extreme melt in 2012 and 2019.
  • North Atlantic Oscillation (NAO): its negative phase favours warm southerly winds over Greenland and more melting.
  • Jet stream changes: a wavier jet stream lets warm air reach the ice sheet.
  • Atmospheric rivers carry warm, moist air that brings rain and melting.

3. Consequences

  • Sea-level rise: Greenland is the largest single contributor from ice; threatening coasts worldwide, including India's.
  • Freshwater input may weaken the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC), affecting the monsoon and European climate.
  • Changes in marine ecosystems and Arctic communities.

Reducing greenhouse gas emissions is the only way to slow this loss.
free.ifm-2020-gk-4b:
Black SummerDrought and heatIndian Ocean DipoleEcological loss

The 2019–20 Australian bushfires, called the "Black Summer", were among the worst in the country's history.

1. Causes

  • Record heat and drought: 2019 was Australia's hottest and driest year on record; vegetation and soils were extremely dry.
  • Positive Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD): one of the strongest positive IODs on record in 2019 reduced rainfall over Australia.
  • Negative Southern Annular Mode: a rare sudden warming over Antarctica pushed hot, dry westerly winds over south-eastern Australia.
  • Climate change has lengthened fire seasons and increased fire weather danger.
  • Fuel load: dense eucalyptus forests rich in flammable oils.
  • Ignition: mainly dry lightning, with some human causes.
  • Fire-generated storms (pyrocumulonimbus) spread fires and created their own lightning.

2. Impact

  • Ecological: loss of habitats for koalas and many endemic species; some species pushed towards extinction; rainforests that rarely burn were damaged.
  • Health: smoke blanketed Sydney, Canberra and Melbourne; air quality was among the worst in the world.
  • Global: smoke travelled to New Zealand and South America and reached the stratosphere.
  • Economic: damage to tourism, agriculture and property worth billions of dollars.
  • Policy: a Royal Commission (2020) recommended better national coordination and preparedness.

3. Lessons

Fire-prone countries, including India (forest fires in Uttarakhand, Odisha), need early warning, fuel management, community preparedness and climate action.
free.ifm-2020-gk-4c:
Cultural landscapeFarming systemsTraditional knowledgeGIAHS

A cultural landscape is a landscape shaped by the interaction of people and nature over time. UNESCO recognises such landscapes, and the FAO lists Globally Important Agricultural Heritage Systems (GIAHS). The way people cultivate, graze, worship and live creates distinctive landscapes.

Examples

  • Apatani valley, Ziro (Arunachal Pradesh): wet rice cultivation with fish farming in terraced fields and bamboo-pine groves — a sustainable system linked to the Apatani way of life.
  • Kuttanad (Kerala): rice farming below sea level on reclaimed wetlands (a GIAHS site).
  • Koraput (Odisha): tribal farming that conserves rice and millet diversity (GIAHS).
  • Saffron fields of Pampore (Kashmir): GIAHS-recognised traditional saffron farming.
  • Jhum (shifting cultivation) in the North-East shapes hill landscapes and community life.
  • Bishnoi villages (Rajasthan): khejri trees and protected blackbuck reflect a religious commitment to conservation.
  • Banni grasslands (Kutch): Maldhari pastoralists and their cattle.
  • Ladakh's Changthang: Changpa nomads and pashmina goats.
  • Tea gardens of Darjeeling and Assam: colonial plantation landscapes.
  • Sacred groves of the Western Ghats and Meghalaya.
  • Abroad: the rice terraces of the Philippine Cordilleras (UNESCO).

Significance: such landscapes conserve biodiversity, soil and water, and traditional knowledge. Modernisation, migration and climate change threaten them, so their protection needs community support and recognition.
free.ifm-2020-gk-4d:
Arithmetic densityPhysiological densityAgricultural densityPressure on land

1. Population (arithmetic) density

  • Total population ÷ total area.
  • India: 382 persons per km² (Census 2011); highest in Bihar (1,106), lowest in Arunachal Pradesh (17).
  • Shows the general distribution of people but not their relation to productive land.

2. Physiological density

  • Total population ÷ net cultivated (arable) area.
  • India's is roughly 860 persons per km² of net sown area (2011 figures).
  • Shows the pressure of the whole population on land that produces food; very high in States with less cultivable land, such as Kerala and the hill States.

3. Agricultural density

  • Agricultural population (cultivators and agricultural labourers with their families) ÷ net cultivated area.
  • Shows the number of farm people supported by each unit of farmland; high values indicate small holdings, disguised unemployment and low productivity.

Difference: arithmetic density uses total area; physiological and agricultural densities use cultivated area. Physiological density covers everyone; agricultural density covers only farm households. Together they help plan land use, agriculture and migration.
free.ifm-2020-gk-5a:
Shock absorbersEnvironment (Protection) ActWestern GhatsCommunity reserves

1. What are ESZs or EFAs?

Eco-Sensitive Zones (ESZs) are areas around protected areas (national parks and wildlife sanctuaries) that act as "shock absorbers" or transition zones, regulating activities that could harm the protected area. Ecologically Fragile Areas (EFAs) are areas with fragile ecosystems (such as Dahanu, Matheran, Mahabaleshwar, Doon Valley and Aravallis) notified to regulate development.

What is regulated:

  • Prohibited: commercial mining, polluting industries, major hydropower projects, timber felling for commerce.
  • Regulated: hotels, construction, tree felling, roads.
  • Permitted: agriculture, organic farming, rainwater harvesting, renewable energy.

2. Statutory backing

  • Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 — Section 3 (power to restrict industries and processes) and Rule 5 of the Environment (Protection) Rules, 1986.
  • The National Wildlife Action Plan (2002–2016) and a 2002 decision of the National Board for Wildlife proposed ESZs up to 10 km around protected areas; MoEFCC guidelines (2011).
  • Supreme Court: in Goa Foundation (2006) it applied the 10-km rule where no ESZ was notified; in June 2022 it ordered a minimum 1-km ESZ around every protected area, later relaxed in April 2023.

3. Controversies

  • Western Ghats: the Gadgil Committee (2011) proposed treating the entire Ghats as ecologically sensitive; the Kasturirangan Committee (2013) limited it to about 37%; the final notification is still pending after several drafts.
  • Protests by farmers and residents in Kerala and other States after the 2022 one-kilometre order, fearing loss of land use and livelihoods.
  • Delays in notification, lack of consultation, and conflict with development projects and tourism.
  • Weak enforcement and rights of forest dwellers.

4. How community reserves differ

Examples of community reserves: Keshopur–Chhamb (Punjab) and many in Meghalaya and Nagaland. They show how conservation can be shared with people.
free.ifm-2020-gk-5b:
Mitochondrial and chloroplast DNAEndosymbiosisMaternal inheritancePlastid transformation

1. Organellar genomes

Mitochondria and chloroplasts (plastids) have their own DNA, separate from the nuclear genome.

  • Circular, small and without histones, like bacterial DNA.
  • Human mitochondrial DNA: about 16,569 base pairs, 37 genes. Chloroplast DNA: about 120–160 kb, around 100–130 genes for photosynthesis and protein synthesis.
  • Many copies per cell — a leaf cell may have thousands of plastid genome copies.
  • They have their own 70S ribosomes and machinery, though most organelle proteins are now coded by the nucleus.
  • Inheritance is usually maternal (uniparental) in animals and most flowering plants.

2. Link with the endosymbiotic theory

Yes. The endosymbiotic theory (popularised by Lynn Margulis, 1967) says that mitochondria came from aerobic alpha-proteobacteria and chloroplasts from cyanobacteria that were engulfed by an ancestral cell and became permanent partners. Evidence:

  • Own circular DNA similar to bacteria;
  • 70S ribosomes and sensitivity to bacterial antibiotics;
  • Double membranes;
  • Division by binary fission;
  • DNA sequences closely related to bacteria;
  • Gene transfer from organelles to the nucleus over evolution.

3. Organellar genomes for transgene containment

A major worry about GM crops is gene flow — transgenes escaping through pollen to wild relatives or non-GM crops. Inserting transgenes into the chloroplast genome (plastid transformation) helps because:

  • Maternal inheritance: in most crops, chloroplasts are not transmitted through pollen, so the transgene does not spread by pollination.
  • High expression: thousands of genome copies per cell produce large amounts of protein (useful for insect resistance, vaccines and bio-pharmaceuticals).
  • Precise insertion by homologous recombination; no gene silencing or position effects.
  • Several genes can be inserted together in operons.

Limitations: occasional paternal leakage in some species, and difficulty in transforming chloroplasts of cereals like rice and wheat. Successful examples include tobacco, tomato and lettuce.
free.ifm-2020-gk-5c:
Nano-fertilisersNano-pesticidesNano-sensorsPrecision farming

Nanotechnology uses materials at the scale of 1–100 nanometres, where they show special properties such as high surface area and reactivity.

Uses in agriculture

  • Nano-fertilisers: slow, targeted release of nutrients reduces losses; for example IFFCO's Nano Urea (2021) and Nano DAP (2023), though their field performance is still debated.
  • Nano-pesticides and herbicides: encapsulation releases chemicals slowly and in smaller doses.
  • Nano-sensors: detect soil moisture, nutrients, pathogens and pesticide residues for precision farming.
  • Seed treatment to improve germination and protect seeds.
  • Post-harvest: nano-coatings and packaging extend shelf life.
  • Water purification and soil remediation.

Prominent nanoparticles

Concerns: toxicity to soil organisms and humans, accumulation in food chains, high cost and the need for clear regulation (India issued guidelines for nano-agri inputs in 2020).
free.ifm-2020-gk-5d:
ArabidopsisDrosophilaMouseConserved genes

Model organisms are species studied in depth to understand biological processes that apply to many other organisms, including humans.

Three model organisms

Others include E. coli, yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae, about 12 Mb, the first eukaryote sequenced in 1996), the nematode C. elegans and zebrafish.

Advantages of using model organisms

  • Short life cycle and many offspring — fast experiments across generations.
  • Small size, easy and cheap to grow.
  • Simple, well-mapped genomes and powerful genetic tools.
  • Conserved genes — findings apply to humans and crops (genes for development, ageing, cancer).
  • Ethical: experiments not possible on humans.
  • Shared resources: mutant stocks and databases worldwide.

Specialities of their genomes: small size with little repetitive DNA (Arabidopsis), few chromosomes (Drosophila), and close similarity to humans (mouse), which together make genetic analysis easier.
free.ifm-2020-gk-6a:
Satellite constellationTrilaterationFour satellitesNavIC

GPS (Global Positioning System) is a satellite navigation system owned by the United States, which gives position, speed and time anywhere on Earth, in all weather.

1. Components

  • Space segment: about 31 operational satellites in six orbital planes at about 20,200 km altitude, each orbiting twice a day.
  • Control segment: ground stations that monitor and correct satellite orbits and clocks.
  • User segment: GPS receivers in phones, vehicles and aircraft.

2. How it works

  • Each satellite carries atomic clocks and continuously broadcasts its position and the exact time.
  • The receiver measures the time taken by signals to arrive and calculates the distance (distance = speed of light × time).
  • Using distances from several satellites, it finds its position by trilateration — the point where the spheres around each satellite intersect.
  • Corrections for the atmosphere and for relativity (satellite clocks gain about 38 microseconds a day) are applied.

3. Minimum number of satellites: four

  • Three satellites would be enough to find latitude, longitude and altitude if the receiver's clock were perfect.
  • But receivers have cheap clocks; even a tiny clock error causes large distance errors (1 microsecond = 300 m).
  • A fourth satellite solves for the receiver's clock error — four unknowns (x, y, z and time) need four equations.
  • More satellites improve accuracy.

4. Uses and Indian system

Navigation, mapping, disaster management, agriculture, banking time stamps and defence. India has its own regional system, NavIC (IRNSS), with seven satellites covering India and 1,500 km around it; it is being upgraded with the NVS series of satellites. Other global systems are Russia's GLONASS, Europe's Galileo and China's BeiDou.
free.ifm-2020-gk-6b:
Magnetic Resonance ImagingProton spinRadiofrequency pulsesNo ionising radiation

MRI stands for Magnetic Resonance Imaging.

Physics behind it

  • The body is mostly water, rich in hydrogen nuclei (protons), which behave like tiny magnets.
  • A strong magnetic field (usually 1.5–3 tesla) aligns these protons.
  • A radiofrequency pulse at the resonance (Larmor) frequency knocks them out of alignment.
  • When the pulse stops, protons relax back, emitting radio signals; different tissues relax at different rates (T1 and T2 relaxation).
  • Gradient coils locate the signals in space, and a computer builds images using Fourier transforms.
  • Paul Lauterbur and Peter Mansfield received the Nobel Prize (2003) for developing MRI.

Advantages over X-ray and CT scans

  • No ionising radiation, so it is safer, especially for children and pregnant women (with caution).
  • Excellent soft-tissue contrast — brain, spinal cord, muscles, ligaments, cartilage and tumours.
  • Images in any plane without moving the patient.
  • Functional MRI shows brain activity; MR angiography shows blood vessels, often without contrast dye.

Limitations: costly, slow, noisy and confined; not suitable for patients with some pacemakers or metal implants; CT remains better for bones, lungs and emergencies.
free.ifm-2020-gk-6c:
ElectrolysisZero emissionsPEM fuel cellGreen Hydrogen Mission

1. Hydrogen energy

Hydrogen is an energy carrier — it stores energy that is released when it is burned or used in a fuel cell. It has a very high energy content per kilogram (about three times that of petrol), and its use produces only water.

2. Why it is called "green"

Hydrogen is "green" when produced by electrolysis of water using renewable electricity (solar, wind). Then the whole chain emits almost no greenhouse gases.

Today most hydrogen is grey; green hydrogen can decarbonise steel, fertiliser, refineries, shipping and heavy transport.

3. Fuel cell technology

A fuel cell converts hydrogen's chemical energy directly into electricity, without burning it.

Proton Exchange Membrane (PEM) fuel cell:

  • At the anode, a platinum catalyst splits hydrogen into protons and electrons: H₂ → 2H⁺ + 2e⁻.
  • Electrons flow through an external circuit — this is the electric current.
  • Protons pass through the membrane to the cathode.
  • At the cathode, oxygen combines with protons and electrons to form water: O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ → 2H₂O.
  • Cells are stacked to get the required power; efficiency is about 40–60%, higher than engines.

Uses: fuel-cell cars and buses, trucks, trains, backup power and drones.

4. India's efforts

The National Green Hydrogen Mission (2023), with about ₹19,744 crore, targets 5 million tonnes of green hydrogen a year by 2030, with incentives for electrolysers (SIGHT programme), green hydrogen hubs, and hydrogen buses and trains.

Challenges: high cost, storage and transport (it is light and leaks easily), safety, and the need for cheap renewable power and water.
free.ifm-2020-gk-6d:
CERN27 km ringHiggs bosonStandard Model

Large Hadron Collider (LHC)

  • The world's largest and most powerful particle accelerator, built by CERN near Geneva on the Swiss–French border.
  • A 27-km ring, about 100 m underground, with superconducting magnets cooled to –271 °C (1.9 K).
  • It accelerates protons (and heavy ions) to nearly the speed of light and smashes them together; Run 3, since 2022, has collisions at 13.6 TeV.
  • Major detectors: ATLAS, CMS, ALICE and LHCb.
  • A High-Luminosity LHC upgrade is planned to increase collisions several times.
  • India is an Associate Member of CERN (since 2017), and Indian scientists work on CMS and ALICE.

Why the Higgs boson is important

  • Discovered at the LHC in 2012; Peter Higgs and François Englert won the Nobel Prize in Physics (2013).
  • It is the particle of the Higgs field, which gives mass to fundamental particles such as electrons and quarks. Without it, particles would be massless and atoms could not form.
  • It completed the Standard Model of particle physics.
  • Studying its properties helps test theories beyond the Standard Model — dark matter, supersymmetry and the stability of the universe.
  • It is called a "boson" after the Indian physicist Satyendra Nath Bose.
free.ifm-2021-ge-1a:
Segregation at sourceCircular economyLegacy landfillsSwachh Bharat Mission

Our Urban Survival Depends upon Efficient Waste Management

In March 2023, a fire at the Brahmapuram dumpsite in Kochi burned for nearly two weeks, covering the city in toxic smoke. Delhi's Ghazipur landfill has grown so high that it is jokingly compared to the Qutub Minar, and fires and collapses there have killed people. These are not isolated accidents. They are warnings that our cities are being buried under their own waste. As India urbanises rapidly, how we manage waste will decide whether our cities remain liveable.

The scale of the problem

Indian cities generate about 1.6 lakh tonnes of municipal solid waste every day, and the amount is rising with incomes and consumption. Though collection has improved greatly, a large share is still dumped without treatment in open landfills. Add to this sewage, plastic waste, construction and demolition debris, biomedical waste and fast-growing electronic waste, and the challenge becomes enormous. Most cities treat only a fraction of their sewage, which flows into rivers and lakes.

Why waste threatens urban survival

First, public health. Uncollected garbage breeds flies, mosquitoes and rats, spreading dengue, malaria, cholera and typhoid. Burning waste releases toxic dioxins and fine particles that worsen the air pollution that already shortens lives in Indian cities.

Second, water and soil pollution. Leachate from landfills seeps into groundwater, and untreated sewage turns rivers like the Yamuna into drains.

Third, urban flooding. Plastic bags and debris choke drains, so even moderate rain floods streets, as Mumbai, Chennai and Bengaluru have seen.

Fourth, climate change. Rotting organic waste in landfills produces methane, a powerful greenhouse gas, and landfill fires add more emissions.

Fifth, loss of land and resources. Landfills occupy valuable land, and materials that could be recycled — plastic, metal, paper, organic matter — are wasted.

Finally, social injustice. Lakhs of waste-pickers, often women and children, work without protection or recognition, exposed to disease and danger.

Signs of hope

The Swachh Bharat Mission (Urban), launched in 2014, and its second phase from 2021 aim at garbage-free cities, segregation at source, scientific processing and the remediation of legacy dumpsites. The Solid Waste Management Rules, 2016 and the Plastic Waste Management Rules with extended producer responsibility set clear duties for citizens, municipalities and producers. Indore, repeatedly ranked India's cleanest city in the Swachh Survekshan, shows what is possible: near-total segregation into wet and dry waste, door-to-door collection, composting, a bio-CNG plant that runs city buses, and the clearing of its old dumpsite. Cities such as Ambikapur have built models around women's self-help groups managing waste.

What efficient waste management requires

  • Segregation at source: households and businesses must separate wet, dry and hazardous waste — the foundation of everything else.
  • Reduce and reuse: cutting single-use plastics, encouraging refill and repair, and the "LiFE" lifestyle.
  • Decentralised processing: composting and biogas at the level of homes, colonies and markets.
  • Recycling and the circular economy: material recovery facilities, waste-to-wealth enterprises and extended producer responsibility.
  • Integrating waste-pickers into the formal system with identity cards, safety gear and fair pay.
  • Scientific landfills only for inert residue, and biomining of old dumpsites.
  • Sewage treatment and reuse of treated water.
  • Financing and governance: user charges, capable municipal bodies and public–private partnerships.
  • Citizen behaviour: awareness, penalties for littering and community ownership.

Conclusion

A city is like a living body: if it cannot get rid of its waste, it sickens and dies. Our urban future depends not only on metro lines and flyovers but on what happens to the garbage we throw away each morning. If we treat waste as a resource rather than a nuisance, we can make our cities cleaner, healthier and more sustainable. Efficient waste management is not a municipal chore; it is a condition of urban survival.
free.ifm-2021-ge-1b:
LibertyDutyHarm principleFundamental Duties

Paradox of Freedom and Responsibility

Freedom is the most cherished of human values. Revolutions have been fought for it, and constitutions are written to protect it. Yet the more freedom we have, the more responsibility we must carry. This is the paradox: freedom seems to mean doing what we like, but true freedom can survive only when it is limited by responsibility.

The meaning of freedom

Freedom has two faces. Negative freedom is freedom from interference — no one should stop me from speaking, believing or moving. Positive freedom is freedom to — the ability to shape one's own life, which needs education, health and opportunity. Both are precious. India's Constitution guarantees freedom of speech, movement, religion and occupation, and the Supreme Court has expanded the right to life and personal liberty to include dignity and privacy.

Why freedom needs responsibility

First, my freedom ends where another's begins. John Stuart Mill's harm principle holds that people may do as they wish so long as they do not harm others. Freedom of speech does not include the freedom to spread hatred or false rumours that incite violence. That is why Article 19(2) allows reasonable restrictions in the interests of public order, decency and the rights of others.

Second, freedom without responsibility destroys itself. If every driver ignored traffic rules in the name of freedom, no one would be able to drive safely. If citizens refused to pay taxes or obey laws, the State that protects their liberty would collapse. Anarchy leads not to freedom but to the rule of the strongest.

Third, freedom brings the burden of choice. The philosopher Jean-Paul Sartre said that human beings are "condemned to be free": since we choose our actions, we are responsible for them and cannot blame fate or others. The psychiatrist Viktor Frankl, who survived Nazi concentration camps, once suggested that America's Statue of Liberty on the East Coast should be balanced by a Statue of Responsibility on the West Coast.

The paradox in modern life

Social media has given every person a megaphone. This has empowered ordinary citizens to expose injustice and share ideas. But the same freedom has spread fake news, cyberbullying and hate, sometimes leading to mob violence. Technology companies enjoy freedom to innovate, but they must take responsibility for privacy and the harm caused by their platforms. Economic freedom has created wealth, but without responsibility towards workers and the environment, it has also caused inequality and pollution. Even personal freedom — to eat, drink or travel as we like — affects public health and the planet.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, the paradox became visible to all. The freedom to move about and gather had to be balanced against the responsibility to protect the vulnerable from infection.

The Indian view

Indian thought has long linked rights with duties. The idea of dharma stresses duty to family, society and nature. Mahatma Gandhi argued that rights flow from duties well performed. The Fundamental Duties (Article 51A), added by the 42nd Amendment, remind citizens to respect the Constitution, promote harmony, protect the environment and develop a scientific temper.

Resolving the paradox

The paradox dissolves when we see freedom and responsibility not as opposites but as two sides of the same coin. Responsibility is the price of freedom, and freedom is the reward of responsibility. Children are given more freedom as they show more responsibility; nations that act responsibly earn the trust and freedom of the international community. A free press remains free when it is responsible; a free market stays free when it is fair.

This requires:

  • Education that teaches critical thinking and ethics, not merely rights;
  • Laws that protect liberty while restraining harm;
  • Institutions that hold the powerful accountable;
  • Personal self-discipline — what Indian philosophy calls atma-sanyam.

Conclusion

Freedom is not a licence to do anything; it is the opportunity to do what is right. As citizens of a democracy, we are free because we accept the responsibility of respecting the freedom of others. The true test of a free society is not how much people can do as they please, but how willingly they choose to do what is just.
free.ifm-2021-ge-1c:
Zoonotic spilloverPreparednessInequalityOne Health

COVID-19: A Natural Calamity or a Man-Made Disaster

In early 2020, a new coronavirus, SARS-CoV-2, spread from Wuhan in China across the world. Within months, cities fell silent, hospitals overflowed and economies collapsed. The World Health Organization (WHO) declared a pandemic in March 2020, and by the time it ended the global health emergency in May 2023, about seven million deaths had been officially reported — and the WHO estimates that the true number of excess deaths was far higher. Was this a natural calamity, like an earthquake, or a disaster created by human beings? The honest answer is that it was both: a natural hazard turned into a catastrophe by human choices.

The natural element

Viruses are part of nature. They mutate constantly, and many jump from animals to humans — a process called zoonotic spillover. HIV, Ebola, SARS, MERS and Nipah all came from animals. Most scientists believe SARS-CoV-2 also originated in bats and reached humans, possibly through an intermediate animal at a wildlife market. In this sense, COVID-19 resembled earlier pandemics such as the 1918 influenza, which no human planned. The question of its exact origin remains debated; the WHO's advisory group reported in 2025 that the available evidence points mainly to natural spillover, but that a laboratory-related origin cannot be ruled out because key data have not been shared.

The human element

Even if the virus came from nature, human actions explain why it became so deadly.

First, we created the conditions for spillover. Deforestation, mining, wildlife trade and intensive farming bring humans into close contact with wild animals. Scientists had warned for years that a new pandemic was likely.

Second, globalisation spread it at lightning speed. Air travel carried the virus to every continent within weeks.

Third, early warnings were delayed or ignored. Information sharing in the first weeks was slow, and many countries were late to act.

Fourth, health systems were unprepared. Years of low investment in public health left hospitals short of beds, oxygen, ventilators and staff. India's devastating second wave in 2021, with shortages of oxygen and hospital beds, showed this painfully.

Fifth, inequality magnified the suffering. Migrant workers walked hundreds of kilometres home during the lockdown; the poor lost jobs and income; children without internet lost two years of schooling. Rich countries stocked vaccines while poorer nations waited — a failure of global solidarity that prolonged the pandemic.

Finally, misinformation about masks, vaccines and false cures cost lives.

What humanity did right

The pandemic also showed human ingenuity. Vaccines were developed in under a year — an unprecedented scientific achievement. India produced and administered over two billion doses through the CoWIN platform, and supplied vaccines to many countries under its Vaccine Maitri initiative. Health workers, scientists and volunteers showed extraordinary courage and compassion.

Lessons for the future

  • One Health: human, animal and environmental health are linked; we must protect forests, regulate wildlife trade and monitor animal diseases.
  • Strong public health systems, with surveillance, laboratories and trained staff.
  • Global cooperation: the WHO's member states adopted a Pandemic Agreement in 2025 to improve preparedness and fair access to vaccines and medicines.
  • Transparency and quick sharing of data.
  • Social protection for the poor during crises.

Conclusion

Nature supplied the virus, but human beings shaped the disaster — through how we treat the environment, how we prepare, how we govern and how we share. To call COVID-19 merely a natural calamity would excuse us from responsibility; to call it purely man-made would ignore the power of nature. The real lesson is that in an interconnected world, our choices decide whether a natural hazard becomes a human catastrophe. The next pandemic is a question of when, not if. Whether it becomes another disaster depends on us.
free.ifm-2021-ge-1d:
Planetary boundariesAir and water pollutionLand degradationSustainable development

Perils of Ecodegradation

The Earth has supported human civilisation for thousands of years with clean air, fertile soil, fresh water and a stable climate. But in barely two centuries of industrial growth, we have damaged these life-support systems more than in all previous history. Ecodegradation — the deterioration of the environment through pollution, deforestation, overuse of resources and climate change — is no longer a distant threat. It is a present danger to our health, economy and survival.

The many faces of ecodegradation

  • Air pollution: Indian cities regularly rank among the most polluted in the world. Studies have linked air pollution to well over a million premature deaths a year in India.
  • Water crisis: rivers such as the Yamuna carry untreated sewage and industrial waste; groundwater is falling rapidly in Punjab, Haryana and Rajasthan; many cities face severe water shortages in summer.
  • Land degradation: about 30% of India's land is degraded by erosion, salinity and desertification.
  • Deforestation and biodiversity loss: forests are cleared for mining, roads and farms; species such as the Great Indian Bustard are close to extinction.
  • Climate change: heat waves, erratic monsoons, floods, cyclones and melting glaciers are becoming more frequent and intense.
  • Plastic and chemical pollution in soil, rivers and oceans.

Scientists studying planetary boundaries — the safe limits of Earth systems — found in 2023 that six of nine boundaries had already been crossed.

The perils

First, health. Polluted air and water cause respiratory disease, heart disease, cancer and diarrhoea. Heat waves kill the elderly and outdoor workers.

Second, food and water security. Degraded soils, falling groundwater, pollinator decline and climate extremes threaten harvests in a country where nearly half the workforce depends on farming.

Third, disasters. The destruction of forests, wetlands and mangroves removes natural protection. The Kedarnath floods (2013), Kerala floods (2018), Joshimath's sinking (2023) and Wayanad landslides (2024) showed how unplanned development in fragile areas turns rain into catastrophe.

Fourth, economic loss. Pollution and disasters cost India several percent of GDP every year through illness, lost productivity and damage.

Fifth, social injustice. The poor, tribal communities, women and children suffer most because they depend directly on natural resources and cannot buy their way out of pollution. Ecodegradation can also cause conflict over water and land, and climate migration.

Finally, inter-generational injustice. We are borrowing the Earth from our children and returning it damaged.

Causes

The root causes are an economic model that values short-term growth over long-term sustainability, unplanned urbanisation, overconsumption by the rich, poverty that forces overuse of resources by the poor, weak enforcement of laws and a lack of environmental awareness.

The way forward

  • Green growth: renewable energy, energy efficiency and clean transport — India's non-fossil power capacity has already crossed half of its total.
  • Protecting ecosystems: forests, wetlands, grasslands and coasts, with the participation of local communities.
  • Strong enforcement of environmental laws and honest environmental impact assessments.
  • Circular economy: reduce, reuse and recycle; extended producer responsibility.
  • Sustainable agriculture: water-efficient irrigation, natural farming, crop diversification.
  • Climate adaptation: resilient infrastructure, early warnings and disaster planning.
  • Lifestyle change: Mission LiFE asks citizens to consume mindfully and avoid waste.
  • Education that builds ecological responsibility from childhood.

Conclusion

Mahatma Gandhi said that the Earth provides enough to satisfy every man's needs, but not every man's greed. Ecodegradation is the result of forgetting this truth. The environment is not a resource to be exploited endlessly but the very foundation of life. If we continue to degrade it, no economic growth will be able to save us; if we protect it, it will continue to sustain us for generations to come. The choice is ours, and the time to make it is now.

ABC XYZ Locality

16 November 2021

The Editor XYZ (an English daily) City

Subject: Refusal by police to register an FIR for vehicle theft

Sir/Madam,

Through the columns of your esteemed newspaper, I wish to draw the attention of the authorities to the refusal of the Station House Officer (SHO) of our local police station to register a First Information Report (FIR) in a case of vehicle theft.

Last week, my motorcycle was stolen from outside my house at night. The next morning I went to the police station with the registration papers and details of the theft. The SHO refused to register an FIR, asked me to "search for a few days" and offered only to take a written complaint without any receipt. Several neighbours have had similar experiences. Without an FIR, a vehicle owner cannot claim insurance, and the stolen vehicle may be misused for crimes.

Theft is a cognizable offence. The Supreme Court in Lalita Kumari v. Government of Uttar Pradesh (2013) made it mandatory for the police to register an FIR when information discloses a cognizable offence. The law also allows complaints to be filed online (e-FIR) and at any police station (zero FIR). Refusal to register FIRs is often done to show lower crime figures, but it denies justice to citizens and encourages criminals.

Through your newspaper, I request the senior police officers to: 1. take action against officers who refuse to register FIRs; 2. ensure that e-FIR facilities for vehicle theft are widely publicised and functional; 3. increase night patrolling in our area, where thefts have risen.

I hope this letter will prompt the authorities to act.

Yours faithfully, ABC

Local NGO Leads the Way in Adolescent Mental Health

By ABC

At a time when stress, anxiety and depression among young people are rising, a local non-governmental organisation, XYZ, has emerged as a lifeline for adolescents and teenagers in our district.

Founded five years ago by a group of psychologists, teachers and social workers, XYZ works with schools, colleges and families. Its volunteers say that examination pressure, competition, family conflicts, bullying, excessive screen use and the isolation of the pandemic years have affected the mental health of many teenagers, while stigma prevents them from seeking help.

The NGO runs free counselling centres and a telephone helpline, and holds weekly sessions in more than thirty schools. Trained counsellors teach students about emotions, stress management, healthy sleep and safe internet use. Peer educators — older students trained by the NGO — encourage classmates to speak up. Teachers and parents are trained to recognise warning signs such as withdrawal, sudden changes in behaviour and falling grades, and to respond with empathy rather than punishment.

The NGO also refers serious cases to the district hospital's psychiatric unit and links families with the Government's Tele-MANAS helpline (14416). It organises sports, art and music activities to help young people express themselves.

"Earlier, no one in my class talked about feeling low. Now we know it is okay to ask for help," said a class XI student.

The district education officer praised the NGO's work and said the department plans to extend its programme to all government schools. The NGO's main challenges are a shortage of trained counsellors and funds.

Change as remedyTired mindNew interestsHobbies

People who bear heavy responsibilities for long are offered many remedies for worry and mental strain — exercise or rest, travel or retreat, solitude or gaiety. Each may suit some temperament, but their common element is change.

Change is the master key. Like a coat's elbows, a part of the mind wears out through constant use; but, unlike a coat, a tired mind can be refreshed by using its other parts. Mere rest is not enough, for the mind goes on weighing or worrying. Relief comes only when a new interest calls fresh cells into activity. Worry is an emotional spasm in which the mind clings to something; arguing with it is futile. One can only gently slip in another interest, which, if well chosen, loosens the grip and starts recovery. Hence cultivating hobbies is vital for a public man, but such interests must be nurtured patiently over years to be ready when needed.

(154 words)
free.ifm-2021-ge-4a: The Antapala was an officer who collected small road tolls from merchants travelling from place to place. He was responsible for the upkeep of the road and its safety. According to the Arthasastra, these tolls worked as a kind of insurance: the Antapala was expected to make good any loss that merchants suffered from thieves.
free.ifm-2021-ge-4b: According to the Arthasastra, essential goods such as grain, oil, sugar, pots and cheap textiles were to be taxed at one-twentieth (5%) of their value, while other goods were taxed at rates ranging from one-fifteenth to one-fifth of their value. In addition, craftsmen were expected to give one or two days' work a month to the king, a labour tax often converted into a tax on average daily earnings.
free.ifm-2021-ge-4c: Land records were kept by local officers. The Jataka stories call them "holders of the surveyor's cord" (rajjugahaka), probably the same as the rajjukas of Ashoka's inscriptions, and Megasthenes says the land was thoroughly surveyed. Land was transferred to a new owner only after checking the local land records, and this fact, with the names of the record keepers who certified it, was often noted in copper-plate title deeds. Well-organised kingdoms kept full, up-to-date ownership records like England's Domesday Book, but these were written on perishable materials and have been lost.
free.ifm-2021-ge-4d: Tax defaulters faced harsh punishment. South Indian inscriptions mention whole village councils being imprisoned for failing to pay tax, and the looting of a village as punishment for tax default — an action that the Chola emperor Rajaraja I upheld when villagers appealed. A defaulting taxpayer was also liable to eviction, although he might be given a year's grace or more in genuine need. Harsh exactions sometimes drove peasants to leave their villages en masse.

SuvarnabhumiFunan, Champa, KambujaAngkor WatRamayana traditions

From the early centuries CE, Indian merchants, Brahmanas and Buddhist monks travelled to Suvarnabhumi (South-East Asia). Their influence spread mainly through trade and voluntary cultural exchange, not conquest, and local rulers adopted Indian ideas to strengthen their kingship.

1. Indianised kingdoms

  • Funan (lower Mekong, 1st–6th century): legend says it was founded by a Brahmana, Kaundinya, who married a local Naga princess.
  • Champa (central Vietnam): Sanskrit inscriptions and the Shaiva temple complex of My Son.
  • Kambuja (Khmer Empire, Cambodia): Jayavarman II (802 CE) began the devaraja cult; Angkor Wat, built by Suryavarman II in the 12th century as a Vishnu temple, is the largest religious monument in the world; Angkor Thom and the Bayon of Jayavarman VII are Buddhist.
  • Dvaravati (Mon, Thailand), Pyu and Pagan (Myanmar — Ananda temple), and Vat Phou in Laos.

2. Religion

  • Shaivism and Vaishnavism under royal patronage; temples of Shiva and Vishnu.
  • Mahayana, and later Theravada Buddhism (via Sri Lanka), which remains the main religion of Myanmar, Thailand, Laos and Cambodia.

3. Language and script

  • Sanskrit was the language of royal inscriptions (the Vo Canh inscription in Vietnam is among the oldest).
  • The Pallava Grantha script of south India gave rise to the Khmer, Thai, Lao, Burmese and Mon scripts.
  • Thai and Khmer have many Sanskrit and Pali words (for example Rama, Siam, Ayutthaya from Ayodhya).

4. Literature and performing arts

  • The Ramayana became part of local culture: Reamker (Cambodia), Ramakien (Thailand), Phra Lak Phra Lam (Laos); Thai kings took the title Rama.
  • The Mahabharata, Jataka tales and Puranic stories appear in sculpture and shadow plays; classical dances drew on Indian forms.

5. Polity, law and architecture

  • Ideas of kingship, the Manusmriti-based law codes, the use of Brahmana priests in court rituals (the Thai royal court still keeps them).
  • Temple architecture inspired by Indian styles, adapted to local forms.

Assessment: Indian culture was adapted, not imposed — local traditions blended with Indian ideas. Today the shared heritage supports India's Act East Policy: the Archaeological Survey of India has helped restore Angkor Wat, Ta Prohm, My Son and Vat Phou, and the Mekong–Ganga Cooperation (2000) builds on these links.

Chausa and KannaujSarkars and parganasLand revenueGrand Trunk Road

Sher Shah Suri (r. 1540–1545) ruled for only five years, but he is remembered both as a great general and as one of medieval India's finest administrators.

1. Military genius — comparable to Babur

  • Defeated Humayun at Chausa (1539) and Kannauj/Bilgram (1540), driving the Mughals out of India.
  • Brilliant use of strategy, surprise and diplomacy: he took the Rohtas fort by a ruse and timed the Chausa attack for when Humayun's camp was unprepared.
  • Conquered Malwa, Raisen, Multan, Sindh and fought the Rajputs of Marwar at Sammel (1544), a hard-won victory after which he remarked that he had nearly lost the empire of Hindustan for a handful of millet.
  • Died at Kalinjar (1545) while besieging it.
  • Army reforms: a large standing army under his direct control; dagh (branding of horses) and huliya (descriptive rolls of soldiers) to stop fraud, following Alauddin Khalji.

Like Babur (Panipat 1526, Khanwa 1527, Ghaghra 1529), he was a master of battlefield tactics; but his success came mostly through planning and diplomacy rather than new weapons such as Babur's artillery.

2. Administrative genius — forerunner of Akbar

  • Provincial structure: empire divided into sarkars and parganas, with officials like the shiqdar-i-shiqdaran (law and order) and munshif-i-munshifan (revenue and justice).
  • Land revenue: measurement of land with the jarib; crop rates (rai); the state's share fixed at one-third of produce; patta (title deed) and qabuliyat (agreement) given to peasants; relief for crop failure.
  • Currency: the silver rupiya (about 178 grains) and copper dam — the basis of later currency.
  • Communication and trade: the Sarak-i-Azam (Grand Trunk Road) from Sonargaon to Peshawar, and other roads; sarais along roads that served as dak (postal) stations and markets; abolition of internal customs duties.
  • Law and order: village headmen (muqaddams) held responsible for crimes in their area.
  • Justice: strict and impartial.

3. Comparison with Akbar

Raja Todar Mal, who served Sher Shah, later framed Akbar's revenue system. Akbar's administration thus built on Sher Shah's foundations.

Conclusion: although his reign was brief and his dynasty ended soon after, Sher Shah's achievements in war and administration justify comparisons with both Babur and Akbar. His tomb at Sasaram is a reminder of his greatness.

DevanampiyaPaternal kingshipSelf-restraintDhamma

Ashoka called himself Devanampiya Piyadasi ("beloved of the gods, of gracious appearance"), but he did not claim divinity. For him, the sacredness of kingship lay in ruling through moral example.

How he ruled by example

  • Remorse for violence: in Rock Edict XIII he publicly expressed regret for the suffering caused by the Kalinga war — a rare confession by a ruler — and gave up conquest by arms for conquest by Dhamma.
  • Paternal kingship: "All men are my children" (Kalinga Separate Edict); he saw his duty as the welfare and happiness of all beings.
  • Personal conduct: he gave up royal hunting, reduced meat in the royal kitchen, and replaced pleasure tours with Dhamma yatras to meet people.
  • Accessibility: officials could report to him at any time, whether he was eating or in his private quarters (Rock Edict VI).
  • Tolerance: he honoured all sects and asked people to respect others' faiths (Rock Edict XII).
  • Public welfare: hospitals for people and animals, wells and shade trees.
  • Teaching by edicts: he inscribed his moral messages on rocks and pillars in local languages.

Significance: Ashoka made morality the basis of political legitimacy. His idea of ethical rule influenced later Indian thought — the Ashokan lion capital and the Dharma Chakra are national symbols today.

Dadabhai Naoroji (1825–1917), called the "Grand Old Man of India", was a leading figure of the Moderate phase of the national movement.

Contributions (1885–1905)

  • Economic critique — the drain theory: in Poverty and Un-British Rule in India (1901) and earlier papers, he showed that Britain drained India's wealth through Home Charges, salaries, pensions and profits. He estimated India's per-capita income at about ₹20 a year (1867-68). This became the most powerful argument against colonial rule.
  • Founding the Congress: he was among the founders of the INC and was its president three times — 1886, 1893 and 1906. At Calcutta (1906) he declared Swaraj as the goal.
  • Voice in Britain: he was elected to the British House of Commons in 1892 from Finsbury Central — the first Indian MP — and raised Indian issues there.
  • Welby Commission (1895–97): as a member of the Royal Commission on Indian Expenditure, he exposed unfair costs imposed on India.
  • Demands: simultaneous civil service examinations in India and England, more Indians in administration, reduction of military expenditure.
  • Organisations and press: the East India Association (1866) in London, the newspaper Rast Goftar.
  • Mentor: he inspired Gokhale, Gandhi and Tilak.

His economic nationalism gave the freedom struggle an intellectual foundation and prepared the ground for the demand for self-rule.

Over-leveraged firmsNPA-laden banksNARCLIDRCL

Twin balance sheet (TBS) problem

The Economic Survey 2016-17 described India's twin balance sheet problem: two balance sheets were stressed at the same time —

  • Over-leveraged corporates: companies in infrastructure, power, steel and telecom borrowed heavily during the 2000s boom; when projects were delayed and demand fell, they could not repay.
  • Banks with bad loans: banks, especially public sector banks, were burdened with non-performing assets (NPAs). Gross NPAs of scheduled commercial banks peaked at over 11% in 2018.

The result was low investment, weak credit growth and slow economic growth.

How a State-sponsored bad bank deals with it

The Budget 2021-22 announced a bad bank, set up as the National Asset Reconstruction Company Ltd (NARCL), with the India Debt Resolution Company Ltd (IDRCL) to manage and resolve the assets. In September 2021, the Government guaranteed security receipts worth up to ₹30,600 crore.

  • Transfers bad loans out of banks: NARCL buys large stressed loans (above ₹500 crore) from banks.
  • Payment structure: 15% in cash and 85% in security receipts (SRs), backed by a government guarantee in case recovery falls short.
  • Aggregation: loans from many banks to the same borrower are consolidated, making resolution faster.
  • Resolution: IDRCL, with professional managers, restructures, sells or revives the assets.
  • Cleaner bank balance sheets: banks free up capital and management time and can lend more.

Other steps that helped: the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (2016), recapitalisation of public sector banks, the RBI's asset quality review, and bank mergers. Gross NPAs fell to about 2.3% by March 2025.

Concerns: moral hazard, slow acquisition of assets by NARCL, the risk of under-valuation, and the cost to taxpayers if recoveries are poor. Better credit appraisal and governance in banks are essential to prevent a repeat.

The 26th Conference of the Parties (COP26) to the UNFCCC was held at Glasgow in November 2021. Its outcome, the Glasgow Climate Pact, aimed to speed up action under the Paris Agreement (2015).

1. Actions on temperature control

  • Keep 1.5 °C within reach: recognised that limiting warming to 1.5 °C requires cutting global CO2 emissions by 45% by 2030 relative to 2010 and reaching net zero around mid-century.
  • Stronger NDCs: asked countries to revisit and strengthen their 2030 targets by the end of 2022, rather than waiting five years.
  • Coal and fossil fuel subsidies: for the first time a COP text called for the phase-down of unabated coal power and the phase-out of inefficient fossil fuel subsidies (the language changed from "phase-out" to "phase-down" at India's intervention).
  • Methane and forests: the Global Methane Pledge (30% cut by 2030 from 2020 levels) and the Glasgow Leaders' Declaration on Forests (halt deforestation by 2030).
  • Paris Rulebook completed: rules for carbon markets (Article 6), a common reporting framework, and common timeframes for NDCs.
  • India's "Panchamrit": 500 GW non-fossil capacity by 2030, 50% of energy needs from renewables by 2030, cut projected emissions by one billion tonnes by 2030, reduce the carbon intensity of the economy by 45%, and net zero by 2070.

2. Transfer of funds from developed to developing countries

  • $100 billion a year: expressed regret that developed countries missed the goal of mobilising $100 billion a year by 2020 and urged them to deliver it urgently through 2025.
  • Adaptation finance: urged developed countries to at least double adaptation finance by 2025 from 2019 levels.
  • New finance goal: began a process to set a new collective quantified goal for after 2025 (later fixed at COP29 in Baku at $300 billion a year by 2035).
  • Loss and damage: set up the Glasgow Dialogue on funding for loss and damage and strengthened the Santiago Network for technical help; a loss and damage fund was agreed at COP27 (2022).
  • Technology transfer and capacity building for developing countries.

Assessment: COP26 kept the 1.5 °C goal alive and finished the Paris Rulebook, but pledges still fall short of what is needed, and developing countries criticised the slow delivery of climate finance and the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities being diluted.

DeprivationAverages hide inequalityHPI-1MPI

The Human Development Index (HDI), published by UNDP since 1990, measures average achievements in health (life expectancy), education (years of schooling) and income (GNI per capita). The Human Poverty Index (HPI), introduced by UNDP in 1997, measured deprivation in the same dimensions:

  • Longevity: probability at birth of not surviving to age 40;
  • Knowledge: adult illiteracy rate;
  • Decent standard of living: share of people without safe water and share of underweight children.

Why HPI can be a better measure

  • Focus on the deprived: HDI is an average and can hide inequality — a country with a rich elite may score well even if many are poor. HPI shows how many are left out.
  • Non-income measures: it captures deprivation directly rather than through income.
  • Policy targeting: it highlights where action is most needed.

Limitations

  • HPI does not show overall progress or capabilities; HDI and HPI complement each other.
  • HPI was replaced in 2010 by the Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI), which measures overlapping deprivations at the household level in health, education and living standards. NITI Aayog's MPI estimates that about 24.8 crore Indians escaped multidimensional poverty between 2013-14 and 2022-23.

So, deprivation measures like HPI and MPI are better at revealing poverty, while HDI shows average development; both are needed.
