RBI Retail Direct Scheme, launched on 12 November 2021, allows individual investors to open a Retail Direct Gilt (RDG) account directly with the RBI through an online portal (and a mobile app since 2024), free of charge.

Investors can buy and sell:

  • Central Government securities, Treasury bills, State Development Loans and Sovereign Gold Bonds;
  • in primary auctions through non-competitive bidding, and in the secondary market through the RBI's NDS-OM trading platform.

Advantages

  • Safe investment: government securities carry no default risk.
  • Direct access without intermediaries such as mutual funds or banks; no fees.
  • Steady returns — often better than bank fixed deposits for long tenures.
  • Wider investor base for government borrowing, reducing dependence on banks and institutions.
  • Financial inclusion and savings culture: small investors can invest with low amounts.
  • Deepens the bond market and improves liquidity.
  • Diversification of household savings away from gold and real estate.

Many countries (the US "TreasuryDirect", Brazil) have similar schemes; India's is one of the few that gives retail investors direct access to both primary and secondary markets.
free.ifm-2021-gk-3a:
Basic structureFlexibility with stabilityKesavanandaLiving document

The Indian Constitution has been amended over 100 times, yet its core philosophy and structure remain the same.

1. Why so many amendments?

  • The Constitution is detailed — it covers Centre–State relations, services, elections and administration — so many changes are technical or administrative.
  • Flexibility under Article 368: some provisions can be changed by simple majority, others by special majority, and federal provisions need ratification by half the States.
  • Social and economic change: land reforms (1st, 4th, 17th Amendments), the reorganisation of States, anti-defection (52nd), local government (73rd, 74th), the right to education (86th), GST (101st), EWS reservation (103rd), women's reservation (106th).

2. Why the basic premises remain intact

  • Basic structure doctrine (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973): Parliament can amend any part but cannot destroy its basic features — supremacy of the Constitution, democracy, republican and secular character, federalism, separation of powers, judicial review, rule of law, free and fair elections and the essence of Fundamental Rights.
  • Courts as guardians: the 39th Amendment (Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain, 1975), parts of the 42nd Amendment (Minerva Mills, 1980) and the 99th Amendment (NJAC, 2015) were struck down.
  • Restoration: the 44th Amendment (1978) undid many Emergency-era changes and protected Articles 20 and 21 during emergencies.
  • Preamble's values — justice, liberty, equality, fraternity — remain the guiding philosophy.

3. Assessment

Amendments have helped the Constitution adapt to changing needs — it is a living document. The basic structure doctrine has ensured that change does not become destruction. As Granville Austin noted, the Constitution has provided both stability and change, which explains its long life compared with many other post-colonial constitutions.
free.ifm-2021-gk-3b:
Separation of functionsChecks and balancesJudicial reviewParliamentary accountability

India does not follow a rigid separation of powers like the US, but its Constitution creates a balance of power among the executive, legislature and judiciary, each with its own domain and each checking the others.

1. Separation of functions

  • Legislature makes laws (Articles 79–122, 168–212).
  • Executive implements them (Articles 52–78, 153–167).
  • Judiciary interprets laws and the Constitution (Articles 124–147, 214–231).
  • Article 50 directs the separation of judiciary from executive; Articles 121 and 211 bar legislatures from discussing judges' conduct; Articles 122 and 212 bar courts from questioning legislative proceedings.

2. Checks and balances

  • Collective responsibility of the Council of Ministers to the Lok Sabha (Article 75).
  • The judiciary can strike down unconstitutional laws (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973) and executive orders (S.R. Bommai, 1994).
  • Parliament can override judgments by changing the law (within the basic structure).

3. Fusion in the parliamentary system

The executive is drawn from and accountable to the legislature, so there is a fusion of executive and legislative powers. This is balanced by an independent judiciary.

4. Tensions

  • Judicial activism or overreach (environmental and administrative directions) versus executive and legislative dominance (ordinances, weak scrutiny of bills).
  • Disputes over judicial appointments (NJAC case, 2015) and Governors' assent to bills (2025).

The Supreme Court in Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975) and Ram Jawaya Kapur (1955) held that while India has no strict separation, each organ must respect the others' domain. This "nice balance" has kept Indian democracy stable.
free.ifm-2021-gk-3c:
Means and endsMinerva MillsHarmonious constructionWelfare state

Fundamental Rights (Part III) are justiciable rights of individuals; Directive Principles of State Policy (Part IV) are non-justiciable guidelines for the State. They are not in conflict; they serve the same goal — a just and democratic society.

How they complement each other

  • Means and ends: DPSPs are the goals (social and economic justice); FRs are the means of protecting liberty while pursuing them.
  • Political and economic democracy: FRs secure political democracy; DPSPs aim at economic and social democracy.
  • Interpretation: courts use DPSPs to give content to FRs — the right to life (Article 21) now includes livelihood, health, education, a clean environment and legal aid, drawing on Articles 39A, 41, 45, 47 and 48A.
  • DPSPs into rights: Article 21A (right to education) came from Article 45.
  • Reasonable restrictions: laws to implement DPSPs (land reforms, prohibition) have been upheld as reasonable restrictions on rights.

Judicial view

  • Champakam Dorairajan (1951): FRs prevailed over DPSPs.
  • Kesavananda Bharati (1973): both are complementary.
  • Minerva Mills (1980): the Constitution rests on the balance and harmony between Parts III and IV; giving absolute primacy to one destroys the basic structure.

Together they form the conscience of the Constitution (Granville Austin).
free.ifm-2021-gk-3d:
Money powerCriminalisationMCCECI appointments

India's Constitution (Articles 324–329), the Representation of the People Acts and an independent Election Commission of India (ECI) have ensured regular, free elections. But several regulatory gaps remain.

Areas that need improvement

  • Money power: spending limits for candidates but no limits for parties; opaque funding — the Supreme Court struck down the electoral bonds scheme in February 2024.
  • Criminalisation: a large share of elected MPs face criminal cases; disqualification applies only after conviction.
  • Model Code of Conduct is not statutory, so enforcement is limited.
  • ECI appointments and independence: the Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners Act, 2023 created a selection committee of the PM, a Union Minister and the Leader of the Opposition; critics want a more independent process.
  • Paid news, social media and deepfakes.
  • Inner-party democracy and transparency of parties.
  • Anti-defection law: delays by Speakers in deciding cases.
  • Accurate voter rolls, migrant voters and remote voting.
  • Frequent elections — the proposal of simultaneous elections (Constitution 129th Amendment Bill, 2024) is under study.

Suggested reforms

  • Cap on party expenditure; State funding of elections (Indrajit Gupta Committee, 1998).
  • Bar candidates facing serious charges once courts frame charges (Law Commission's 244th report); fast-track courts for cases against legislators.
  • Statutory backing for the MCC; power to the ECI to deregister parties.
  • Regulation of political advertising and AI-generated content online.
  • Time-bound decisions on defection petitions by an independent authority.
  • Strengthening VVPAT verification and transparency to maintain trust.
free.ifm-2021-gk-4a:
Land degradationWater and wind erosionWatershed managementAfforestation

Soil erosion is the removal of the fertile top layer of soil by water, wind and human activity. According to ISRO's Desertification and Land Degradation Atlas (2021), about 97.85 million hectares (about 30% of India's area) was degraded in 2018-19, and water erosion is the biggest cause.

Why it is increasing

  • Deforestation and loss of vegetation cover.
  • Overgrazing by livestock.
  • Faulty farming practices: ploughing up and down slopes, shifting cultivation (jhum) with shorter cycles, leaving fields bare.
  • Intense rainfall events and floods, increasing with climate change.
  • Mining, road building and construction on slopes.
  • Wind erosion in Rajasthan and Gujarat.
  • Ravines in the Chambal valley; gullies in the Himalaya and Western Ghats.

Consequences: loss of fertility and crop yields, siltation of dams and rivers, floods, desertification and rural poverty.

Remedial measures

  • Watershed management: treating whole catchments under PMKSY–Watershed Development (WDC 2.0).
  • Afforestation and agroforestry, Green India Mission.
  • Conservation agriculture: minimum tillage, residue retention.
  • Soil Health Cards and organic manure to improve soil structure.
  • Community participation: village watershed committees, MGNREGA works on land development.
  • International commitment: India aims to restore 26 million hectares of degraded land by 2030 under the UNCCD.

Protecting soil is protecting food security; "soil once lost is lost for generations".
free.ifm-2021-gk-4b:
Demographic dividendHuman capitalJobsWomen's participation

India became the world's most populous country in 2023 (UN), with about 1.46 billion people in 2025. A large population puts pressure on land, water, jobs, housing, health and education — and is often seen as a bane. Yet with the right strategies it can be a boon.

Why it can be a boon

  • About two-thirds of Indians are of working age and the median age is under 30 — a demographic dividend that lasts until about the 2050s.
  • A huge domestic market attracts investment.
  • A large pool of talent for science, technology and services.

Strategies to make it a boon

  • Education and skills: foundational literacy (NIPUN Bharat), NEP 2020, vocational training (Skill India), and higher education linked to industry.
  • Health and nutrition: Ayushman Bharat, Poshan Abhiyaan, safe water and sanitation, to build a productive workforce.
  • Job-rich growth: labour-intensive manufacturing (textiles, electronics assembly, food processing), MSMEs, tourism, construction and the care economy; PLI and the National Manufacturing Mission.
  • Women's participation: education, safe transport, childcare and flexible work can add crores of workers.
  • Entrepreneurship and start-ups: Startup India, Mudra loans.
  • Global workforce: migration and mobility agreements so that skilled Indians can work abroad, bringing remittances (India is the largest recipient).
  • Urban planning: well-planned cities to absorb migrants.
  • Population stabilisation: voluntary family planning, education of girls and better health care; India's fertility rate has already fallen to about 2.0.
  • Regional focus: northern States with high fertility and weak human development need special attention, while ageing southern States need elder care.

With these measures, India's population can become its greatest resource rather than its biggest burden.
free.ifm-2021-gk-4c:
ConvectionWarmingDeadliest natural hazardEarly warning

Lightning is the largest killer among natural disasters in India. NCRB data show about 2,800–2,900 deaths a year from lightning in recent years. Reports by the Climate Resilient Observing Systems Promotion Council recorded about 1.85 crore lightning strikes in 2020-21, a 34% rise over the previous year.

Causes of rising frequency and intensity

  • Global warming: a warmer, moister atmosphere increases convection and thunderstorms; studies suggest each 1 °C rise may increase lightning by about 10–12%.
  • More moisture from warmer seas.
  • Aerosols and air pollution provide more nuclei for cloud droplets and charge separation.
  • Land-use changes: deforestation, urban heat islands and drying of water bodies.
  • Pre-monsoon heating in eastern and central India.

Consequences

  • Deaths and injuries, mostly among farmers, labourers and herders working in open fields; Odisha, Jharkhand, Bihar, West Bengal and Madhya Pradesh are worst affected.
  • Loss of livestock, damage to houses, power lines and electronics.
  • Forest fires.
  • Disruption of aviation and communication.

Measures: early warnings through the Damini app (IITM Pune) and IMD's nowcasts; lightning arresters in schools and public buildings; awareness of "30-30" safety rules; some States, like Odisha and Bihar, treat lightning as a State-specific disaster for compensation.
free.ifm-2021-gk-4d:
Net zeroRenewablesElectrificationGreen hydrogen

Carbon neutrality (net zero) means balancing greenhouse gas emissions with removals. The energy sector — electricity, industry, transport and buildings — causes about three-quarters of global emissions, so changing how we produce and use energy is the most important step.

What energy transition means

A shift from fossil fuels (coal, oil, gas) to clean energy (solar, wind, hydro, nuclear, green hydrogen), together with energy efficiency and electrification.

Why it is the best measure

  • Replacing coal power with renewables cuts the largest source of CO2.
  • Electrifying transport (EVs) and cooking, and powering them with clean electricity.
  • Green hydrogen for steel, fertiliser and refineries where electrification is hard.
  • Efficiency — LED bulbs (UJALA), efficient appliances and buildings — reduces demand.
  • Co-benefits: cleaner air, energy security, lower import bills and new jobs.

India's path

  • Net zero by 2070; non-fossil sources crossed 50% of installed power capacity in 2025.
  • Target of 500 GW non-fossil capacity by 2030, the National Green Hydrogen Mission, ethanol blending (E20), PM Surya Ghar and PM-KUSUM, and the Carbon Credit Trading Scheme (2023).

Limits: energy transition alone is not enough — emissions from agriculture, land use and industrial processes need other measures, such as carbon sinks (forests), carbon capture and sustainable farming. It must also be a just transition for coal-dependent regions and workers.
free.ifm-2021-gk-5a:
Subhash PalekarJeevamruthaOn-farm inputsNatural farming

Zero Budget Natural Farming (ZBNF), promoted by Subhash Palekar, is a method of chemical-free farming with almost no purchased inputs, so the cost of cultivation is close to zero; income from intercrops covers the cost of the main crop.

1. Features — the four "wheels"

  • Jeevamrutha: a ferment of cow dung, cow urine, jaggery, pulse flour and soil that boosts soil microbes.
  • Bijamrita: seed treatment with cow dung, urine and lime to protect seedlings.
  • Acchadana (mulching): covering the soil with crop residue or a cover crop to conserve moisture and organic matter.
  • Whapasa (soil aeration): creating conditions where air and moisture are balanced in the soil, reducing irrigation needs.

Other features: intercropping and multi-cropping, contour bunds, use of local seeds and indigenous cows, and natural pest repellents (neemastra, brahmastra, agniastra).

2. Spread in India

  • Andhra Pradesh Community-managed Natural Farming (APCNF) since 2016 covers lakhs of farmers.
  • Promoted under the Bharatiya Prakritik Krishi Paddhati and the National Mission on Natural Farming (2024), which aims to reach about one crore farmers.

3. How it differs from organic farming

4. Assessment

ZBNF reduces costs, debt and chemical use, and improves soil health. But critics, including some agricultural scientists, question whether yields can be sustained without external nutrients, and call for more research. A balanced approach — natural farming where suitable, with scientific monitoring — is advisable.
free.ifm-2021-gk-5b:
rDNAAgrobacteriumGene flowPest resistance

1. What is GM of crops?

Genetic modification is the direct alteration of a crop's DNA using biotechnology to introduce a desired trait — for example, the cry gene from the bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis in Bt cotton to resist bollworms.

2. How it is done

  • Gene identification and cloning from any organism.
  • Transformation by Agrobacterium tumefaciens (a natural genetic engineer) or a gene gun (biolistics) that shoots DNA-coated particles into cells.
  • Selection of transformed cells using marker genes, regeneration into whole plants by tissue culture.
  • Testing in labs, contained trials and field trials; approval by India's Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee (GEAC).

3. GM versus conventional breeding

Genome editing (CRISPR) is a newer tool; India released its first two genome-edited rice varieties in 2025.

4. Environmental impacts

  • Positive: less insecticide spraying (Bt cotton), lower fuel use, higher yields on less land; possible drought-tolerant varieties.
  • Negative:

- Resistance in pests: pink bollworm has become resistant to Bt cotton in India. - Superweeds: herbicide-tolerant crops encourage overuse of herbicides, leading to resistant weeds. - Gene flow to wild relatives and non-GM crops. - Effects on non-target organisms such as pollinators and soil microbes. - Loss of crop diversity if a few GM varieties dominate.

5. India's status

Only Bt cotton (2002) is commercially grown. GM mustard (DMH-11) was approved for environmental release in 2022, but the matter is before the Supreme Court, which in 2024 asked the Government to frame a national policy on GM crops. Strong biosafety assessment and transparent regulation are essential.
free.ifm-2021-gk-5c:
Stratospheric ozoneTropospheric ozoneMontreal ProtocolSecondary pollutant

"Ozone is good up high, bad nearby." Its effects depend on where it is found.

1. Stratospheric ozone — useful

  • Found mainly 15–35 km above the Earth (the ozone layer).
  • It absorbs harmful ultraviolet (UV-B and UV-C) radiation, protecting humans from skin cancer and cataracts, and protecting crops and marine life.
  • Damaged by ozone-depleting substances (CFCs, halons) that caused the Antarctic ozone hole.
  • The Montreal Protocol (1987) phased them out; the ozone layer is expected to recover to 1980 levels by around 2066 over Antarctica (UNEP–WMO assessment, 2023). The Kigali Amendment (2016) phases down HFCs.

2. Tropospheric (ground-level) ozone — harmful

  • A secondary pollutant formed when nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds react in sunlight; a key part of smog.
  • Causes respiratory problems, asthma and lung damage.
  • Reduces crop yields (wheat and rice losses in India) and damages forests.
  • It is also a greenhouse gas.
  • It is a growing problem in Indian cities in summer, and is one of the pollutants measured in the Air Quality Index.

So ozone is useful only in the stratosphere; near the ground it is a pollutant.
free.ifm-2021-gk-5d:
Bollgard IIGlyphosate toleranceIllegal cultivationWeed management

Bt cotton carries genes from Bacillus thuringiensis (cry1Ac, and in Bollgard II also cry2Ab) that make the plant toxic to bollworms. Herbicide-tolerant (HT) Bt cotton adds another layer — a gene (cp4-epsps) that makes the plant tolerant to the herbicide glyphosate. Farmers can spray glyphosate to kill weeds without harming the cotton crop. This "stacked" trait is sometimes called Bollgard III or BG-III.

Why farmers want it

  • Labour shortage and high cost of manual weeding; herbicide use saves time and money.

Concerns

  • Not approved in India: the GEAC has not cleared it, yet illegal HT seeds have spread in Maharashtra, Gujarat, Telangana and Andhra Pradesh.
  • Health risks of glyphosate: classified as "probably carcinogenic" by the WHO's cancer agency (2015); India in 2022 restricted its use to licensed pest-control operators.
  • Superweeds: weeds develop resistance to glyphosate.
  • Gene flow and loss of biodiversity.
  • Loss of jobs for women who do manual weeding.
  • Spurious seeds without quality control hurt farmers.

Way forward: a science-based decision by the GEAC, strict action against illegal seed trade, integrated weed management, and better regulation of herbicides.
free.ifm-2021-gk-6a:
2015Light-based technologiesAnniversariesSustainable development

The UN General Assembly (December 2013) declared 2015 the International Year of Light and Light-based Technologies (IYL 2015).

Why 2015?

It marked several important anniversaries in the science of light:

  • 1015: about 1,000 years since the work of Ibn al-Haytham on optics (Book of Optics).
  • 1815: Fresnel's wave theory of light.
  • 1865: Maxwell's electromagnetic theory of light.
  • 1905: Einstein's explanation of the photoelectric effect; 1915: general relativity, showing light's role in space-time.
  • 1965: discovery of the cosmic microwave background by Penzias and Wilson, and Charles Kao's work on optical fibres for communication.

Purpose of IYL 2015

  • To raise global awareness of how light-based technologies promote sustainable development and solve challenges in energy, education, agriculture, communication and health.
  • Examples: solar energy and LED lighting (energy efficiency), optical fibres and the internet, lasers in medicine and industry, imaging and diagnostics.
  • To promote science education among young people, especially in developing countries.
  • To highlight light pollution and the importance of dark skies.
  • To promote international cooperation in science.

Legacy: UNESCO now celebrates the International Day of Light on 16 May every year (since 2018), the anniversary of the first laser (1960). In India, light-based technologies such as LED lighting under UJALA, solar power and optical-fibre broadband (BharatNet) show its practical impact.
free.ifm-2021-gk-6b:
Fission chain reactionReactor componentsPHWRThree-stage programme

Nuclear power is produced by using the heat released in nuclear fission to make steam and drive turbines.

1. Principle

When a heavy nucleus such as uranium-235 absorbs a neutron, it splits into lighter nuclei, releasing large energy and 2–3 neutrons, which split more nuclei — a chain reaction. In a reactor, the chain reaction is controlled so that energy is released steadily.

2. Main parts of a reactor

  • Fuel: natural or enriched uranium, plutonium or thorium.
  • Moderator: slows down neutrons so they cause more fission — heavy water, light water or graphite.
  • Control rods: absorb neutrons (boron, cadmium) to control or stop the reaction.
  • Coolant: carries heat away — water, heavy water, gas or liquid sodium.
  • Steam generator, turbine and generator.
  • Shielding and containment for safety.

3. Types of reactors

  • Pressurised Heavy Water Reactors (PHWR) — the mainstay of India (700 MWe indigenous units at Kakrapar and Rawatbhata).
  • Light water reactors (LWR/VVER) — Kudankulam.
  • Fast Breeder Reactors — produce more fuel than they consume (the Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor at Kalpakkam).
  • Small Modular Reactors (SMRs) — the future option.

4. India's three-stage programme (Homi Bhabha)

1. PHWRs using natural uranium produce plutonium. 2. Fast breeder reactors use plutonium and convert thorium into uranium-233. 3. Thorium-based reactors use India's large thorium reserves.

5. Status and advantages

India has about 8.9 GW from 25 reactors (2025) and plans 100 GW by 2047, including Bharat Small Reactors under the Nuclear Energy Mission. Nuclear power gives reliable, low-carbon base-load electricity and energy security. Challenges include high cost, long construction times, waste disposal, safety concerns after Fukushima, and limited uranium.
free.ifm-2021-gk-6c:
MTCR memberPeaceful recordSeparate programmesTransparency

Some countries fear that satellite launch vehicles (SLVs) can be converted into long-range missiles. India can answer these fears as follows:

  • Different purposes and design: launch vehicles are built to place satellites in orbit, not to carry warheads; they lack re-entry vehicles, heat shields for warheads, guidance for targets and quick-launch readiness. PSLV and LVM3 need days of preparation on fixed launch pads, unlike military missiles.
  • Separate institutions: ISRO is a civilian space agency; missiles are developed separately by DRDO.
  • Non-proliferation record: India is a member of the Missile Technology Control Regime (2016), the Wassenaar Arrangement (2017) and the Australia Group (2018), and received the NSG waiver (2008). It has never transferred sensitive technology to others.
  • Responsible nuclear doctrine: credible minimum deterrence and no first use.
  • International obligations: party to the Outer Space Treaty; registers launches with the UN; supports the peaceful use of outer space.
  • Commercial record: PSLV has launched hundreds of foreign satellites for over 30 countries, including 104 satellites in one launch (2017) — showing trust in India as a peaceful partner.
  • Peaceful achievements: Chandrayaan-3, Aditya-L1, NavIC, weather and disaster satellites that serve humanity.
  • Transparency: openness about launches and cooperation with NASA, ESA and others.

India thus can show that its space programme is for development and science, not for threatening others.
free.ifm-2021-gk-6d:
C.V. RamanA.P.J. Abdul KalamRaman effectMissile programme

Several Indians have received the Bharat Ratna for science and technology — C.V. Raman (1954), M. Visvesvaraya (1955), A.P.J. Abdul Kalam (1997), C.N.R. Rao (2014) and M.S. Swaminathan (2024). Two of them:

1. Sir C.V. Raman (1888–1970)

  • Discovered the Raman effect (1928): when light passes through a transparent substance, a small part of it is scattered with a change in wavelength, revealing the structure of molecules.
  • Awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics (1930) — the first Asian to win a Nobel in science.
  • Raman spectroscopy is used today in chemistry, medicine and materials science.
  • Founded the Raman Research Institute in Bengaluru and the Indian Academy of Sciences.
  • National Science Day (28 February) marks his discovery.

2. Dr A.P.J. Abdul Kalam (1931–2015)

  • Led India's first indigenous satellite launch vehicle, SLV-3, which placed Rohini in orbit in 1980.
  • Headed the Integrated Guided Missile Development Programme (Agni, Prithvi, Akash, Trishul, Nag) — the "Missile Man of India".
  • Played a key role in the Pokhran-II nuclear tests (1998) as Scientific Adviser.
  • Promoted low-cost medical devices (the Kalam–Raju stent) and inspired youth through his books (Wings of Fire).
  • Served as the 11th President of India (2002–07).

Both showed how Indian science could achieve world-class results and serve the nation.
free.ifm-2022-ge-1a:
BiasAccountabilityPrivacyHuman control

Ethical Dilemmas and Artificial Intelligence

Artificial intelligence has moved from science fiction into everyday life. It recommends what we watch, screens our job applications, reads our X-rays, translates our languages and, through tools such as ChatGPT, even writes essays like this one. AI promises enormous benefits — faster diagnosis of disease, better weather forecasts, personalised education and higher productivity. But because AI systems make or shape decisions that affect human lives, they raise difficult ethical dilemmas: questions of fairness, responsibility, privacy, truth and control.

Bias and fairness

AI learns from data, and data reflects the prejudices of the society that produced it. A recruitment algorithm trained on past hiring data may learn to prefer men; facial recognition systems have been found to be less accurate for women and people with darker skin; risk-assessment software used in some American courts was accused of rating Black defendants as more likely to reoffend. In a country as diverse as India, an AI system trained mostly on English-speaking urban users may misunderstand or exclude rural people, women and speakers of other languages. The dilemma is that AI can make decisions appear objective while hiding discrimination inside a "black box".

Accountability and transparency

When a self-driving car causes an accident, or an AI system denies a loan or a medical treatment, who is responsible — the programmer, the company, the user or the machine? Many advanced AI models are so complex that even their designers cannot fully explain their decisions. Yet people have a right to know why a decision affecting them was made and to challenge it. The classic "trolley problem" — whether a self-driving car should protect its passengers or pedestrians — shows how engineers are now forced to encode moral choices into machines.

Privacy and surveillance

AI feeds on data. Facial recognition in public places, predictive policing and the profiling of consumers can turn societies into surveillance states. Personal data may be collected without meaningful consent and used to manipulate opinions and behaviour, as the Cambridge Analytica scandal showed.

Truth, deepfakes and democracy

Generative AI can produce realistic fake images, voices and videos. Deepfakes have been used to spread misinformation, defame individuals — often women — and commit fraud by imitating a relative's voice. In an age when anyone can create convincing falsehoods, trust in information and in democratic debate is threatened.

Work and inequality

AI can automate routine jobs in offices, call centres and factories. While it will also create new jobs, the transition may leave many workers behind and concentrate wealth in a few technology companies and countries. Should those who profit from automation share the gains with those who lose their jobs?

Autonomy and lethal weapons

Perhaps the gravest dilemma is the use of AI in warfare. Autonomous weapons that can select and kill targets without human intervention raise the question of whether a machine should ever decide to take a human life. There are also concerns about AI systems becoming so powerful that humans lose meaningful control over them.

Towards ethical AI

These dilemmas do not mean we should reject AI. They mean we must shape it. Several principles are now widely accepted:

  • Fairness: test systems for bias and use diverse data.
  • Transparency and explainability: people should know when they are dealing with AI and why it decided as it did.
  • Accountability: clear legal responsibility for harm.
  • Privacy: data protection laws such as India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023.
  • Human oversight: humans must remain "in the loop" for high-stakes decisions.
  • Safety and security testing before deployment.

The UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of AI (2021) and the European Union's AI Act (2024), which bans some uses and strictly regulates high-risk ones, are steps in this direction. India's IndiaAI Mission emphasises "AI for All" and responsible, inclusive AI, and India has led global discussions on AI governance. Companies too must build ethics into design, not add it as an afterthought.

Conclusion

AI is a mirror and a magnifier: it reflects our values and multiplies their effects. Whether it becomes a tool for justice and prosperity or for discrimination and control depends not on the machine but on us. The central ethical task of our time is to ensure that intelligent machines remain servants of human dignity, and that in the race to make machines smarter, we do not make humans less free.
free.ifm-2022-ge-1b:
KabaddiKho-khoMallakhambKhelo India

The Revival of Traditional Indian Sports

Long before cricket and football arrived in India, children in its villages ran, wrestled, chased and climbed in games passed down through generations. Kabaddi, kho-kho, gilli-danda, mallakhamb, kalaripayattu, wrestling in the akhada, boat races in Kerala and archery in the North-East were part of the country's culture. Chess itself grew out of the ancient Indian game of chaturanga. For decades, these sports were neglected, seen as rustic pastimes rather than serious sport. Today they are enjoying a remarkable revival.

Signs of revival

The most striking example is kabaddi. The Pro Kabaddi League, launched in 2014, turned a village game into a television spectacle watched by crores of people, with professional players, sponsors and international stars. India has dominated kabaddi at the Asian Games and in World Cups.

Kho-kho has followed. A professional league, Ultimate Kho Kho, began in 2022, and India hosted the first Kho Kho World Cup in New Delhi in January 2025, with Indian teams winning both the men's and women's titles.

The government's Khelo India programme has included indigenous sports such as gatka, kalaripayattu, thang-ta and mallakhamb in the Khelo India Youth Games, and yogasana has been recognised as a competitive sport. Mallakhamb, the gymnastic art performed on a wooden pole, has spread to dozens of countries. Martial arts such as kalaripayattu and silambam attract learners worldwide, and traditional boat races, bull races and rural games draw large crowds at festivals.

Why revival matters

First, cultural heritage. Traditional sports carry local stories, music, festivals and values. Reviving them keeps alive a living heritage and strengthens community identity.

Second, accessible fitness. Most indigenous games need little or no equipment and can be played in any open space. In an age of sedentary lifestyles, obesity and screen addiction among children, they offer cheap, enjoyable exercise for all.

Third, inclusion. Rural youth, girls and people from poor families, who cannot afford expensive equipment and coaching, can excel in these sports. Many kabaddi and kho-kho stars come from small towns and farming families.

Fourth, values and skills. Games like kho-kho and kabaddi build speed, strategy, teamwork and quick decision-making; martial arts teach discipline and self-control.

Fifth, economic opportunity. Leagues, broadcasting, tourism and equipment create jobs and incomes; traditional sports can become part of India's soft power, much as yoga has.

Challenges

  • Lack of infrastructure, coaching and scientific training in rural areas.
  • Weak federations and poor governance in some sports.
  • Limited international recognition, which keeps these sports out of the Olympics and reduces funding.
  • Dominance of cricket in media attention and sponsorship.
  • Lack of documentation of many folk games, which are disappearing with urbanisation.

The way forward

  • Include traditional games in school physical education and inter-school competitions.
  • Standardise rules and build professional federations that can promote them internationally, as was done with kabaddi.
  • Use leagues and digital media to build fan bases.
  • Provide scholarships, jobs and recognition to players under schemes like Khelo India and the Target Olympic Podium Scheme, and in government service.
  • Document and revive dying folk games through cultural ministries and local communities.
  • Promote them through tourism and festivals.

Conclusion

The revival of traditional sports is not about turning back the clock or rejecting modern games. It is about recognising that India's own sporting heritage can produce champions, healthier citizens and pride in local culture. When a girl from a village wins a kho-kho world title, or a kabaddi raider from a farming family becomes a household name, India discovers that the playgrounds of its villages hold treasures worth preserving. As the nation dreams of becoming a sporting power, its roots can give it strength.
free.ifm-2022-ge-1c:
NEP 2020Holistic educationEthics of technologyInnovation

Liberal Education is not Antithetical to Technical Education

In India, the choice between "arts" and "science" has often felt like a choice between a dream and a job. Engineering and medicine were seen as respectable, secure careers; history, philosophy or literature as subjects for those who could not get into technical courses. This division assumes that liberal education and technical education are opposites. In truth, they are partners. The best engineers, doctors and scientists are those who can also think, question, communicate and care — and these are precisely the gifts of a liberal education.

What each offers

Technical education provides specialised knowledge and skills — how to design a bridge, write software, cure a disease or run a power plant. It is essential for economic growth and national development. Liberal education, which includes the humanities, social sciences, arts and basic sciences, aims at developing the whole person: critical thinking, ethical reasoning, communication, creativity, an understanding of society and history, and the ability to learn throughout life.

Why they need each other

First, technology does not exist in a social vacuum. An engineer designing a dam must understand the people who will be displaced; a software developer creating an app must consider privacy and addiction; a doctor must communicate with patients and respect their dignity. Without the insights of ethics, economics and sociology, technology can cause harm.

Second, innovation thrives at the meeting point of disciplines. Many of the most successful technology companies were built by people who combined technical skill with design, psychology and storytelling. User-friendly products, from the smartphone to India's UPI, succeed because their creators understood human behaviour.

Third, the job market is changing rapidly. Specific technical skills become outdated quickly; the ability to learn, adapt, collaborate and solve new problems endures. Employers increasingly complain that graduates are technically trained but lack communication, teamwork and critical thinking.

Fourth, ethical challenges of new technology — artificial intelligence, genetic engineering, climate engineering — require technologists who can think about values and consequences, not only about efficiency.

Fifth, democracy needs informed citizens. Technical experts are also voters and leaders; they must understand constitutional values, history and the diversity of society.

India's tradition and policy

Ancient Indian universities such as Nalanda and Takshashila taught medicine, logic, grammar, astronomy and the arts together, and the idea of the "64 kalas" combined practical skills with fine arts. Rabindranath Tagore's Visva-Bharati sought an education in which science, art and life were one.

The National Education Policy 2020 revives this vision. It calls for a holistic and multidisciplinary education, ending hard separations between arts and sciences and between curricular and vocational subjects. Students can now combine majors and minors across streams, and IITs and other technical institutes have expanded departments of humanities, social sciences and design. Many engineering curricula include courses on ethics, economics and communication.

Avoiding the extremes

Integration does not mean diluting either. Technical education must remain rigorous, and liberal education must not become a set of superficial "soft skill" modules. The aim is for every student to have depth in one field and breadth across others — the so-called "T-shaped" professional.

Conclusion

Science tells us how to do things; the humanities help us ask whether and why we should do them. A nation that produces brilliant technologists without wisdom risks building powerful tools without direction, while one that produces thinkers without technical capacity cannot turn ideas into reality. Liberal and technical education are not rivals but two wings of the same bird. India's future depends on graduates who can build machines and also understand the human beings they are meant to serve.
free.ifm-2022-ge-1d:
Demographic windowEducationHealthSkills and jobs

To Reap the Demographic Dividend, Investment in Human Capital is Crucial for India

India has the world's largest population, and one of its youngest. More than half its people are below 30, and the working-age population will keep growing for about two more decades. This creates a demographic dividend — a period when a large share of working people supports a smaller share of dependants, allowing faster growth, higher savings and more investment. East Asian economies such as Japan, South Korea and China used their dividend to become prosperous. But a dividend is not automatic. A young population is an asset only if it is healthy, educated and productively employed. Otherwise, it becomes a burden of unemployment and frustration. That is why investment in human capital is crucial.

What human capital means

Human capital is the knowledge, skills, health and capabilities of people that make them productive. It is built through education, health care, nutrition, skill training and opportunities for women. Economists have shown that countries investing early in human capital grew faster and more equitably.

Where India stands

India has made progress. Almost all children now enrol in primary school, life expectancy has risen, and maternal and infant mortality have fallen sharply. Digital public infrastructure has expanded access to services.

But serious gaps remain:

  • Learning poverty: surveys such as ASER show that many children in upper primary classes cannot read simple texts or do basic arithmetic.
  • Malnutrition: about a third of children under five are stunted (NFHS-5), which affects brain development and lifetime earnings.
  • Low skills: only a small share of the workforce has formal vocational training; many graduates are considered unemployable by industry.
  • Low female participation in the workforce, which wastes half the nation's talent.
  • Health spending is low, and out-of-pocket costs push families into poverty.
  • Regional disparities: the young populations of Bihar, Uttar Pradesh and Madhya Pradesh have the weakest education and health outcomes, while southern States are already ageing.

Why it is urgent

India's dividend is a window that will close. By the 2040s, the share of the elderly will rise sharply. If today's young people do not get good jobs, they will grow old without savings, pensions or assets. Moreover, technology and automation are changing the nature of work: low-skill jobs are shrinking, and the jobs of the future need higher skills.

What needs to be done

  • Foundational learning: the NIPUN Bharat mission and NEP 2020's focus on early childhood care and foundational literacy and numeracy must succeed.
  • Quality higher education and research, linked to industry and innovation.
  • Skilling at scale: vocational education from school, apprenticeships and industry partnerships under Skill India; re-skilling for new technologies.
  • Health and nutrition: stronger primary health care, Ayushman Bharat, Poshan Abhiyaan, clean water and sanitation.
  • Women's empowerment: education, safety, childcare and flexible work to raise female participation.
  • Jobs: labour-intensive manufacturing, services, tourism and the care economy to absorb the growing workforce.
  • Public spending: raise education spending towards 6% of GDP and health spending towards 2.5% of GDP, as recommended by national policies.

Conclusion

Population is not destiny; people are. India's young millions can be the engine that makes it a developed nation by 2047 — or a source of social unrest if neglected. The difference lies in the classrooms, clinics, kitchens and training centres where human capital is built. Investing in people is not a cost but the most productive investment a nation can make. As the saying goes, if you plan for a hundred years, educate people.

ABC XYZ Locality XYZ Constituency

16 November 2022

Shri/Smt. XYZ Hon'ble Member of the Legislative Assembly XYZ Constituency

Subject: Request to address the problem of waste management in our locality

Respected Sir/Madam,

I am a resident of your constituency and write on behalf of the residents of our locality to draw your attention to the serious problem of waste management here.

Garbage is not collected regularly from our streets. Waste piles up at corners and on vacant plots, and is often burnt in the open, filling the air with toxic smoke. Plastic waste blocks the drains, which overflow during the rains. Stray animals scatter the garbage, and the stench has become unbearable. Cases of dengue, malaria and stomach infections have increased, especially among children and the elderly. There is no system for separating wet and dry waste, and no compost or recycling facility nearby.

I request you to take the following steps: 1. Ensure daily door-to-door collection of waste by the municipal body. 2. Provide separate bins for wet and dry waste and create awareness about segregation at source. 3. Set up a composting unit and a material recovery facility for recycling. 4. Clear the existing garbage dumps and clean the drains before the monsoon. 5. Impose penalties for littering and open burning, and install dustbins in public places. 6. Involve residents' associations, self-help groups and waste-pickers in the effort.

These measures can be supported under the Swachh Bharat Mission (Urban) and will make our locality clean and healthy.

We shall be grateful for your prompt action.

Thanking you,

Yours faithfully, ABC

Rural schoolsLearning gapsInfrastructureTeachers

Challenges of Learning in Rural Schools: A Field Report

By ABC

During a recent visit to three government schools in the XYZ block — XYZ Primary School, ABC Upper Primary School and XYZ High School — I observed the conditions in which rural children learn. While enrolment was high and students were eager to learn, several challenges stood out.

Teachers: in two schools, a few teachers handled several classes at once; one primary school had only two teachers for five classes. Teachers also spent much time on non-teaching duties such as surveys, mid-day meal records and election work.

Learning levels: many children in classes IV and V could not read a short paragraph in their mother tongue or solve simple division sums. Teaching focused on completing the syllabus rather than ensuring basic reading and arithmetic.

Infrastructure: classrooms were crowded and poorly lit. One school had no working toilet for girls and no boundary wall. The science laboratory and library of the high school were locked for want of staff. Computers supplied under a scheme lay unused because of power cuts and the absence of a trained teacher.

Language and attendance: many children from tribal families spoke a home language different from the medium of instruction. Attendance dropped during the harvest season, when children helped their parents, and some older girls had dropped out.

Digital divide: few families owned smartphones, and internet connectivity was weak, so online resources could not be used.

Positive signs: the mid-day meal was regular and nutritious, and children's attendance had improved because of it. Some teachers were using activity-based methods and local materials, and a community volunteer conducted remedial classes in the evening.

Suggestions: filling teacher vacancies, reducing non-teaching duties, remedial programmes for foundational literacy and numeracy under NIPUN Bharat, mother-tongue teaching in early classes, toilets and electricity in all schools, and active School Management Committees to involve parents.
free.ifm-2022-ge-3:
Air pollutionTaj MahalAcid corrosionRemedies

Air pollution has silently damaged art objects and ancient monuments throughout the industrialised world. The Taj Mahal is gravely threatened by pollutants from foundries, power houses, railway yards and other industries. Some environmentalists believe the Mathura refinery, 40 km away, has aggravated the danger, though this is disputed and its safeguards may limit the harm. Black and brown patches, gypsum formation, scaling and flaking already disfigure its white marble, as sulphur dioxide combines with moisture to form sulphuric acid that corrodes and discolours it. Saving the Taj may cost more than building it. The remedies are to shift foundries and power houses from Agra, supervise the refinery's anti-pollution measures, replace coal locomotives with diesel engines and raise a dense green belt to absorb pollutants. Similarly, soot from a nearby plywood factory is discolouring the Chennakeshava temple at Belur.

(138 words)
free.ifm-2022-ge-4a: The four terms are psychology, psychotherapy, psychoanalysis and psychiatry. All of them describe different approaches to understanding and helping people with psychological and emotional problems. They are confusing because there is a great deal of overlap among them, and the work of the same highly qualified person can sometimes be described by several of these terms.
free.ifm-2022-ge-4b: Experimental psychologists conduct experiments to explore the basics of mental functioning, such as perception, memory, arousal and risk-taking. They study not only humans but also animals, both for their own sake and as models to understand human behaviour. Their work follows the same scientific principles of investigation as physics or chemistry, so experimental psychology is regarded as a "hard science".
free.ifm-2022-ge-4c: Behaviour therapy was an early and clear example of applying psychology to treatment. It uses learning theory — consistent rewards and punishments — to shape behaviour. It has been particularly successful with disturbed children and those with learning difficulties, helping them modify their behaviour, and it works without the patient needing a detailed understanding of their problems. It paved the way for more sophisticated treatments such as cognitive behaviour therapy.
free.ifm-2022-ge-4d: In psychoanalysis, the patient is asked to relax and say the first thing that comes to mind ("free association"), and to pay attention to dreams and irrational thoughts. The analyst listens carefully, gradually detects patterns and clues to repressed conflicts, and shares these insights to help the patient confront and resolve them. The treatment is intensive and long — traditionally an hour a day, up to five times a week, for several years — with the patient lying on a couch and the analyst sitting behind.
free.ifm-2022-ge-4e: Several schools of psychoanalysis were developed by Freud's disciples, such as Jung, Adler and Klein, while others, like those of Reich and Lacan, moved far from the original model. Beyond psychiatry, psychoanalysis has had an enormous influence on literature and the arts, and terms like "Freudian" and "Freudian slip" have entered everyday speech. However, because it lacks firm scientific evidence of effectiveness, it is increasingly marginalised in modern psychiatric practice.
