free.ifm-2022-gk-1a:
Grid planningCitadel and lower townDrainageStandardisation

The Harappan (Indus Valley) Civilization (c. 2600–1900 BCE, mature phase) built some of the earliest planned towns in the world — Harappa, Mohenjo-daro, Dholavira, Lothal, Kalibangan, Rakhigarhi and Banawali.

Main features of Harappan townships

1. Planned layout

  • Streets cut each other at right angles, dividing the town into rectangular blocks (grid pattern).
  • Main streets were wide (up to 10 m at Mohenjo-daro) and ran north–south and east–west.

2. Division of the town

  • A raised, fortified citadel on the west for public buildings and the elite; a larger lower town on the east for residences.
  • Dholavira had three parts — citadel, middle town and lower town.

3. Burnt-brick construction

  • Standardised baked bricks in the ratio 1:2:4, used across the whole civilization.

4. Drainage and sanitation

  • Covered drains along streets with manholes; house drains joined street drains — a remarkable civic sense.
  • Bathrooms and wells in many houses; Mohenjo-daro had about 700 wells.

5. Public buildings

  • Great Bath of Mohenjo-daro — waterproofed with bitumen, probably for ritual bathing.
  • Granaries at Harappa and Mohenjo-daro; an assembly hall.
  • Dockyard at Lothal for maritime trade.

6. Houses

  • One- or two-storey houses around a courtyard; doors opened into side lanes, not main streets, for privacy.

7. Water management

  • Dholavira had large reservoirs and channels to harvest rainwater in a dry region.

8. Uniformity

  • Standard weights (binary system), seals and bricks suggest a strong civic authority.

Significance: such town planning reflects a well-organised administration, trade and civic life, and has no parallel in contemporary Egypt or Mesopotamia in sanitation. Dholavira became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2021.
free.ifm-2022-gk-1b:
Jnana kandaBrahman and AtmanCritique of ritualVedanta

The Upanishads (c. 800–500 BCE) are the last part of the Vedic literature — hence Vedanta. They grew out of the Vedic tradition but shifted its focus so much that they are often seen as different in essence.

1. How they differ from earlier Vedic literature

  • Brahman and Atman: the central idea that the individual self (Atman) is identical with the universal reality (Brahman) — "Tat tvam asi" (Chandogya) and "Aham Brahmasmi" (Brihadaranyaka).
  • Criticism of ritual: the Mundaka Upanishad calls sacrifices "unsafe boats" for crossing the ocean of rebirth.
  • Karma, samsara and moksha appear clearly for the first time.
  • Dialogue and inquiry: teachings through questions — Yajnavalkya and Gargi, Nachiketa and Yama.
  • Ethics: self-control, truth and compassion over ritual purity.

2. Continuity with the Vedas

  • They are part of the Vedic corpus and use its language and symbols (Om, Gayatri).
  • Some earlier hymns, such as the Nasadiya Sukta, already asked philosophical questions.
  • They reinterpret the sacrifice as an inner, symbolic act rather than rejecting it entirely.

3. Significance

The Upanishads laid the basis of Vedanta, influenced Buddhism and Jainism, Shankaracharya and later thinkers such as Vivekananda and Gandhi. So they were different in emphasis and spirit, though not a complete break from the Vedic tradition.
free.ifm-2022-gk-1c:
DukkhaSamudayaNirodhaAshtangika Marga

The Four Noble Truths (Arya Satyani) formed the core of the Buddha's first sermon at Sarnath (Dhammachakrapravartana).

1. Dukkha: birth, old age, disease, death and separation from what we love all bring suffering. 2. Samudaya: the cause of suffering is trishna (craving or desire) — for pleasure, existence and non-existence — rooted in ignorance. 3. Nirodha: suffering ends when craving is destroyed; this state is nirvana. 4. Marga: the way is the Eightfold Path (Ashtangika Marga) — right view, right resolve, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness and right concentration. These fall under wisdom (prajna), ethics (shila) and meditation (samadhi).

Related teachings: the Middle Path between luxury and extreme asceticism; anicca (impermanence) and anatta (no permanent self); karma; and Pratityasamutpada (dependent origination), which explains how suffering arises. The Buddha stressed ethical conduct, compassion and non-violence, and rejected ritual and caste privileges.
free.ifm-2022-gk-1d:
Enfield rifleGreased cartridgesMangal PandeyMeerut

The immediate cause of the Revolt of 1857 was the introduction of the new Enfield rifle, whose cartridges were said to be greased with the fat of cows and pigs. Sepoys had to bite off the paper cover before loading. This offended both Hindu and Muslim sepoys, who saw it as a deliberate attempt to destroy their religion and caste and convert them to Christianity.

Sequence of events

  • January–February 1857: rumours spread at Dum Dum and Barrackpore; the 19th Native Infantry at Berhampore refused the cartridges and was disbanded.
  • 29 March 1857: Mangal Pandey of the 34th Native Infantry attacked officers at Barrackpore; he was hanged and the regiment disbanded.
  • 9 May 1857: 85 sepoys at Meerut who refused the cartridges were court-martialled, given long sentences and publicly put in chains.
  • 10 May 1857: sepoys at Meerut rose in revolt, freed their comrades, killed officers and marched to Delhi, where they proclaimed Bahadur Shah Zafar emperor.

Although the authorities withdrew the cartridges, the distrust had already spread. The cartridge issue was a spark that ignited deeper causes — annexations (Doctrine of Lapse, Awadh in 1856), economic exploitation, land revenue policies, and the sepoys' grievances over pay and overseas service.
free.ifm-2022-gk-2a:
Imported inflationRepo rateSupply shocksInflation targeting

Globalised inflation means that price rises are driven by worldwide factors. In 2022, the Russia–Ukraine war, high crude oil, gas, fertiliser and edible-oil prices, post-pandemic supply-chain disruptions and the US Federal Reserve's sharp rate hikes pushed up inflation across the world. India's CPI inflation peaked at about 7.8% in April 2022, above the RBI's upper tolerance limit of 6%.

RBI's monetary response

  • Raised the repo rate by 250 basis points, from 4.0% (May 2022) to 6.5% (February 2023).
  • Withdrew surplus liquidity and introduced the Standing Deposit Facility as the floor of the corridor.
  • Changed its stance to "withdrawal of accommodation" and gave forward guidance.
  • Intervened in the forex market to limit rupee depreciation and the imported inflation it causes.

How effective was it?

  • Core inflation fell steadily, and headline inflation returned within the band; by 2025 it fell well below 4%, allowing the RBI to cut rates.
  • But much of the inflation was due to imported and supply-side factors, which interest rates cannot fix. Government action — cutting excise duty on fuel, export curbs on wheat and rice, releasing food stocks and lowering import duties on edible oils — played a big role.

Conclusion: monetary policy was effective in containing demand and expectations, but controlling globalised inflation needed coordination with fiscal and supply-side measures.
free.ifm-2022-gk-2b:
Incremental sales14 sectorsAtmanirbhar BharatGlobal value chains

The Production Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme, launched in 2020, gives companies cash incentives on incremental sales of goods made in India, to make domestic manufacturing globally competitive.

Main features

  • 14 sectors with an outlay of about ₹1.97 lakh crore: mobile phones and electronic components, pharmaceuticals, medical devices, automobiles and auto components, advanced chemistry cell batteries, telecom and networking products, food processing, white goods (ACs, LED lights), high-efficiency solar PV modules, textiles (man-made fibre and technical textiles), speciality steel, IT hardware, drones and drone components.
  • Incentives of about 4–6% (varying by sector) on incremental sales over a base year, for five years.
  • Thresholds of investment and sales so that only serious, large-scale players qualify.
  • Selection through a transparent, sector-specific process by the ministries concerned.
  • Linked to Make in India and Atmanirbhar Bharat.

Expected outcomes

  • Higher manufacturing output and exports; reducing imports in electronics, APIs and solar modules.
  • Investment and jobs: by 2025, the scheme had brought in investment of over ₹1.7 lakh crore, production of over ₹16 lakh crore and about 12 lakh jobs (Government figures).
  • Global value chains: attract firms shifting from China (Apple suppliers now make iPhones in India; India is the second-largest mobile phone maker).
  • Economies of scale, technology and R&D.
  • Strategic autonomy in pharmaceuticals and batteries.

Concerns: slow progress in some sectors (textiles, steel, batteries), low domestic value addition in assembly-based industries, and benefits concentrated in large firms. Reforms in logistics, labour and skills must accompany it.
free.ifm-2022-gk-2c:
e₹Legal tenderWholesale and retailProgrammable money

Meaning

The digital rupee (e₹) is a Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC) — a digital form of the Indian rupee, issued by the RBI and backed by it, just like currency notes. It is legal tender and a direct liability of the RBI, unlike bank deposits or private cryptocurrencies. The RBI launched pilots of the wholesale e₹ (e₹-W) on 1 November 2022 and the retail e₹ (e₹-R) on 1 December 2022. Retail users hold e₹ in digital wallets offered by banks.

Advantages

  • Lower cost of currency management: less printing, storage and transport of notes.
  • Safe and trusted: backed by the central bank, without the volatility of crypto assets.
  • Faster and cheaper settlement in inter-bank and cross-border payments.
  • Offline payments in areas with poor connectivity.
  • Programmability: money can be tied to a purpose — for example, subsidies used only for fertiliser.
  • Financial inclusion and a digital alternative to cash with some privacy.
  • Better monetary policy transmission and reduced shadow economy.
  • Cross-border use to reduce dependence on the dollar.

Challenges: cyber security, privacy concerns, possible withdrawal of deposits from banks, and low adoption because UPI already works well.
free.ifm-2022-gk-2d:
Strong dollarCapital outflowsCurrent account deficitImported inflation

The rupee fell from about ₹74 per dollar in early 2022 to over ₹82 by the end of that year, and weakened past ₹88 in 2025.

Reasons

  • Strong US dollar: US Federal Reserve rate hikes attracted money to the US.
  • Foreign portfolio outflows from Indian markets.
  • High crude oil and commodity prices raised the import bill.
  • Wider trade and current account deficits.
  • Geopolitical tensions — the Russia–Ukraine war, and US tariffs on India in 2025.
  • Inflation differential between India and its trading partners.

Impact on the economy

The RBI uses its forex reserves to smooth sharp falls, while promoting rupee trade settlement and export competitiveness to reduce vulnerability.
free.ifm-2022-gk-3a:
Unity in diversityUnion of StatesCooperative federalismLinguistic states

India is a continental-sized country with hundreds of languages, many religions, tribes and regions. The Constitution chose federalism — "a Union of States" (Article 1) — to hold this diversity together.

1. Why federalism suits India

  • Accommodation of diversity: the linguistic reorganisation of States (1956), the creation of new States (Jharkhand, Uttarakhand, Chhattisgarh, Telangana) and special provisions (Articles 371, 371A–J; Fifth and Sixth Schedules) gave regions self-rule and identity.
  • Governance closer to people: States govern police, agriculture, health and land, which differ from region to region.
  • Prevents secession: sharing power reduced separatist demands in Tamil Nadu, Punjab and parts of the North-East.
  • Laboratories of democracy: policies such as Tamil Nadu's mid-day meals and Kerala's literacy were later adopted nationally.

2. Constitutional features

  • Division of powers — Union, State and Concurrent Lists (Seventh Schedule).
  • Bicameral Parliament with the Rajya Sabha representing States.
  • Independent judiciary to settle disputes (Article 131).
  • Fiscal federalism through the Finance Commission and the GST Council — an example of pooled sovereignty.
  • Local government (73rd and 74th Amendments) — a third tier.

3. "Strong centre" and cooperative federalism

India's federalism is called "holding together" rather than "coming together". The strong Union (Articles 249, 252, 356, all-India services) was meant to preserve unity after Partition. Over time, cooperative federalism (NITI Aayog, GST Council, Inter-State Council) and competitive federalism (ranking States) have grown. In S.R. Bommai (1994) the Supreme Court declared federalism a basic feature.

4. Strains

Misuse of Article 356 in the past, the role of Governors, disputes over GST compensation, river waters and tax devolution.

Federalism has thus turned diversity into strength, making India a durable democracy.
free.ifm-2022-gk-3b:
Coalition eraConsensusRegional voicesCommon Minimum Programme

From 1989 to 2014, India was mostly ruled by coalition governments (National Front, United Front, NDA and UPA); since 2024 the government again depends on coalition partners.

How coalitions strengthen and deepen democracy

  • Wider representation: regional and smaller parties — representing States, castes and communities — get a share in national power.
  • Federalism: regional parties ensure that States' interests are heard in Delhi; it reduced the misuse of Article 356 after the Bommai judgment.
  • Consensus-based policy: coalitions work through a Common Minimum Programme and coordination committees, which demands compromise and dialogue among parties with different ideologies.
  • Checks on dominance: no single party can impose its agenda; allies act as internal checks.
  • Moderation of ideologies: parties have to moderate extreme positions to win partners.
  • Important reforms happened under coalitions — economic reforms (1991, minority government), RTI (2005), MGNREGA (2005), and nuclear deal debates.
  • Peaceful transfer of power among rival groups shows the maturity of Indian democracy.

Problems

  • Instability: frequent collapse of governments (1996–98).
  • Policy paralysis and "coalition dharma" compromises; pressure from small partners.
  • Opportunism: post-poll alliances that ignore the mandate; horse-trading.

Conclusion: despite instability, coalitions have made Indian democracy more inclusive, federal and consensual. Stable coalitions with clear agreements and the anti-defection law can combine diversity with good governance.
free.ifm-2022-gk-3c:
Sarva Dharma SambhavaPrincipled distanceArticles 25–30Pluralism

Indian secularism differs from the Western model of a strict "wall of separation" between religion and the State. It is based on equal respect for all religions (Sarva Dharma Sambhava) and principled distance (Rajeev Bhargava).

Why it is regarded as a model of inter-faith coexistence

  • Freedom of religion for all: Articles 25–28 guarantee freedom of conscience and the right to practise and propagate religion.
  • Minority rights: Articles 29–30 protect the culture, language and educational institutions of minorities.
  • No State religion; no discrimination on grounds of religion (Articles 14, 15, 16).
  • Positive engagement: the State can reform unjust practices within religions (abolition of untouchability, temple entry, the end of triple talaq) and help all communities equally.
  • Civilisational tradition of pluralism — Ashoka's tolerance, Akbar's sulh-i-kul, the Bhakti and Sufi movements, Gandhi's sarva dharma samabhava.
  • Basic structure: the Supreme Court declared secularism a basic feature (S.R. Bommai, 1994).
  • A vast country with followers of all major religions lives in democratic coexistence.

Challenges: communal violence, politicisation of religion and hate speech. Upholding constitutional values and inter-faith dialogue keeps the model strong.
free.ifm-2022-gk-3d:
Security of tenureCollegiumSeparation of powersContempt power

The Constitution ensures judicial independence through several provisions:

  • Security of tenure: judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts can be removed only by impeachment on grounds of proved misbehaviour or incapacity, with a special majority in both Houses (Articles 124(4), 217).
  • Appointment process: through the collegium system (Second and Third Judges cases, 1993 and 1998); the NJAC was struck down in 2015 to keep executive influence out.
  • Fixed salaries and service conditions, charged on the Consolidated Fund and not reduced to their disadvantage except in a financial emergency (Article 125).
  • Ban on practice after retirement in courts of the Union (Article 124(7)).
  • No discussion of a judge's conduct in Parliament or State legislatures except in a removal motion (Articles 121, 211).
  • Power to punish for contempt (Articles 129, 215).
  • Separation of judiciary from executive (Article 50).
  • Judicial review and the basic structure — the judiciary can strike down laws.
  • Expenses of the Supreme Court charged on the Consolidated Fund; the Court controls its own staff.

Concerns about post-retirement appointments, opacity in the collegium and vacancies remain, but these provisions make the Indian judiciary one of the most independent in the world.
free.ifm-2022-gk-4a:
Thermal expansionGlacier meltCoastal floodingSaltwater intrusion

Effects of climate change on sea level

According to the IPCC (AR6), the global mean sea level rose by about 20 cm between 1901 and 2018, and the rate has accelerated to about 3.7 mm a year (2006–2018). By 2100, it may rise by about 0.3–1 m depending on emissions, and more if ice sheets collapse.

Causes

  • Thermal expansion of warming ocean water.
  • Melting of glaciers and ice caps (Himalaya, Alps, Andes).
  • Loss of the Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets — the biggest long-term threat.
  • Changes in land-water storage (groundwater pumping).
  • Local factors: land subsidence in deltas (Ganga–Brahmaputra, Mahanadi) adds to relative sea-level rise.

Impacts on coastlines

  • Coastal erosion and land loss: about a third of India's shoreline is eroding (National Centre for Coastal Research).
  • Flooding and storm surges: higher sea levels make cyclones and high tides more destructive.
  • Saltwater intrusion into groundwater, rivers and farmland (Sundarbans, Kerala's Kuttanad).
  • Loss of wetlands and mangroves, coral reefs and turtle nesting beaches.
  • Small islands such as Lakshadweep and the Maldives face existential threats.

Impacts on coastal communities

  • Loss of homes and livelihoods of fishers and farmers; displacement and "climate refugees" (Ghoramara island in the Sundarbans).
  • Damage to infrastructure: ports, roads and cities such as Mumbai, Kolkata, Chennai and Surat.
  • Health: water-borne diseases, salinity in drinking water.
  • Economic losses to tourism, fisheries and agriculture.

India has a long coastline (re-measured at about 11,098 km in 2024) and crores of people live in its coastal districts, making adaptation urgent.

Adaptation: coastal zone management (CRZ rules), mangrove restoration (MISHTI scheme), early warning, climate-resilient infrastructure, planned retreat, and global emission cuts.
free.ifm-2022-gk-4b:
HIPPOEndemismHabitat lossMyers' criteria

1. Factors causing biodiversity loss (often summed up as HIPPO)

  • Habitat loss and fragmentation: clearing forests for agriculture, mining, roads, dams and cities — the biggest driver.
  • Invasive alien species: Lantana camara, water hyacinth and Prosopis juliflora displace native species.
  • Pollution: pesticides, fertilisers, plastics and industrial effluents; vulture populations collapsed due to the drug diclofenac.
  • Population growth and over-consumption.
  • Over-exploitation: poaching, overfishing, illegal wildlife trade and unsustainable harvesting.
  • Climate change: coral bleaching, shifting ranges, loss of alpine species.
  • Others: forest fires, diseases, loss of traditional crop varieties due to monocultures.

2. Characteristics of a biodiversity hotspot

The concept was given by Norman Myers (1988) and adopted by Conservation International. A region qualifies as a hotspot if:

  • it has at least 1,500 species of endemic vascular plants (over 0.5% of the world's total), and
  • it has lost at least 70% of its original natural vegetation.

Thus hotspots are rich in endemic species and highly threatened.

Other characteristics: high species richness, many threatened and endemic species, and high human pressure. Conserving these small areas protects a large share of the world's biodiversity at relatively low cost.
free.ifm-2022-gk-4c:
Warm oceansCoriolis forceSuper cycloneSundarbans

Tropical cyclones are intense low-pressure systems that form over warm tropical oceans with strong winds spiralling inward (anticlockwise in the Northern Hemisphere) around a calm eye.

Conditions for formation: sea-surface temperature above 26.5 °C, enough Coriolis force (they do not form at the equator), low vertical wind shear, moist mid-troposphere and a pre-existing disturbance. They weaken over land because they lose their supply of moisture.

Cyclone Amphan (May 2020)

  • Genesis: formed in the south-east Bay of Bengal around 16 May 2020 and intensified rapidly — within about a day — into a super cyclonic storm, the first in the Bay since the 1999 Odisha super cyclone. Unusually warm waters (around 30–33 °C) fuelled it.
  • It weakened slightly and made landfall on 20 May near the Sundarbans between Digha (West Bengal) and Hatiya (Bangladesh), with wind speeds of about 155–165 km/h.

Impact on India

  • Severe damage in West Bengal (Kolkata, North and South 24 Parganas) and parts of Odisha; dozens of deaths.
  • Uprooted trees, destroyed houses, power and telecom outages; flooding of farmland with saline water.
  • Estimated losses of about US$ 13 billion — the costliest cyclone in the North Indian Ocean at that time.
  • It struck during the COVID-19 lockdown, complicating evacuation of millions.
  • The Sundarbans mangroves absorbed part of the storm's force.

Accurate forecasts by IMD and large evacuations kept the death toll much lower than in past cyclones.
free.ifm-2022-gk-4d:
Water-bearing rockOver-extractionFree electricityRecharge

An aquifer is an underground layer of permeable rock, sand or gravel that stores and transmits groundwater, from which water can be drawn through wells.

  • Unconfined aquifer: the upper surface is the water table, open to recharge from rain.
  • Confined aquifer: lies between impermeable layers and is under pressure (artesian wells).
  • Perched aquifer: a small saturated zone above the main water table.

Groundwater in India: India is the world's largest user of groundwater. The Dynamic Groundwater Assessment (2024) shows the stage of extraction at about 60%, but about 11% of assessment units are over-exploited, mainly in Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan, Delhi and parts of the south.

Main causes of depletion

  • Over-extraction for irrigation — about 87% of extracted groundwater is used for farming.
  • Water-intensive crops such as paddy and sugarcane in dry regions.
  • Free or subsidised electricity for pumps, encouraging over-pumping.
  • Urbanisation: cities depend on borewells; concrete surfaces reduce recharge.
  • Industrial use and pollution of shallow aquifers.
  • Loss of recharge zones: encroachment on lakes, ponds and wetlands; deforestation.
  • Erratic rainfall due to climate change.
  • Weak regulation: groundwater is linked to land ownership, so it is treated as private property.

Remedies: Atal Bhujal Yojana (community management), Jal Shakti Abhiyan "Catch the Rain", Amrit Sarovars, micro-irrigation, crop diversification and aquifer mapping.
free.ifm-2022-gk-5a:
Minor forest produceTribal livelihoodsFRA 2006Van Dhan

Non-timber forest products (NTFPs), also called minor forest produce (MFP), are all biological products from forests other than timber. Examples: tendu leaves, mahua flowers and seeds, sal seeds and leaves, bamboo, honey, lac, gums and resins, tamarind, amla, medicinal plants, mushrooms, chironji and broom grass.

Importance

About 27.5 crore people in India depend on forests for their livelihood, and NTFPs give many tribal households a large part of their cash income, especially in the lean season.

How NTFPs ensure sustainable livelihoods

  • Regular income without cutting trees, so forests remain standing.
  • Food and nutrition security: fruits, tubers, mushrooms and honey.
  • Women's empowerment: women do most of the collection and processing.
  • Value addition and enterprise: processing into products such as mahua drinks, honey, lac bangles and herbal medicines.
  • Traditional knowledge is preserved.

Legal and policy support

  • Forest Rights Act, 2006: gives forest dwellers ownership rights over minor forest produce, including the right to collect, use and sell.
  • PESA, 1996: gives Gram Sabhas ownership of MFP in Scheduled Areas.
  • The Indian Forest Act was amended (2017) so that bamboo grown outside forests is no longer a "tree", allowing free trade.
  • MSP for MFP scheme (from 2013-14), covering about 87 items.
  • Pradhan Mantri Van Dhan Yojana (2018): Van Dhan Vikas Kendras with self-help groups for processing and marketing; TRIFED and Tribes India outlets.

Challenges: exploitation by middlemen, lack of storage and processing, State monopolies on some products (tendu), over-harvesting, and weak awareness of rights. Strengthening Gram Sabhas, cooperatives and fair markets can make NTFPs a pillar of both livelihoods and conservation.
free.ifm-2022-gk-5b:
Forest (Conservation) Act 1980Stage I approvalCompensatory afforestationFRA concerns

The Forest Conservation Rules, 2022 were notified on 28 June 2022 under the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980, replacing the 2003 rules. They govern the process of diverting forest land for non-forest purposes.

1. Main features

  • Committees: an Advisory Committee at the Centre, Regional Empowered Committees at Integrated Regional Offices, and a Project Screening Committee in each State to examine proposals.
  • Timelines for each stage of approval to speed up decisions.
  • Compensatory afforestation (CA):

- Allowed private persons and companies to raise plantations on non-forest land, which can later be traded to project developers needing land for compensatory afforestation (a "land bank" system). - In hilly or mountainous States with forest cover over two-thirds of their area, or States with forest cover above one-third, CA may be done in other States with low forest cover.

  • Exemptions and relaxations for linear projects (roads, railways) near borders, strategic and security projects, and small projects.
  • Forest Rights Act compliance: the Central Government may grant final approval and leave it to the State Government to settle forest rights under the FRA after approval, instead of requiring the Gram Sabha's consent before the Stage I clearance as under earlier guidelines.

2. Why they were considered more liberal towards development

  • Diluted the role of Gram Sabhas: forest-dwellers' consent was no longer a precondition for Central clearance; critics, including the National Commission for Scheduled Tribes, said this weakened the FRA.
  • Faster clearances with fixed timelines and fewer stages.
  • Compensatory afforestation land banks let projects buy ready-made plantations — critics feared that natural forests would be replaced by plantations of poor ecological value.
  • Wider exemptions for linear and strategic projects.
  • Ease of doing business: aimed to reduce delays in infrastructure and mining.

3. Later developments

The Forest (Conservation) Act was amended in 2023 and renamed the Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam; new rules were issued in 2023. The Supreme Court in 2024 directed that the broad definition of "forest" from the T.N. Godavarman (1996) case continue to apply.

A balance requires respecting forest rights and ecological value while allowing essential development.
free.ifm-2022-gk-5c:
GI Act 1999Origin-linked qualityPremium priceRural branding

A Geographical Indication (GI) is a sign used on products that have a specific geographical origin and possess qualities or a reputation due to that origin. India's GI of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999 (in force from 2003) governs GI tags; Darjeeling tea was the first GI (2004). India now has more than 600 GI tags.

Examples of agricultural and horticultural GIs: Basmati rice, Kashmir saffron, Nagpur orange, Ratnagiri Alphonso mango, Banaganapalle mango, Malabar pepper, Coorg arabica coffee, Joha rice (Assam), Kandhamal haldi, Madurai malli (jasmine), Bhalia wheat (Gujarat) and Dalle khursani (Sikkim).

How GI tags add value

  • Premium prices: consumers pay more for authentic origin-linked quality.
  • Protection from imitation: only authorised users can use the name; it prevents misuse at home and abroad.
  • Export promotion: recognised brands in global markets (Bhalia wheat and Madurai malli have been exported).
  • Rural livelihoods and FPOs: collective branding by farmer groups.
  • Conservation of traditional varieties and knowledge.
  • Tourism and regional identity.

Challenges: low awareness among farmers, weak quality control and enforcement, few authorised users, and limited marketing. Linking GIs with the "One District One Product" scheme and better post-registration support can maximise value.
free.ifm-2022-gk-5d:
HYV seedsGroundwater depletionSoil degradationRegional imbalance

The Green Revolution (from the mid-1960s) used high-yielding varieties (HYV) of wheat and rice, chemical fertilisers, pesticides and irrigation. It made India self-sufficient in food grains and ended dependence on food aid. But it is considered unsustainable because:

  • Groundwater depletion: rice and wheat in Punjab and Haryana need heavy irrigation; water tables are falling fast, and most blocks in Punjab are over-exploited.
  • Soil degradation: excessive and imbalanced use of fertilisers (too much urea), loss of organic matter, micronutrient deficiencies, salinity and waterlogging.
  • Pesticide overuse: residues in food and water, health problems and resistance in pests.
  • Monoculture of rice and wheat: loss of crop diversity — pulses, millets and oilseeds were neglected, harming nutrition.
  • Stubble burning of paddy residue pollutes the air in north India.
  • High input costs and farmer indebtedness.
  • Regional and social inequality: benefits went mainly to irrigated regions and larger farmers.
  • Declining returns: yields have plateaued despite more inputs.
  • Climate stress: heat and water scarcity threaten this input-intensive model.

The way forward is an "evergreen revolution" (M.S. Swaminathan) — crop diversification, water-efficient irrigation, balanced fertilisers (Soil Health Cards), natural and organic farming, and climate-resilient varieties.
free.ifm-2022-gk-6a:
Layer by layerDigital designCustomisationLess waste

Additive manufacturing (3D printing) builds a three-dimensional object layer by layer from a digital design (CAD file), by adding material — plastic, metal, resin, ceramic, concrete or even living cells. It is the opposite of subtractive manufacturing, where material is cut away from a block.

Main techniques: fused deposition modelling (melting plastic filament), stereolithography (curing liquid resin with light), selective laser sintering and melting (fusing powder, including metals).

Usefulness in diverse fields

  • Healthcare: custom prosthetics, implants, dental crowns, hearing aids; surgical models; bioprinting of tissues; India has made low-cost 3D-printed prosthetic limbs.
  • Aerospace and space: light, complex engine parts. Agnikul Cosmos launched a rocket with a single-piece 3D-printed engine from Sriharikota in May 2024.
  • Defence: spare parts on demand, drones.
  • Construction: India's first 3D-printed post office opened in Bengaluru in 2023; low-cost houses can be built quickly.
  • Automobile and manufacturing: rapid prototyping, tools and spare parts.
  • Education and research: models for teaching and experiments.
  • Consumer goods: jewellery, footwear, fashion and customised products.
  • Food and architecture: printed foods and complex designs.

Advantages: customisation, complex shapes, less waste, faster prototyping, and local, on-demand production.

Limitations: high cost of machines and metal printing, slow speed for mass production, limited materials, and concerns about printed weapons and intellectual property.

India's National Strategy on Additive Manufacturing (2022) aims to build a strong 3D-printing industry.
free.ifm-2022-gk-6b:
Cyber-physical systemsAI and automationReskillingPlatform economy

The Fourth Industrial Revolution (4IR), a term popularised by Klaus Schwab of the World Economic Forum (2016), is the fusion of digital, physical and biological technologies. It follows steam (1st), electricity and mass production (2nd), and computers and the internet (3rd).

1. Key technologies

2. Impact on the future of work

  • Job displacement: routine tasks in manufacturing, clerical work, data entry and customer service are being automated.
  • New jobs: in AI, data science, cyber security, renewable energy and the care economy. The WEF's Future of Jobs Report 2025 expects about 170 million jobs to be created and 92 million displaced by 2030 — a net gain, but with major churn.
  • Changing skills: analytical thinking, creativity, technological literacy and lifelong learning become essential.
  • Gig and platform work: flexible work through apps, but with insecurity and weak social protection.
  • Remote and hybrid work across borders.
  • Inequality: a gap between high-skill, high-pay jobs and low-skill workers; a digital divide.
  • Productivity gains in agriculture (precision farming), health (telemedicine) and governance.

3. India's response

Skill India, FutureSkills Prime, the IndiaAI Mission (2024), Digital India, Samarth Udyog Bharat 4.0, and social security for gig workers under the Code on Social Security, 2020.

The 4IR can boost growth if workers are reskilled and its benefits are widely shared.
free.ifm-2022-gk-6c:
27% dark matter68% dark energyRotation curvesGravitational lensing

Dark matter is matter that does not emit, absorb or reflect light and so cannot be seen, but its presence is known from its gravitational effects. It makes up about 27% of the universe's mass–energy.

Dark energy is a mysterious form of energy that causes the expansion of the universe to accelerate. It makes up about 68% of the universe. It was inferred in 1998 from observations of distant Type Ia supernovae (Nobel Prize in Physics, 2011). Ordinary matter is only about 5%.

How we know dark matter exists

  • Galaxy rotation curves: stars in the outer parts of galaxies move as fast as those near the centre (Vera Rubin, 1970s); visible mass is not enough to hold them, so unseen mass must exist.
  • Galaxy clusters: Fritz Zwicky (1933) found galaxies in the Coma cluster moving too fast for the visible mass.
  • Gravitational lensing: light from distant objects bends more than visible matter can explain; the Bullet Cluster shows mass separated from hot gas.
  • Cosmic microwave background: patterns measured by WMAP and Planck require dark matter.
  • Structure formation: galaxies could not have formed so quickly without extra gravity.

Missions such as Euclid (2023) and surveys such as DESI are mapping the universe to understand both mysteries.
free.ifm-2022-gk-6d:
Caesium-133Hyperfine transitionDefinition of the secondNavIC and IST

Atomic clocks measure time using the natural, extremely stable frequency of radiation emitted or absorbed when electrons in atoms move between two energy levels. Since 1967, the second has been defined as 9,192,631,770 oscillations of the radiation from the hyperfine transition of the caesium-133 atom. Other atomic clocks use rubidium, hydrogen masers, or optical transitions in strontium and ytterbium.

Why they are more accurate than mechanical clocks

  • Identical atoms: every caesium atom has the same transition frequency, so the "pendulum" never changes.
  • High frequency allows finer division of time.
  • No mechanical wear.

Uses: GPS and NavIC satellite navigation (each satellite carries atomic clocks), telecom and internet synchronisation, power grids, stock markets, space missions and scientific research. In India, the National Physical Laboratory maintains Indian Standard Time using atomic clocks.
free.ifm-2023-ge-1a:
Ecosystem servicesSixth mass extinction30x30Coexistence

Biodiversity and Human Existence

Every breath we take, every meal we eat and almost every medicine we use comes to us from the web of life. Bees pollinate our crops, microbes make our soils fertile, forests and oceans absorb the carbon we emit, and wetlands clean our water. Biodiversity — the variety of genes, species and ecosystems on Earth — is not a luxury to be admired in zoos and documentaries. It is the foundation of human existence. Yet we are destroying it at a speed never seen in human history.

What biodiversity gives us

Scientists call the benefits of nature ecosystem services. Provisioning services give us food, timber, fibre, fuel and fresh water. Nearly all our crops and livestock were domesticated from wild species, and their wild relatives still hold the genes we need to breed varieties that resist heat, drought and disease. Regulating services control climate, floods, pests and diseases: mangroves blunt cyclones, forests regulate rainfall, and predators keep pests in check. About three-quarters of the world's food crop types depend at least partly on animal pollinators. Supporting services such as soil formation and nutrient cycling make all life possible. Cultural services — the sacred groves of the Western Ghats and Meghalaya, the reverence for the tiger and the peepal tree, the joy of a bird's song — give meaning to human life.

Biodiversity is also a pharmacy. Aspirin came from willow bark, the anti-malarial artemisinin from a plant, and many cancer drugs from forest and marine organisms. Traditional systems such as Ayurveda and the knowledge of tribal healers rely on thousands of medicinal plants.

A crisis of our making

The Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services (IPBES) warned in 2019 that about one million species face extinction. The WWF's Living Planet Report 2024 found that monitored wildlife populations have declined by an average of 73% since 1970. Many scientists speak of a sixth mass extinction, the first caused by a single species.

The drivers are well known: land-use change as forests and grasslands become farms, mines and cities; over-exploitation through overfishing, poaching and logging; climate change, which bleaches coral reefs and pushes species uphill; pollution by plastics, pesticides and fertilisers; and invasive species such as Lantana in Indian forests.

Why the loss threatens us

When biodiversity declines, ecosystems become fragile. A forest with fewer species is more vulnerable to pests and fire; a farm landscape without pollinators produces less food. The loss of natural habitat brings humans into closer contact with wildlife and raises the risk of diseases that jump from animals to people — COVID-19, Nipah and Ebola remind us of this danger. Fisheries collapse when oceans are overfished, threatening the protein supply of millions. Poor and indigenous communities, who depend most directly on nature, suffer first and most.

India's responsibility

India is one of the world's megadiverse countries, holding about 7–8% of recorded species on 2.4% of the world's land, and parts of four of the 36 global biodiversity hotspots — the Himalaya, the Western Ghats, the Indo-Burma region and Sundaland. Project Tiger has more than doubled the tiger population since 2006; the Asiatic lion has recovered in Gir; community efforts by the Bishnois and the Chipko movement are celebrated around the world. But wetlands are shrinking, grasslands are neglected, and species such as the Great Indian Bustard are close to extinction.

What must be done

The Kunming–Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (2022) commits countries to protect 30% of land and sea by 2030 and to restore degraded ecosystems. India has updated its National Biodiversity Strategy and Action Plan and amended the Biological Diversity Act in 2023. Real progress requires:

  • protecting and connecting habitats through corridors;
  • respecting the rights and knowledge of indigenous and local communities, who are often the best conservators;
  • sustainable agriculture and fisheries that work with nature;
  • fair sharing of benefits from the use of genetic resources;
  • valuing nature in economic decisions, and reducing wasteful consumption, as the Mission LiFE campaign urges.

Conclusion

Chief Seattle is often quoted as saying that man did not weave the web of life; he is merely a strand in it, and whatever he does to the web he does to himself. Biodiversity is not something separate from us that we can choose to save or spend. It is the living system that sustains us. To protect it is not charity towards other species — it is the condition for our own survival.
free.ifm-2023-ge-1b:
PuttaswamyDPDP Act 2023ConsentSurveillance capitalism

Data Privacy in the Digital Age

Every time we unlock a phone, pay through UPI, search the internet or walk past a CCTV camera, we leave a trail of data. That data reveals where we go, what we buy, whom we talk to, what we believe and even how we feel. In the digital age, data has been called the new oil. But unlike oil, data is about people. Who controls it, and how it is used, has become one of the central questions of freedom in our time.

Why privacy matters

Privacy is not about having something to hide. It is about autonomy and dignity — the freedom to think, communicate and live without being watched, profiled or manipulated. In Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017), a nine-judge bench of the Supreme Court held that privacy is a fundamental right under Article 21, including informational privacy.

Without privacy, democracy itself is at risk. The Cambridge Analytica scandal of 2018 showed how personal data of millions of Facebook users could be harvested to target political messages. Targeted advertising, credit scoring by algorithms and facial recognition can lead to discrimination, manipulation and surveillance.

The threats

  • Data breaches and cybercrime: hospitals, government portals and companies have suffered breaches; the ransomware attack on AIIMS Delhi in 2022 crippled its systems. Leaked data feeds fraud and identity theft.
  • Surveillance capitalism: many "free" apps earn money by collecting and selling behavioural data, often without meaningful consent.
  • State surveillance: powerful tools such as spyware can be misused against journalists, activists and opponents.
  • Artificial intelligence: AI systems are trained on huge datasets, including personal data, and deepfakes can misuse a person's face and voice.
  • Children are especially vulnerable to tracking and exploitation online.

India's legal response

After years of debate, India enacted the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023. It requires consent for processing personal data, limits use to specified purposes, gives citizens rights to access, correct and erase their data and to nominate someone, requires verifiable parental consent for children, and sets up a Data Protection Board that can impose penalties of up to ₹250 crore. The DPDP Rules were notified in November 2025, with obligations coming into force in phases over 18 months.

Critics point out that the Act gives the government wide powers to exempt its own agencies, and that amendments to the RTI Act could restrict access to information. Supporters argue that it balances privacy with innovation and the needs of a digital economy. Its success will depend on how independently the Board functions and how seriously companies comply.

Building a privacy culture

Laws are necessary but not enough. We need:

  • Privacy by design: systems that collect only the data they need and protect it with encryption;
  • Strong cyber security for government and private databases;
  • Clear, simple consent instead of long, unreadable terms and conditions;
  • Digital literacy, so that citizens know their rights and can protect themselves from fraud;
  • Oversight of surveillance by Parliament and the courts;
  • Ethical AI, with transparency about how personal data is used.

India's digital public infrastructure, such as Aadhaar, UPI and the Account Aggregator framework, can show the world how to combine scale with consent-based data sharing — if privacy is built into its foundations.

Conclusion

Technology has given us immense convenience and opportunity, but it must remain our servant and not become our master. A digital society that does not respect privacy can slide into a surveillance society. The challenge of our age is to enjoy the benefits of data while ensuring that every person remains the owner of their own life story. As the Supreme Court reminded us, privacy is the constitutional core of human dignity.
free.ifm-2023-ge-1c:
Demographic windowAgeingSocial securitySkilling

Today's Demographic Dividend is Tomorrow's Crisis of Elderly Population

India is a young nation. Its median age is under 30, and about two-thirds of its people are of working age. This demographic dividend — a large working population supporting relatively few dependants — is often described as India's greatest asset. But demography is destiny only for those who ignore it. The young workers of today will be the elderly of tomorrow, and if India does not prepare, today's dividend may turn into tomorrow's crisis.

The coming age wave

India's fertility rate has fallen to about 2.0 children per woman (NFHS-5), below the replacement level of 2.1. States such as Kerala, Tamil Nadu and Andhra Pradesh have much lower rates. At the same time, life expectancy has risen to about 70 years. According to the India Ageing Report 2023 (UNFPA), the share of people aged 60 and above, about 10.5% in 2022, is expected to double to about 20.8% — some 34.7 crore people — by 2050. By the mid-2040s, the elderly may outnumber children. Southern States and Himachal Pradesh are already ageing fast, while northern States remain young.

Why it could become a crisis

First, India risks growing old before it grows rich. Japan, Korea and China became wealthy before they aged; India's per-capita income is still low.

Second, social security is weak. Most Indians work in the informal sector and have no pension. Only a small share of the elderly receive regular pensions, and old-age pensions under the National Social Assistance Programme are meagre.

Third, health care costs will rise sharply as chronic diseases such as diabetes, heart disease and dementia increase. Out-of-pocket health spending already pushes many families into poverty.

Fourth, family support is weakening. Migration of the young to cities and abroad, smaller families and nuclear households leave many old people, especially widowed women, living alone and poor.

Fifth, a smaller workforce will have to support more dependants, putting pressure on public finances and growth.

Why the dividend itself is not guaranteed

A demographic dividend is only a window of opportunity. It pays off only if the young are educated, healthy and productively employed. If millions of young people remain unskilled or unemployed, as many are today, they will reach old age without savings, assets or pensions — the dividend will have been wasted and the crisis will be deeper.

Turning the challenge into opportunity

  • Use the dividend now: invest in quality education, skills and job-rich growth, especially for women, whose low participation in work is a missed opportunity.
  • Universal pensions: expand contributory schemes such as the Atal Pension Yojana and the National Pension System, and extend social security to gig and informal workers under the labour codes.
  • Health care for the elderly: Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY now covers all citizens aged 70 and above (2024); geriatric care, palliative care and health insurance need to expand.
  • Active ageing: flexible work and re-skilling for older people who want to keep working; the "silver economy" of products and services for the elderly can create jobs.
  • Protection and dignity: enforce the Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007, build day-care centres and community support, and encourage inter-generational bonds.
  • Learn from others: Japan's long-term care insurance and Korea's pension reforms offer lessons.

Conclusion

Ageing is a sign of success — of better health, education and control over fertility. It becomes a crisis only when society fails to prepare. India has perhaps two to three decades in which its working population will remain large. What it does with this window — whether it builds the skills, savings, health systems and social security of its people — will decide whether its old age is one of dignity or of distress. The time to plan for tomorrow's grandparents is today.

Life Skills Education should be an Essential Part of School Curriculum

A student may know the formula for the area of a circle and the dates of the Mughal emperors, yet feel helpless when faced with failure, peer pressure, an online scam or an angry friend. Schools have long measured success by marks, but life tests us in ways no examination does. That is why life skills education must become an essential part of the school curriculum.

What are life skills?

The World Health Organization defines life skills as abilities for adaptive and positive behaviour that enable individuals to deal effectively with the demands and challenges of everyday life. It lists ten core skills: decision-making, problem-solving, creative thinking, critical thinking, effective communication, interpersonal relationships, self-awareness, empathy, coping with emotions and coping with stress. To these we may add financial literacy, digital safety, health and hygiene, and civic responsibility.

Why they matter today

First, young people face growing pressures. Competitive examinations, social media and comparison with others have led to rising stress, anxiety and mental-health problems among students. Coping skills and emotional awareness can help them seek help and bounce back from setbacks.

Second, the world of work has changed. Employers increasingly value communication, teamwork, adaptability and problem-solving — skills that machines cannot easily replace. The World Economic Forum lists analytical thinking, resilience and curiosity among the most important skills for the future.

Third, the digital world brings new risks: cyberbullying, online fraud, misinformation and addiction to screens. Critical thinking and digital literacy are now survival skills.

Fourth, health and safety depend on informed choices — about nutrition, substance abuse, road safety and reproductive health.

Fifth, democracy needs citizens who can listen, argue respectfully, empathise with others and resolve conflicts peacefully.

What India is doing

The National Education Policy 2020 calls for holistic education that develops not only cognitive abilities but also social, ethical and emotional capacities, and for experiential learning, vocational exposure and reduced rote learning. The National Curriculum Framework for School Education (2023) builds these goals into the syllabus. The School Health and Wellness Programme under Ayushman Bharat trains teachers as health and wellness ambassadors, and some States have introduced happiness and well-being curricula, mindfulness sessions and entrepreneurship programmes. CBSE has published life-skills manuals.

Challenges

  • Exam-centred culture: parents and schools focus on marks and coaching; life skills are seen as an "extra".
  • Teacher capacity: teaching empathy or stress management needs trained teachers and counsellors, who are scarce.
  • Assessment: life skills are hard to measure in a marks-based system.
  • Time and resources in overcrowded classrooms.

How to make it work

  • Make life skills a graded, regular part of the timetable, not an occasional workshop.
  • Integrate them into all subjects through projects, group work, debates and role plays.
  • Train teachers and appoint school counsellors.
  • Involve parents and communities, and use local contexts and languages.
  • Use holistic report cards, as recommended by NEP 2020, to value these skills.

Conclusion

Education, as Swami Vivekananda said, is the manifestation of the perfection already in man. Its purpose is not merely to fill minds with information but to prepare young people to live wisely, work well and care for others. Life skills are the bridge between knowledge and life. A school that teaches them is preparing its students not just for examinations, but for living.

Style as conventionArt as social activityGenius and milieuKroeber

A style is the conventional way of executing formal designs. All art appeals through some formal arrangement of lines, surfaces, sounds, colours or rhythms. A new design that wins social acceptance becomes a fashion and, in time, a style. Styles arise and change because art is a social activity: society frames the individual artist, whose creative joy lies in being seen, appreciated and copied.

Since styles are born and die within a society, and an innovator succeeds only by creating a taste others imitate, genius is a product of its social setting and of the opportunity and appreciation society offers. Even unrecognised masters owed their achievement to their age. Genius is not inherited; sensitivity, emotional intensity, imagination and the power to fuse perception, thought and feeling are essential, but they flourish only in a favourable climate. Hence Kroeber treated the number and quality of creative geniuses as an index of a culture's flowering or decline.

free.ifm-2023-ge-4a: Agriculture is no longer the only viable activity because its relative economic value has fallen sharply — it now contributes only about one-sixth of GDP, though most rural people still depend on it. As a result, more villagers are taking up non-farm work such as transport services, business enterprises and craft manufacturing, and those living close enough commute daily to nearby towns for work while continuing to live in the village.
free.ifm-2023-ge-4b: Mass media and communication now bring images of urban lifestyles and consumption into villages, so urban norms and standards are known even in remote areas. This creates new desires and aspirations for consumer goods. With mass transport and communication bridging the rural–urban gap, rural areas are being more closely integrated into the consumer market; people also have to buy things they once got free, such as fuel, fodder and supplementary food.
free.ifm-2023-ge-4c: Common property resources are resources owned and used collectively by the village community, such as ponds, forests and grazing lands. They are important because they allowed poor people with little or no land to survive in the villages — giving them fish, fuel, fodder and supplementary food free of cost. As these resources are privatised or exhausted, the poor must buy these things in the market, their hardship increases, and many are pushed to migrate to cities.
free.ifm-2023-ge-4d: The city offers relative anonymity, since people mostly interact with strangers. For socially oppressed groups such as Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, this gives partial protection from the daily humiliation they face in villages where everyone knows their caste. It also allows the poorer members of dominant rural groups to take up low-status work that would be socially unacceptable for them in the village. Thus anonymity makes the city an attractive destination and encourages migration.
free.ifm-2023-ge-4e: The passage points out that although urbanisation is rapid and the big metropolises are growing fastest — with more than two-thirds of the urban population in million-plus cities whose infrastructure cannot keep pace — and although the media's focus makes the public face of India increasingly urban, the country remains largely rural, and rural areas are still the decisive force in political power. In other words, India looks urban but is politically governed by its rural majority.

Kalinga warEdictsDhamma mahamattasEthical code

After the Kalinga war (c. 261 BCE), whose bloodshed he regretted in Major Rock Edict XIII, Ashoka replaced bherighosha (the sound of war drums) with dhammaghosha (the sound of Dhamma). His Dhamma was not the Buddhist creed as such but a code of moral conduct and social responsibility meant for all his subjects.

1. Main principles of Ashoka's Dhamma

  • Respect and kindness: obedience to parents and elders, respect for teachers, kindness to slaves and servants, generosity to Brahmanas and Shramanas.
  • Non-violence: restrictions on animal slaughter and a ban on sacrifices and festive gatherings (samajas) involving killing (Rock Edict I); the royal kitchen cut meat dishes.
  • Tolerance (Rock Edict XII): honour all sects; restraint in speech (vachaguti); one who disparages others' sects harms his own.
  • Self-examination: avoid anger, cruelty, pride and envy.
  • Welfare (Rock Edict II, Pillar Edict VII): medical care for humans and animals, wells, rest houses and shade trees along roads.

2. How it was practised

  • Dhamma mahamattas (from the 13th regnal year, Rock Edict V) to spread Dhamma and look after the welfare of all sects, women and prisoners.
  • Dhamma yatras replaced royal hunting tours; the king met people and officials.
  • Rajukas and yuktas toured every five years to teach Dhamma and give justice.
  • Edicts in Prakrit in Brahmi and Kharosthi (and Greek and Aramaic in the north-west) so that ordinary people could understand them.
  • Missions abroad to Sri Lanka (Mahinda and Sanghamitra) and to Hellenistic kingdoms.
  • Lenient justice: a three-day respite for those sentenced to death.

3. Significance

Dhamma gave a common ethical bond to a vast, diverse empire and is an early example of a welfare state and of religious tolerance. Critics (H.C. Raychaudhuri) argue that the stress on non-violence weakened the army and contributed to the decline of the empire, while Romila Thapar sees it as a practical policy to unify the empire.

KannaujHiuen TsangPulakeshin IINalanda

Harshavardhana (606–647 CE) of the Pushyabhuti dynasty ruled from Thanesar and later Kannauj. His reign was the last great attempt to unify north India before the Rajput period. Our sources are Banabhatta's Harshacharita, the account of the Chinese pilgrim Hiuen Tsang (Xuanzang), and the Banskhera and Madhuban inscriptions.

1. Political significance

  • Unification of north India: he avenged his brother and sister (Rajyashri), took over Kannauj, and controlled Punjab to Bengal and Odisha; he was called Sakalottarapathanatha (lord of the whole north).
  • Kannauj became the political centre of north India, later contested by the Pratiharas, Palas and Rashtrakutas (the tripartite struggle).
  • Limits: he was defeated by Pulakeshin II of the Chalukyas on the Narmada (Aihole inscription), which fixed the Narmada as the southern boundary.
  • Administration: a feudal structure in which samantas held land; land grants to officials and priests; light taxation according to Hiuen Tsang; the king toured constantly.
  • Diplomacy: an embassy to the Tang emperor of China (641 CE).

2. Cultural significance

  • Patron of learning: he gave large grants to Nalanda, which Hiuen Tsang described as a great centre with thousands of students.
  • Author: he wrote three Sanskrit plays — Nagananda, Ratnavali and Priyadarshika; court poets included Banabhatta and Mayura.
  • Religious tolerance: he worshipped Shiva and the Sun and later favoured Mahayana Buddhism; he held the Kannauj assembly to honour Hiuen Tsang and the Prayag assembly (Mahamoksha Parishad) every five years, where he gave away his wealth.
  • Hiuen Tsang's account is a valuable record of society, religion and the economy of the time.

His empire did not survive him, but Harsha's reign was a bridge between the classical Gupta age and early medieval India.

Bal Gangadhar Tilak rejected the Moderates' "prayers and petitions" and made passive resistance — peaceful refusal to cooperate with the colonial government — a method of struggle.

How he introduced it

  • Mass mobilisation: the Ganapati (1893) and Shivaji (1895) festivals, and his papers Kesari and Mahratta, took politics to ordinary people.
  • No-revenue campaign (1896–97): during the famine in Maharashtra, he urged peasants to demand relief under the Famine Code and to withhold land revenue if crops had failed.
  • Swadeshi and boycott (1905–08): after the partition of Bengal, he spread the movement to Bombay and Poona through bonfires of foreign cloth, picketing and swadeshi stores.
  • "Tenets of the New Party" (Calcutta, 1907): he said the British ruled with Indian help; if Indians refused to help collect revenue, run the administration or fight their wars, the government could not run. He called for boycott of foreign goods, government schools, courts and services, national education and self-help.
  • "Swaraj is my birthright": the goal of self-rule.

This method — non-violent non-cooperation backed by the masses — anticipated Gandhi's Non-Cooperation Movement, though in Tilak's time it lacked an organised mass base and was suppressed after 1908.

By the late 1920s and early 1930s, socialist ideas became a powerful force in the national movement.

Circumstances that led to it

  • Russian Revolution (1917): the Soviet model of planned growth inspired Indian leaders; Nehru visited the USSR in 1927.
  • Disillusionment after the Non-Cooperation Movement was withdrawn (1922); the young looked for a more radical programme.
  • Great Depression (1929): prices of farm produce collapsed, and peasants and workers suffered; the colonial economy came under question.
  • Rise of organised labour and peasants: the AITUC (1920), the great textile strikes in Bombay (1928) led by the Girni Kamgar Union, and kisan sabhas.
  • Communist and left groups: the Communist Party of India (1925), the Workers' and Peasants' Parties (1926–28); repression in the Meerut Conspiracy Case (1929) made them popular.
  • Revolutionary socialism: the Hindustan Socialist Republican Association (1928) of Bhagat Singh and Chandrashekhar Azad.
  • Youth leadership: Nehru and Subhas Chandra Bose toured the country, spoke of socialism and led youth leagues.

Result: the Congress adopted the Karachi Resolution (1931) on Fundamental Rights and Economic Policy, and the Congress Socialist Party was formed in 1934. Socialism shaped later ideas of planning and social justice.

Human capitalProductivityHDIDemographic dividend

How investment in people drives growth

Spending on education, health, nutrition and skills builds human capital, which raises growth in several ways:

  • Productivity: educated and healthy workers produce more and earn more.
  • Innovation and technology: skilled people create and adopt new technology (endogenous growth theory).
  • Better use of physical capital: machines and infrastructure need skilled workers.
  • Health: fewer sick days and a longer working life.
  • Social returns: educated mothers have healthier children; lower fertility; better governance and participation.

East Asian economies such as South Korea grew fast after investing early in universal education and health.

Why it is crucial for India

  • Demographic dividend: about two-thirds of Indians are of working age; without skills, the dividend can turn into a burden.
  • Low human development: India ranks 130 of 193 (HDI 0.685, HDR 2025); its Human Capital Index (World Bank, 2020) is 0.49.
  • Learning gaps: ASER surveys show many children in class V cannot read class II text.
  • Health and nutrition: stunting in about 35% of children (NFHS-5) and anaemia limit productivity.
  • Skill gaps: only a small share of the workforce has formal vocational training.
  • Female participation depends on education and health.
  • New economy: AI, digital and green jobs need higher skills.

Measures: NEP 2020, Samagra Shiksha, Skill India, Ayushman Bharat, Poshan Abhiyaan and public spending on education towards 6% of GDP and on health towards 2.5% of GDP.

Causes of price volatility in agricultural markets

  • Supply shocks: monsoon failure, floods, heat waves and pests.
  • Perishability and poor storage: tomatoes, onions and potatoes (TOP) show sharp price swings.
  • Cobweb cycle: high prices lead farmers to sow more next season, causing a glut and a price crash.
  • Fragmented markets with many intermediaries and weak price information.
  • Sudden trade policy changes: export bans (onion, wheat, rice) and stock limits.
  • Global prices of edible oil, pulses and fertiliser; exchange rates.
  • Speculation and hoarding.

Ways to tackle price and income fluctuations

  • Stable and predictable trade policy, instead of sudden bans.
  • Futures and options markets for price discovery.
  • Market intelligence and forecasts for farmers.
  • Crop diversification and allied activities (dairy, fisheries) to spread risk.
  • Agriculture Infrastructure Fund for storage and post-harvest facilities.

Why India is called a global agricultural powerhouse

  • Largest producer of milk (about 239 million tonnes, 2023-24), pulses and jute, and the largest producer of millets.
  • Second largest producer of rice, wheat, sugarcane, fruits, vegetables, cotton and groundnut.
  • Largest rice exporter, with about 40% of world trade; a major exporter of spices, marine products and buffalo meat; agri-exports of about $50 billion.
  • Food security: grain stocks feed over 80 crore people under PMGKAY; India supplied food to other countries during crises.
  • Large area under cultivation and diverse agro-climatic zones.

Key priorities for agricultural growth

  • Productivity: yields remain below world averages; better seeds, soil health and research.
  • Irrigation and water efficiency: Per Drop More Crop, micro-irrigation.
  • Climate resilience: heat-tolerant varieties, crop insurance, natural farming.
  • Diversification to horticulture, pulses, oilseeds (National Mission on Edible Oils), dairy and fisheries.
  • Markets and value chains: FPOs, e-NAM, food processing, exports.
  • Digital agriculture: the Digital Agriculture Mission (2024), Agri Stack.

A digitalised society uses digital technology in payments, governance, education, health and work. India's digital public infrastructure — Aadhaar, UPI, DigiLocker, CoWIN — shows its gains.

Economic gains

  • Lower transaction costs and faster payments: UPI handles about 20 billion transactions a month.
  • Financial inclusion: Jan Dhan accounts, digital credit for small businesses (OCEN, Account Aggregator).
  • Formalisation and tax compliance: GST network, e-invoicing.
  • New jobs and start-ups: e-commerce, fintech and gig work; the digital economy was about 11.7% of GDP in 2022-23.
  • Less leakage: Direct Benefit Transfer has saved large sums by removing fake beneficiaries.

Social gains

  • Access to services: telemedicine (eSanjeevani), online education (DIKSHA, SWAYAM), e-governance (UMANG).
  • Transparency and less corruption; citizens can track services.
  • Empowerment of women, farmers (market prices) and remote areas.

Environmental gains

  • Less paper and travel: e-office, online meetings and digital documents.
  • Smart grids, precision farming and better resource management.
  • Monitoring: satellites and sensors track pollution, forests and disasters.

Caution: the digital divide, cyber fraud, data privacy and e-waste must be handled for these gains to be shared by all.
free.ifm-2023-gk-3a:
RightsJusticeDevelopmentGovernance

The Constitution of India is not only a legal framework; it is oriented to four intertwined goals that reinforce each other.

1. Rights

  • Fundamental Rights (Part III) protect liberty and equality; Article 32 makes them enforceable.
  • Courts have expanded rights to include privacy, dignity, livelihood and a clean environment.

2. Justice

  • The Preamble promises social, economic and political justice.
  • Abolition of untouchability, reservations, land reforms and the Directive Principles (Articles 38, 39, 46) aim at a just social order.

3. Development

  • Directive Principles direct the State to secure adequate livelihood, distribution of resources, health, education and living wages.
  • Planning, welfare schemes and laws such as MGNREGA and the Right to Education turn these into action; Article 21A made education a right.

4. Governance

  • The Constitution sets up democratic institutions — Parliament, executive, judiciary, federal structure, local bodies — and independent bodies such as the Election Commission, CAG and UPSC.
  • It provides accountability through elections, judicial review and the separation of powers.

How they are intertwined

  • Rights without development remain empty (the right to life needs food, health and shelter — the Right to Food case).
  • Development without rights can become authoritarian; governance ensures that development is fair and accountable.
  • Justice links them: affirmative action and welfare make rights real for weaker sections.
  • The Supreme Court in Minerva Mills (1980) called the balance between Parts III and IV a basic feature.

The Constitution thus seeks a transformation in which rights, justice, development and good governance advance together.
free.ifm-2023-gk-3b:
Separation of powersJudicial reviewIndependent bodiesFederalism

India's Constitution does not concentrate power in one body; it creates many institutions that check one another, so the failure of one is corrected by another.

1. Main institutions and how they check each other

2. Examples of one institution correcting another

  • Judiciary over the legislature and executive: the basic structure doctrine (Kesavananda, 1973); Bommai (1994) against misuse of Article 356; the electoral bonds scheme struck down (2024).
  • Parliament over the judiciary: amending laws after judgments; the power to remove judges.
  • CAG and Parliament: CAG reports on telecom spectrum and coal allocation led to parliamentary and court action.
  • Election Commission ensures that governments change peacefully.
  • Federal balance: States challenge Union actions in court; the Supreme Court in State of Tamil Nadu v. Governor (2025) checked delays by a Governor, while the Presidential Reference opinion (November 2025) set limits on courts fixing timelines.
  • RTI, Lokpal and human rights commissions add further checks.

3. Assessment

This web of institutions has helped Indian democracy survive crises — the Emergency (1975–77) was followed by restoration through elections and the 44th Amendment. Concerns remain: delays in courts, weakened parliamentary scrutiny, and pressure on independent bodies. Their autonomy must be protected for checks and balances to work.

The 73rd and 74th Amendments (1992) made panchayats and municipalities constitutional bodies, adding a third tier of government.

How they deepened constitutional democracy

  • Wider representation: about 31 lakh elected representatives, among the largest bodies of elected people in the world.
  • Women's empowerment: at least one-third of seats reserved, and about 21 States give 50%; about 14 lakh women representatives.
  • Inclusion of SCs, STs and OBCs through reservations.
  • Direct democracy: the Gram Sabha, especially under PESA (1996) in Scheduled Areas, gives villagers a say in planning, forest and mineral resources.
  • Regular elections by State Election Commissions; State Finance Commissions for funds.
  • Local planning and accountability: social audits of MGNREGA, Gram Panchayat Development Plans.
  • A training ground for future leaders.

Limits: inadequate devolution of funds, functions and functionaries; "sarpanch-pati" proxies; bureaucratic control and delayed elections. Empowering local bodies financially would deepen democracy further.

The Supreme Court, under Article 32, is the guardian of Fundamental Rights; Ambedkar called this article the "heart and soul" of the Constitution.

How its role has evolved

  • Early phase (1950s–60s): a literal approach — A.K. Gopalan (1950) read rights narrowly.
  • Defending the core: Golaknath (1967) and Kesavananda Bharati (1973) — the basic structure doctrine limited Parliament's amending power.
  • Failure and recovery: in ADM Jabalpur (1976) it failed to protect liberty during the Emergency; this was later overruled in Puttaswamy (2017).
  • Expansion of Article 21: Maneka Gandhi (1978) — "procedure established by law" must be fair, just and reasonable; rights to livelihood, shelter, health, clean environment, privacy and dignity followed.
  • PIL and access to justice: relaxed standing for the poor (bonded labour, prisoners); Vishaka (1997) guidelines.
  • Recent rights rulings: decriminalising homosexuality (Navtej Johar, 2018), triple talaq (Shayara Bano, 2017), electoral bonds (2024), sub-classification of SCs (2024) and guidelines against arbitrary demolitions (2024).

Concerns: pendency, delays in hearing habeas corpus and rights cases, and criticism of judicial overreach. Still, the Court has become one of the world's most powerful courts in protecting rights.

Cyclone and anticyclone

How climate change affects tropical cyclones globally (IPCC AR6)

  • Stronger cyclones: the proportion of intense cyclones (categories 3–5) has increased; total numbers may not rise.
  • Rapid intensification: warmer oceans let storms strengthen quickly, leaving little time for warning (Cyclone Ockhi, 2017; Hurricane Otis in Mexico, 2023).
  • Heavier rainfall because warm air holds more moisture.
  • Higher storm surges because of sea-level rise.
  • Slower movement in some regions, causing longer rain over land (Hurricane Harvey, 2017).
  • Poleward shift of the zone of peak intensity in the western North Pacific.
  • Arabian Sea: cyclones have become more frequent and intense; one study found 52% more cyclones in 2001–2019 than in 1982–2000.

Response: better forecasts (India's IMD has cut cyclone deaths sharply), early warning systems, coastal shelterbelts and mangroves, and climate-resilient infrastructure.
free.ifm-2023-gk-4b:
NICDPIndustrial smart citiesPlug-and-playBalanced regional growth

The National Industrial Corridor Development Programme (NICDP), run through the National Industrial Corridor Development Corporation (NICDC), is building 11 industrial corridors with planned industrial cities. In August 2024, the Union Cabinet approved 12 new industrial smart cities costing about ₹28,602 crore.

Corridors and nodes

  • Delhi–Mumbai (DMIC): Dholera (Gujarat), Shendra–Bidkin/AURIC (Maharashtra), Greater Noida, Vikram Udyogpuri (Ujjain) already developed.
  • Chennai–Bengaluru, Amritsar–Kolkata, East Coast (Visakhapatnam–Chennai), Bengaluru–Mumbai, Hyderabad–Nagpur, Odisha and others.
  • New cities (2024): Khurpia, Rajpura–Patiala, Dighi, Palakkad, Agra, Prayagraj, Gaya, Zaheerabad, Orvakal, Kopparthy and Jodhpur–Pali.

How they can promote equitable and sustainable urbanisation

  • New growth centres: planned cities away from crowded metros reduce pressure on Delhi, Mumbai and Bengaluru.
  • Balanced regional development: nodes in backward regions (Gaya, Orvakal, Palakkad) bring jobs closer to rural areas.
  • Plug-and-play infrastructure: ready land, power, water and approvals attract investment.
  • Smart and green planning: walk-to-work design, recycled water, renewable energy, waste management and public transport.
  • Multimodal connectivity under PM Gati Shakti with dedicated freight corridors.
  • Jobs: about 10 lakh direct and 30 lakh indirect jobs are expected from the new cities.

Challenges: land acquisition and displacement, slow occupancy of earlier nodes, water stress, environmental impacts and the need for social infrastructure — housing, schools and hospitals — for workers.

If planned with local communities and environmental safeguards, these corridors can make urbanisation both inclusive and sustainable.
free.ifm-2023-gk-4c:
Carrying capacityJoshimathFragile HimalayaRegulated tourism

Carrying capacity is the maximum number of visitors a place can support without harming its environment, infrastructure and the quality of life of residents.

Why unchecked tourism in hill stations is a disaster

  • Fragile geology: Himalayan slopes are young and unstable. Joshimath's land subsidence (2023) and the Shimla and Himachal floods and landslides (2023) were linked to unplanned construction, blocked drainage and heavy traffic.
  • Water stress: Shimla's water crisis (2018); springs are drying up.
  • Waste: plastic and sewage pollute rivers and lakes (Nainital).
  • Traffic and air pollution: long jams in Manali and Mussoorie in peak season.
  • Loss of forests for hotels and roads; disturbance to wildlife.
  • Disaster risk: crowds in risky places, as in the Kedarnath flood (2013).

Steps being taken: the Supreme Court asked for a carrying-capacity study of Himalayan towns (2023); the Madras High Court made an e-pass system mandatory for Ooty and Kodaikanal (2024); Sikkim and some pilgrim routes limit visitor numbers.

Tourism must be planned according to carrying capacity, with building controls, green fees, waste management and spreading tourists across seasons and places.
